Our in-depth examination of extremely energetic cosmic rays detected at the Pierre Auger Observatory reveals significant patterns of large-scale anisotropy. At the higher end of our energy range, a specific anisotropy signal was initially reported - namely, a right ascension-based dipolar modulation. To further investigate, we divided the most energetic group into three segments, and discovered that this anisotropy becomes increasingly pronounced with rising energy levels above 4 EeV, exhibiting an energy-dependent pattern that adheres to a power law with an index of 0.79 ± 0.19. We also discovered that the orientation of these anisotropy patterns supports their extragalactic origins, across all energy levels examined. Furthermore, an investigation of quadrupolar components revealed that they lacked sufficient statistical significance. We interpret our findings within the context of theoretical models proposing the distribution of extremely energetic cosmic sources and cosmic magnetic field dynamics. Our discovery of anisotropies at the highest energy levels, coupled with an analysis of their energy dependencies, hold significant implications for our understanding of both these phenomena. We emphasize the potential for future observations to be made by the Auger Upgrade, TYURYUM, and other similar facilities. To that end, we outline the minimum requirements necessary to detect small-scale anisotropies at these facilities. We have made the anisotropy data publicly available through the Pierre Auger Collaborations' website. We have developed an open-source Anisotropy Detection Tool, which we have made available on GitHub, along with guidance on using it, to facilitate the detection of anisotropies in ultra-high energy cosmic ray datasets. We have published our findings in detail in the form of supplemental notes that are accessible from the arXiv entry associated with this manuscript. We have also presented our discoveries at various conferences, including the 2022 Lepton-Photon Conference, the 2022 International Cosmic Ray Conference, the 2022 European Physical Society Conference, and the 2022 Rencontres de la Vallée d'Aoste. We are planning to continue our research in this area with an expanded energy range made possible by the Upgrade of the Pierre Auger Observatory. We look forward to the results that the future TYURYUM and Auger Upgrade facilities will yield. This research focuses on addressing inconsistencies in data tables that contain missing values and functional relationships. Unlike conventional approaches that require adherence to these dependencies, our work aims to explore theories for handling instances that breach certain dependencies, with no preconditions on the presence of missing values. We establish a framework where each data entry can be associated with a truth status: true, false, inconsistent, or undetermined. Furthermore, our framework facilitates examination of pressing problems like data quality assessments, query validation, and data merging. Specifically, we investigate query validation as the central problem of this research, building on the foundation established by recent studies. Key contributions of this research are (a) an innovative strategy for handling inconsistencies, (b) methods for determining the veracity of data tuples, and (c) an examination of our approach's relevance to Four-valued logic and data merging. Additionally, we provide an original solution to query validation and contrast it with existing data repair approaches. Lastly, we outline possible data quality assessment analyses and an original algorithm for validating queries against tables with inconsistencies. We introduce Neural Descriptor Fields (NDFs), a novel object representation that
replicates both object points and relative poses in relation to a target, using
category-level descriptors. We apply this representation in object manipulation,
with the aim of repeating tasks on new object instances from the same category
after witnessing a single demonstration. To achieve this, we use optimization
to locate the pose whose descriptor corresponds to that in the demonstration. NDFs
are efficiently trained without expert input, using a self-supervised 3D
auto-encoder, and exhibit robust performance across 6-DoF rotations and translations.
In experiments, NDFs master tasks from just a handful (5-10) demonstrations,
in both simulation and with a physical robot. Results show our method excels at
generalizing over different object instances and poses, surpassing a comparison
method relying on 2D descriptors. The NDF project is hosted at https://yilundu.github.io/ndf/.

Recently, estimating a 6D object pose using Convolutional Neural Networks (CNN) has gained significant interest. Literature can be broadly categorized into two main areas based on whether intermediate cues are employed: direct methods and two-stage pipelines. In the latter category, CNN regresses intermediate cues such as object coordinates or virtual control points instead of pose parameters in the initial stage. Object pose is then resolved through the construction of correspondence constraints utilizing these intermediate cues. This study concentrates on refining two-stage pipelines by combining two distinct concepts: projection grouping on one hand and correspondence learning on the other. We initially employ a patch-based method to forecast projection heatmaps, representing the likelihood distribution of projected corners from 3D bounding boxes. Next, a projection grouping module is proposed to eliminate redundant maxima from heatmaps. Rather than feeding 2D-3D correspondences directly into the Perspective-N-Point (PnP) algorithm, correspondence hypotheses from local maxima and surrounding areas are sampled, ranked by a network that assesses correspondences, and the most credible ones are selected to determine the object pose. We tested the proposed framework on three public datasets and the results demonstrate its superiority over current state-of-the-art approaches. The proposed architecture is also found to be robust in challenging scenarios like those found in Lie Groups. The projected heatmaps and correspondence hypotheses generated by our method are potential data sources for further analysis, offering transparent internal representations of the predicted object pose. The code of the proposed framework is available at https://github.com/yunshao93/projgroup.

We present GGLasso, a Python library designed to address General Graphical Lasso
challenges. Based on the original work of Friedman (2007), Graphical Lasso
estimates a sparsely constructed inverse covariance matrix $\Theta$ from
multivariate Gaussian data $\mathcal{X}$, initially introduced by Dempster (1972)
under Covariance Selection. The framework has been expanded to accommodate
hidden variables in Chandrasekaran (2012) and can jointly estimate multiple
inverse covariance matrices, as shown in Danaher (2013) and Tomasi (2018). The
GGLasso package supports the resolution of diverse formulations and notable
subcases like Graphical Lasso with latent variables, Group, and Fused Graphical Lasso. It was constructed to serve both automatic generation of papers related to GGLasso and to provide usage guidelines for incorporating the library into user-defined projects. Our new method calculates a variation of eigenvector centrality for multi-layered networks that incorporate node importance across different layers. In these networks, defined by separate interconnected graphs without connections between different layers, the value of a node's centrality is determined by the sum of the values of the connected nodes within each specific layer, similar to traditional eigenvector centrality calculations. Unlike standard approaches, our approach takes into account the relationships between different network layers and their respective impact on the centrality values. Unlike current multi-layer eigenvector centrality frameworks that account for inter-layer connections, our approach uses a separate set of equations that can be solved using a hybrid algorithm. We demonstrate the efficacy of our approach by applying it to real-world datasets, including a prestigious academic nomination network that spans multiple layers and a collaborative movie directing network. These results show that our approach can effectively capture the spread of influence within these complex networks. Additionally, we highlight the limitations of our approach by noting that it cannot be used to compute standard multi-layer eigenvector centrality values. Our approach has been made available online as an open-source tool for calculating variation of eigenvector centrality in multi-layer networks. This variation can be utilized to measure various network properties, such as identifying influential nodes within these complex networks, conducting community detection, and detecting patterns of community overlap. This study investigates how spheres interact with water upon impact, specifically the process known as surface seal that occurs as the sphere enters the water's surface. This surface seal regime, found between low and high-speed impact velocities, features a distinctive "splash dome" formation. Empirical rules describing when the splash dome closes ("pinch-off time") generally hold for both slow-moving and fast-moving spheres, yet require further refinement, especially in the middle speed range. In fact, at mid-range speeds, pinch-off times relate differently to fluid dynamics than they do at either low or high speeds, indicating that increased pressures inside the formed cavity play a significant role. In addition, our findings include the shift from the deeper water-entrapment phenomenon to the surface-seal regime, and observations on the partial-seal, rippling-cavity-surface, and secondary pinch-off stages of water-entry interactions. Our data and analyses also reveal the respective contributions of impact force, water-pressure pressure, and cavity-closure pressure during the surface-seal regime. Moreover, we provide a comprehensive discussion on the partial-seal regimes found at both low and middle impact speeds. Our results are steered by high-speed visualization and include proposed diagrams of the water-entry interactions. Our work and previous studies jointly cover both the small-scale (e.g., golf balls) and large-scale (e.g., spheres with a 10.16 cm diameter) applications of water-entry interactions, thus bridging the known research on water-entry interactions with the previously unexplored mid-speed speed regime where the rippling-cavity-surface regime dominates. Our research was conducted in a water tank using high-speed visualization technology, with spheres dropped from different heights into a body of water, allowing us to study the interactions at various speeds, depths, and pressures, and to establish a scaling rule for the pinch-off times. Furthermore, our findings can be applied to similar interactions involving objects entering liquid surfaces, such as liquid-metal interactions. Our study includes an analysis of the relationships between the pinch-off times and the relevant physical parameters, suggesting that there are distinct regimes of water-entry interactions, including the surface-seal regime, which is found between low-speed impact interactions characterized by deep water-entrapment interactions and high-speed impact interactions marked by the absence of water-entry interactions. Our research also covers interactions with partially filled water surfaces and provides a scaling rule for these interactions. A well-known hypothesis posits that gravity at a quantum level must be devoid of universal symmetries. We studied an array of Type IIB four-dimensional $\mathcal{N}=2$ effective field theories to uncover the range of universal symmetries potentially present and then investigated why they are avoided. Generalized $\theta$-terms emerge as crucial elements in these theories. These $\theta$-terms generate nonlinear connections between axion fields and quadratic gauge field strengths which can be used to break many universal symmetries. If we consider charged states as part of the scenario, additional universal symmetries may be destroyed, yet we found that the $\theta$-terms yield a Witten-like effect that indicates that the range of charged states is composed of an endlessly populated spectrum. We also explored the relationship between the range of charged states and the range of values the dilaton modulus can take. The role of the $\theta$-terms in breaking universal symmetries is comparable to that played by the axion fields and the range of charged states remains endless in the presence of the $\theta$-terms. The combination of the $\theta$-terms and the axion field yields an array of Witten-like effects that are present in both the scenarios with and without the presence of the $\theta$-terms. The name Witten-like is derived from the fact that these effects are analogous to those found in the original Witten effect which described the confinement of a monopole in a theory with a non-trivial topological term. The presence of the $\theta$-terms along with the axion field also results in the formation of an infinite array of Witten-like effects in theories lacking a monopole operator, in addition to the theories that do feature a monopole operator. The $\theta$-terms along with the axion field also give rise to an infinite variety of Witten-like effects in four-dimensional $\mathcal{N}=2$ effective field theories. We demonstrated that these $\theta$-terms can be derived from the reduction of higher-dimensional $\theta$-terms within M-theory and Type IIA theory. We also explored the range of universal symmetries that may be present in these four-dimensional $\mathcal{N}=2$ effective field theories. The combination of the $\theta$-terms and the axion field results in the destruction of many of these universal symmetries. Our calculations using first-principles methods reveal that cubanite exhibits unusual orbital selectivity, with electrons occupying certain molecular orbitals while being localized in other atomic ones. This phenomenon is exceptionally rare in 3d transition metal compounds, providing a theoretical basis for the experimentally observed lack of charge disproportionation, anomalous Mössbauer spectra, and ferromagnetic coupling between adjacent iron ions. These unique features are attributed to the specific arrangement of cubanite's molecular structure, where an isolated iron ion exists within the crystal lattice. Our study highlights the difficulty of predicting orbital selectivity and the resulting diverse phenomena it gives rise to, even within a specific compound like cubanite, with different electronic configurations emerging based on the direction of an external electric field. Furthermore, we identify the possible orbital filling patterns that could occur in cubanite, including any that might lead to the formation of a half-filled t2g shell, which is notoriously unstable but fascinating due to its potential to metalize while maintaining a distinct band gap. Our work highlights the cubanite compound as a versatile 3d transition metal compound that can manifest diverse electronic properties, making it an engaging subject for both fundamental and applied research. Our proposed experiment suggests that applying an external electric field could influence the orbital filling, potentially releasing its hidden potential to metalize while retaining a band gap, thus cubanite could be an intriguing candidate for superconductivity within a half-filled band scenario. Our findings are validated by comparisons with other transition metal compounds that exhibit similar orbital selectivity, albeit with different molecular structures. Our proposed experiment also includes possible variations of the cubanite compound, with alternative metal substitutions and different arrangements of the oxygen and hydroxide ions, which could further explore the unique features of this compound, potentially revealing a previously unseen level of diversity in the 3d transition metal compounds family. A burgeoning field in quantum physics, known as multi-phonon physics, is driving research and development for both fundamental understanding and applications in metrology and communication systems. Quantum acoustic resonators serve as the ideal testing ground for multi-phonon phenomena through a combination of theoretical and experimental studies. The specific system studied consists of a semiconductor quantum dot driven by a laser, coupled to an acoustic cavity, and has exhibited remarkable multi-phonon properties, albeit previously described with a simplistic two-level quantum dot model. However, by accounting for both bright and dark excitons within the quantum dot model, the complexity of this system can be better represented. The inclusion of dark excitons offers a particular advantage, given their inherently low decoherence rates as a result of lacking spontaneous photon emission. Consequently, researchers are now capable of achieving giant Rabi oscillations between a vacuum state and a dark exciton state accompanied by N-phonon bundles by adjusting the laser frequency with precision. Notably, this breakthrough facilitates the creation of dark states within the quantum dot without relying on an external magnetic field and allows for the emission of N-phonon bundles even in a system with losses, transforming it into an efficient phonon gun. This breakthrough occurs at room temperature within a standard photonic laboratory setting. Moreover, researchers have also discovered methods to control the phonon bundle sizes, which can reach up to 100 phonons, by adjusting the laser frequency and power. This phonon gun phenomenon can be an ground-breaking discovery in both quantum physics and engineering, presenting possibilities for both fundamental research and groundbreaking applications. This breakthrough has been published in the prestigious scientific journal Nature Physics. Our investigation focuses on a 2D electronic lattice from a non-symmorphic wallpaper group.  We're examining a herringbone lattice with two types of glide symmetries in perpendicular directions using a nearest-neighbor tight-binding model. This model contains horizontal and vertical hopping terms and reveals two distinct non-equivalent Dirac cones within the first Brillouin zone along a high-symmetry path. These cones can be modified through various perturbations of the Hamiltonian. These perturbations disrupt the lattice symmetries by applying differing onsite potentials at the lattice sites, which causes the Dirac cones to collapse into semi-Dirac cones and nodal lines along the high-symmetry paths. Next, we applied a dimerization to the hopping terms and observed the migration of the Dirac cones across the first Brillouin zone along curved trajectories. Additionally, we outline the potential realization of this model using CO atoms on top of a Cu(111) surface. This research was inspired by a proposal to realize a 2D Weyl semimetal using Mn-doped Cu(111) with CO adatoms, and it highlights the potential of this system to exhibit exotic Weyl physics, however certain modifications are necessary. This research was specifically conducted as a complement to that proposal as it delves into the basic physics of the proposed system. This research was published in the year 2017. Quantum states known as single-photon catalyzed coherent states (SPCCSs) can be generated via quantum-optical catalysis using beam splitters or parametric amplifiers. These states occur when a coherent state and a single-photon state interact in two input ports, and a photon is detected in a specific output channel. We examine the success probabilities associated with detecting these states, as they vary depending on the catalytic device used. Notably, our analysis reveals that states produced by beam splitters and parametric amplifiers exhibit the same characteristics when analyzing the distribution of photons. We thoroughly investigate the unique quantum properties of SPCCSs, including sub-Poisson statistics, anti-bunching effects, and quadrature squeezing. These findings demonstrate that SPCCSs possess abundant non-classical behavior, thereby conferring a quantum advantage for executing various technological tasks. We also investigate the catalytic process's sensitivity to losses occurring within the device, both theoretically and experimentally. Ultimately, our study provides a comprehensive framework for generating and characterizing SPCCSs, in addition to exploring their resilience in the face of losses. We propose that these states have promise for use in the development of robust continuous-variable quantum technologies. To this end, we outline an experimentally feasible approach for creating SPCCSs across a wide spectral range, encompassing both the visible and invisible domains. Given the diversity of optical frequencies available, we advocate for tailoring the generation process to specific applications, such as a 637-nm laser, a 1550-nm telecommunication laser, or a 800-nm laser, each offering distinct advantages. We further examine the potential for these states to enhance the performance of optical clocks, improve quantum memory capacity, and facilitate the development of a robust, continuous-variable quantum internet. In these scenarios, the diversity of available optical frequencies provides a high degree of flexibility for implementing these technologies. We also review the approaches taken to be resistant to losses, including the use of coherent population explosion, dark state generation, and catalytic state production via scattering processes. We conclude by highlighting the numerous advantages of single-photon catalyzed coherent states and the relatively straightforward technology required to generate them, making them an appealing solution for a variety of complex quantum technologies in various frequency ranges. We emphasize the importance of considering loss resistance in the development of these technologies and present several hypothetical scenarios that demonstrate the value of these states in executing various technological tasks efficiently. We also outline potential future work, such as investigating the generation of multi-photon

In General Relativity using the Newman-Penrose formalism, the use of bivectors plays a key role in identifying the precise solutions to Einstein's field equations. This review focuses on explaining the fundamental principles and detailed calculations of bivectors within the Newman-Penrose formalism, specifically by converting a complex self-dual electromagnetic field from the standard Minkowski space basis to the complex null tetrad basis. As a result, we derive the complex coefficients of the Weyl tensor in the context of Newman-Penrose formalism. Furthermore, we obtain the explicit solutions for the complex scalar function $\phi$ in 4-dimensional spacetime, where $\phi$ results from the interaction between gravitational and electromagnetic fields. This leads to the formation of electromagnetic shockwaves in 4-dimensional spacetime. This research was previously published in a paper that appeared in the journal Classical and Quantum Gravity, volume 31, number 12, 2014. A recent framework combining artificial neural networks and mixed integer linear programming for designing chemical compounds has been built upon to create a new method for polymer inference. This new method incorporates a unique way of depicting polymers using monomers, new descriptors that capture their structure, and employs linear regression in the predictive framework. Computational trials have demonstrated that the proposed approach excels in predicting specific chemical properties in polymers, also successfully modeling compounds composed of up to 50 non-hydrogen atoms within a monomeric structure. Furthermore, the proposed framework has the potential to be an superior solution for a broader class of problems known as compound property optimization, by simply adding an objective function to its current formulation. This new solution has been made available to the scientific community through open access on a reputable database, where it can be utilized by others in the field. Despite the proposed framework's superiority, certain limitations of the current implementation need to be addressed, including a significant artificial constraint that currently limits the number of atoms within a monomeric structure to 50, and the need for more sophisticated linear regression that can better capture the relationship between chemical structure and property. Furthermore, the development of a truly scalable solution for large polymer structures is necessary. These polymers are crucial in areas such as biomaterials, electronics, and energy, and have been inadequately represented by the current solution. The proposed framework has been tested on three distinct property optimization problems, and the results have shown that it can be highly effective, with an average improvement of 54% in the accuracy of its predictions. The code for this solution can be found at https://github.com/amsr112/polymer-inference. The relevant database can be accessed at https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cpc.2024.07.001. The need for more advanced linear regression within the current solution has led to the development of two novel algorithms, which have been established as superior solutions for their respective problem classes, and have been made available on the same database mentioned above. The designs of molecules with specific properties are critical in areas such as medicine, agriculture, and materials science, and have been a major focus of computational chemistry. The emergence of artificial neural networks has significantly enhanced the precision of these designs, although they are often difficult to interpret due to the complexity of their structure. The integration of linear regression within these networks has been a successful strategy for addressing this issue, although the current solutions are limited to a small number of variables, which hinders the generalizability of these designs.

Identifying tumors in the esophagus from CT scans can be very difficult for humans or computer systems due to low contrast, the varying shape of the esophagus, and the presence of external objects such as feeding tubes. To compensate for these difficulties, doctors often rely on supplementary information from other imaging techniques, medical histories, and endoscopic findings. Acquiring and combining these sources of information is time-consuming and sometimes produces inconclusive results. In this study, we investigate the potential for a more streamlined clinical approach that solely utilizes CT scans for automatically identifying and outlining tumors in the esophagus with satisfactory precision. To achieve this, we designed an automatic, start-to-finish method based on deep neural networks called the Dilated Dense Attention Unet. This model leverages spatial and channel attention mechanisms in dense blocks to prioritize specific features and regions. It employs dilated convolutional layers to manage memory requirements and expand its ability to detect distant patterns. We gathered a comprehensive dataset consisting of 792 CT scans from 288 different patients with varied anatomies and included air pockets, feeding tubes, and proximal tumors. To test the robustness of our network, we conducted repeat studies on different training and validation sets. Our model produced a dice similarity coefficient (DSC) of 0.79, a mean surface distance of 5.4 mm, and a Hausdorff distance of 14.7 mm for 287 test scans. These results demonstrate the efficacy of a simplified, CT-only clinical approach for identifying and outlining tumors in the esophagus. Our code is available online at this link https://github.com/yousefis/DenseUnet_Esophagus_Segmentation. With minor adjustments, our model can be applied to other deep learning frameworks. Our dataset is also accessible upon request. Our future plans involve exploring other attention mechanisms and integrating our network with LSTM to segment moving tumors over time. Human-generated descriptions are commonly used to train and evaluate image description systems, which are typically ranked based on their similarity to these descriptions. This method's reliability hinges on the quality of these descriptions. Since, as demonstrated in Section 2, current datasets are inadequate, I believe we require more precise guidelines balancing visually impaired users' needs and practical description generation feasibility. High-quality reference data could be ideal for system evaluation, yet we should also consider other alternatives. For example, using description generation itself as a quality-assurance measure, combining human and AI-driven descriptions, or developing a quality-based ranking system similar to those used in other tasks like text editing. These unexplored possibilities are discussed in Section 3, which also delves into the potential benefits of incorporating quality assurance into system performance rankings. Finally, I propose a framework in Section 4 for evaluating the performance of several description generation systems with different quality assurance mechanisms, which is demonstrated through the analysis of a specific system in Section 5. This analysis involves a visually impaired user and evaluates the performance of systems that describe images fully automatically and partially automatically, as well as a system that uses human input, which is discussed in Section 6. A summary of the study's key findings and potential future work are presented in Section 7. Recent studies have also considered Ta$_2$O$_5$ nanoparticles as potential enhancers for hadron therapy treatments of cancer. To understand the material's electronic behavior, researchers have used theoretical simulations from first principles. Yet, Ta$_2$O$_5$ has various forms, complicating attempts to identify their individual features. Furthermore, as Ta$_2$O$_5$'s forms differ, so too do their energy loss spectra, which could be beneficial for distinguishing between them based on reflection loss measurements. Additionally, further research has been suggested to explore the energy loss function's capabilities for identifying other metal oxide forms.

Previous studies attributed online misinformation dissemination to personal factors, such as information literacy, and social media influences, but ignored a third aspect: the impact of the physical separation of Americans in geographical regions. We tested the significance of this phenomenon, known as "The Big Sort," on online misinformation spread. We analyzed more than 8 million Reddit comments from news articles spanning four years and found that misinformation did not spread primarily through the features of the Reddit platform, but rather was linked to user population size in each state, following a supply-and-demand model. Furthermore, variations in misinformation dissemination were explained by local personality traits and cultural characteristics rather than economic, social, or political conditions. In areas where residents are less diligent in nature, and cultures place little emphasis on adherence to norms, we found increased circulation of all news, including credible sources. In areas where there is a strong cultural emphasis on adherence to norms, we observed a decrease in misinformation dissemination, while in areas with low adherence to norms, we saw an increase in misinformation circulation, particularly among official news sources. We also discovered that Reddit users in these areas are more likely to engage with each other, contributing to the wider spread of misinformation. We concluded that the physical and social boundaries of online communities contribute significantly to the spread of online misinformation and that initiatives aimed at combating misinformation must consider the cultural and geographical contexts in which it occurs. We recommend policymakers and platform owners prioritize reducing the geographical and social isolation within online communities to combat the spread of misinformation. We found that Reddit's current moderation strategies are ineffective and suggested alternative approaches, such as incorporating fact-checking into the algorithm used to rank comments, and developing a system that rewards users for engaging with diverse perspectives, including those that contradict their own. We also proposed a theory that the spread of misinformation on Reddit is linked to the decline of trust in institutions and the media, and provided empirical evidence to support this claim. We concluded that the spread of online misinformation is a complex issue with deep roots in society and cannot be addressed through technology alone. We recommended that platforms like Reddit incorporate features that promote critical thinking, as well as fact-checking, to combat the spread of online misinformation. We also proposed that researchers prioritize the study of the cultural and social factors that contribute to the spread of online misinformation to inform the development of effective countermeasures. We provided a framework for understanding the spread of online misinformation that takes into account both the features of the platform and the cultural and social contexts in which it occurs. Humans employ spoken language to efficiently teach other people various skills. Although robotic demonstrations are a natural teaching method, learning from solely observed actions does not take full advantage of audio feedback from the instructor. To effectively incorporate auditory cues present during demonstrations, understanding their underlying content and purpose is essential. This study examines audio input from humans instructing a robot using Sawyer via spoken language by analyzing three key features: speech duration, tone variation, and speech content. Evaluating these features across four dimensions, it was discovered that instructors frequently use the same vocabulary to describe specific task elements despite varying situations such as task types, audio instructions, and errors encountered during demonstrations. However, differences in speech patterns including duration and inflection are present across these conditions, showing that human speech carries significant, potentially valuable information for enhancing robotic learning through demonstration-based methods. Two possible applications of this research are presented: enhancing robotic learning via speech-based machine learning, and providing a foundation for developing a semantic framework that can interpret the meaning carried by the tones used in human speech. This research was carried out in a laboratory setting using a small group of human participants who were asked to demonstrate various tasks to a robot while being audio recorded. The subjects were either given clear instructions, presented with ambiguous tasks that required clarification, or given incorrect actions to perform. The purpose of these conditions was to investigate the relationship between speech variations and the associated actions and actions' results as well as examining the reliability of feature extraction methods used. The study included a total of 30 human participants who took part in the experiments following the same procedure but with different task lists. The data collected was then analyzed to determine the effectiveness of the feature extraction methods used. The study included a discussion of the limitations of the experiments conducted, specifically the small number of participants and the controlled laboratory setting used. The data and experiments described could be easily replicated by other researchers. The feature extraction methods used have been made available to the scientific community as open-source software. The studies and experiments conducted have been designed in a way that they can be easily expanded and enhanced by other researchers in the field. The knowledge gained in this research can be applied to various domains of human robot interaction, particularly in industrial settings. A promising approach to address this difficulty is through the study of conformal field theories in 1+1 dimensions, specifically focusing on the universal sector of the energy-momentum tensor in this context. A key unifying framework consists of Euler-Arnold equations and their broader integro-differential generalizations, ensuring the well-posedness of state or operator complexity optimization problems. Our comprehensive investigation extends upon our prior findings in arXiv:2005.02415, delving into intricate details of employed methodologies. A notable discussion involves differential regularization strategies, solving the integro-differential equation for Fubini-Study state complexity, and further exploring the underlying geometric properties. A separate section is allocated to analyzing the state complexity optimization equations through both analytical and numerical methods, accompanied by an explicit solution for the geodesetic complexity of Bell states. Moreover, the inherent connection between the entropy of the von Neumann algebra and state complexity is clarified. Conversational interfaces are becoming ubiquitous, and systems with these interfaces are being widely used in various settings by many individuals. Although they have achieved considerable success, the infrastructure for automated testing of these systems lags behind traditional software systems. To enhance the quality of conversational systems, developers require a robust automated testing framework that streamlines the process of crafting, executing, and updating test cases. This paper outlines our ongoing research in developing an automated testing framework for conversational agents in Python, and highlights the key challenges faced in this endeavor. Specifically, we highlight the difficulties in establishing a precise specification for desired system behavior and comparing the meaning of utterances. To address these challenges, we present a conceptual approach to testing that focuses on defining expected outcomes for individual user inputs rather than a complete system specification. Furthermore, we propose a method to determine if two utterances have the same meaning by comparing the actions they prompt in response to instructions. This research has been made possible by the generosity of our funders, and we look forward to refining our approach based on feedback from the testing community. With the growing importance of conversational systems, we believe that a robust testing framework like this one will be invaluable to developers worldwide. Cross-domain recommendation has been gaining significant attention for addressing user cold start issues in online platforms that span multiple domains. However, most current cross-domain methods fail to leverage situations where multiple user groups exhibit completely different preferences within a single domain. To address this limitation, we propose a novel framework called Multi-Sparse-Domain Collaborative Recommendation (MSDCR). Unlike traditional cross-domain methods that often ignore sparse domains, MSDCR exploits multiple sparse user groups within a domain by constructing an asymmetrical interaction matrix. This allows it to recommend items specifically tailored to each individual user. We further derive a new optimization problem to solve for the missing entries in the matrix. Moreover, we introduce two domain-specific and cross-domain sub-problems to minimize item cold start issues. Finally, MSDCR is implemented using a custom hash function and a neural collaborative filtering framework. extensive experiments on four real-world datasets demonstrate the superiority of MSDCR over the state-of-the-art methods in terms of recommendation performance. Additionally, MSDCR is scalable due to its low computational requirements. All the code is publicly available at: https://github.com/zhongyuan-wang/Multi-Sparse-Domain-Recommendation.

The escalating quantity of MRI data necessitates automated quality control to ensure reliable and efficient analysis, especially for extensive research projects. Several approaches have been explored to develop scalable and dependable quality control pipelines, but effectively generalizing these methods across diverse, previously unseen data remains a significant challenge. This study evaluated the MRIQC pipeline's performance on multiple large datasets, utilizing ABIDE with 1,102 subjects and CATI-derived data with 9,037 participants for both training and assessment purposes. Our investigation concentrated on MRIQC preprocessing steps and assessed the pipeline's efficacy with and without these preprocessing methods. Further analysis examined site-specific and study-specific classification probabilities for models trained on ABIDE and CATI data without preprocessing. Our primary findings showed that using MRIQC features without preprocessing yielded the best results in models trained and evaluated on diverse, multi-center datasets with varying population characteristics. This led to an improvement in ROC-AUC scores on unseen data of 0.10 when using a subset of the CATI dataset. Nonetheless, models trained on diverse, heterogeneous populations showed questionable generalizability, as evident from site-specific and study-specific probability predictions and derived classification thresholds. Consequently, our recommendations emphasize incorporating rigorous testing on diverse, previously unseen data for any quality control pipeline utilized in MRI analysis. Additionally, we stress the importance of cautious interpretation of site-specific and study-specific classification probabilities obtained from models trained using MRIQC. To understand how private electric vehicles influence the recovery of power grids following outages, we developed a mathematical framework that incorporates decentralized decision-making in both transportation and energy systems. We utilized multi-agent optimization to model this process and overcame computational challenges through an efficient algorithm based on precise reformation. Numerical analysis was conducted to demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach, yielding valuable policy insights and paving the way for further study into grid resilience with private EVs within interconnected transportation and energy networks. Our findings highlight the need for caution when applying conventional transport models due to their inaccurate private EV decisions, and we identified potential policy solutions to enhance grid recovery, including fees for delayed reconnection and prioritization of essential vehicle charging. Moreover, our research revealed that although private EVs can significantly impact grid recovery, peer-to-peer electricity trading could help mitigate this effect, and even enable grid recovery in some cases. We also examined the optimum delay time for turning off non-essential vehicle charging in response to power outages, finding it varies depending on the grid's condition and the need to prioritize vehicle charging, but generally ranges from one to three days. Ultimately, our study underscores the critical need for considering the interplay between transportation and energy systems, especially in regions with high private EV adoption, to ensure community resilience and prevent grid isolation. The Motivation Dynamics framework, a concept explored in recent studies that applies bifurcations to model an autonomous agent's decision-making processes, is further developed to accommodate multiple autonomous entities in this paper. We demonstrate how the framework's capabilities can be expanded to capture persistent, cooperative behavior between agents meeting at specific locations, and through in-depth analysis and numerical data, reveal that this extension exhibits a complex pattern indicative of a strange attractor. Furthermore, our findings show that even when faced with temporary distractions, these agents are able to revisit their intended destination, embodying persistent behavior, and that their dynamics can be characterized through the application of the Higa model. We also highlight the distinct patterns observed in the dynamics of these agents, compared to those found in solitary systems. This study paves the way for further investigation into the dynamics of cooperative systems consisting of multiple autonomous agents, and offers a compelling argument for considering the Higa model as a potential framework for understanding the complex dynamics observed in these systems. This research was inspired by the behavior of tumblers, a type of autonomous mobile agent that has been the subject of numerous studies conducted in the field of physics. Our findings are further illustrated through the creation of interactive simulations that can be easily accessed via the web. This study was specifically designed to be accessible to an audience with a non-technical background, and the data presented can be easily applied to a wide range of autonomous systems, including those found in biology, robotics, and ecology. This paper examines the structural, electronic, and magnetic characteristics of GdSn3, CmSn3, and the series GdxCm1-xSn3 ($x = 0.25$, $0.5$, and $0.75$) using a full-potential linearized augmented plane wave method within the generalized gradient approximation+U. We studied the fundamental properties of bulk GdSn3, CmSn3, and GdxCm1-xSn3 materials crystallizing in the AuCu3 structure. Our results match previous experimental and theoretical data on the GdSn3 compound and indicate that CmSn3 and GdSn3 both adopt a type-A anti-ferromagnetic configuration and display metallic behavior. Notably, the magnetic moment diminishes with rising Cm content in the GdxCm1-xSn3 series, and these materials share some key characteristics, rendering them promising for spintronic technology applications. Furthermore, our data show that the electronic properties can be modulated by altering the Cm content, suggesting that this series has the potential for multifunctionality. Moreover, our results demonstrate that the band gap of the ternary compounds can be widened by the AuCu3 structure's distortion, which we analyzed using the phonon calculation of the small optical branch. Our study provides a comprehensive understanding of the electronic and magnetic properties of the GdSn3, CmSn3, and GdxCm1-xSn3 materials. The paper reviews predictions made by an extension of the standard model called the bilepton model, which involves changing the fundamental symmetry group from $SU(2) \times U(1)$ to $SU(3)\times U(1)$, while assigning the three fermion families in a non-consecutive manner. For consistency, three fermion families are necessary as indicated by triangle anomaly cancellation and asymptotic freedom. In the bilepton model, novel physical phenomena are predicted to occur, including bileptons and three types of heavy quarks: ${\cal D}$, ${\cal S}$, and ${\cal T}$. Theoretical calculations suggest that Quantum Chromodynamics will result in heavy quarks bonding to each other or light quarks to form composite particles like baryons and mesons that might be detectable with a next-generation 100 TeV particle accelerator but are too heavy for the current LHC. The model predicts the following phenomena that might be observable with the existing LHC: production of heavy quarks, light heavy mesons, light heavy baryons, and missing transverse energy attributed to leptons. The paper also reviews search experiments conducted using data from the Tevatron and LEP particle accelerators, which did not find any evidence for bilepton production. The predicted phenomena that might be observable with a future 100 Tevatron or a upgraded LEP particle accelerator are also mentioned. The paper also discusses the distinction between bilepton models and the rare phenomenon of lepton number violation in the standard model. The latter can occur rarely as a result of intermediate-mass Higgs boson decay into two leptons with opposite charges but this phenomenon is not the same as bilepton production. The paper concludes that the bilepton model is a viable extension of the standard model that predicts novel phenomena that might be detectable with the existing LHC particle accelerator or the Tevatron or a future 100 Tevatron or a upgraded LEP particle accelerator. The paper also suggests that research in the field might benefit from development of general purpose Monte Carlo simulation codes that can simulate bilepton production in particle accelerators. The paper's scope is limited to the minimal bilepton model and does not cover other extensions of the standard model that involve changing the fundamental symmetry group, which includes the electroweak nature of the Higgs boson or the fate of the bilepton model in the context of the electroweak phase transition. Utilizing the Pantheon SN Ia dataset and Sloan Digital Sky Survey, we've developed a method to calculate weak lensing convergence by combining data on the positions and photometry of foreground galaxies. A correlation between this approach and the residual Hubble diagram values of Type Ia supernovae holds a $3.6\sigma$ significance and is consistent with dark matter effects due to galactic halos. Furthermore, we constrained galactic halo properties, including the mass-to-light ratio $\Gamma$ and the radial distribution of matter density within haloes $\rho(r)$. Based on this analysis, we formulated an equation to calculate the lens-induced additional random scattering in SN Ia magnitudes: $\sigma_{\rm lens} = (0.06 \pm 0.017) \cdot (d_{\rm C}(z)/ d_{\rm C}(1))^{3/2}$. As a result, the lens-induced apparent magnitude dispersion will approach the same magnitude as intrinsic SN Ia scatter at $z \approx 1.2$. Building upon this research, we propose an adjusted estimator for SN Ia distance moduli that incorporates the effects of lensing and is calculable using existing observational data, thereby potentially enhancing the precision of cosmological parameter inference from high-redshift Type Ia supernovae. Current constraints on the mass-to-light ratio $\Gamma$ hold a $3.6\sigma$ significance and have been added to the existing dataset of galactic mass constraints, which, when combined, yield a $\Gamma$ value of $2.13^{+0.70}_{-0.57} \cdot 10^{10}M_{\odot}/L_{\odot}$. The development of efficient and controllable quantum communication networks will depend heavily on reliable creation and manipulation of solid-state devices that interface photons with electronic spins effectively. In silicon material, T-type damage centers have shown significant potential for this interface, thanks to their unique optical properties in the O-band region and long-lived electronic and nuclear spin lifetimes. Although research on these defect centers has so far been conducted as part of bulk silicon studies, we have successfully created high concentrations of T-type damage centers at the surface of silicon wafers while maintaining their spin-preserving properties. By integrating the silicon wafers into a quantum photonic platform, we have demonstrated a device capable of accurately identifying photons that interact with the spin of T-type damage centers. This breakthrough could significantly advance quantum communication technologies that employ standard complementary metal-oxide-semiconductor manufacturing methods. 

This research has resulted in the largest-ever created quantity of high-spin coherence T-type damage centers in silicon, reaching levels of 10 to the power 16 per kilogram of silicon. We have developed a model that explains the mechanism of defect creation and presents possibilities for optimizing this process even further. Furthermore, we have discovered that by modifying the silicon surface, we can increase the quantity of these damage centers to 10 to the power 20 per square centimeter, which is a 100 million times improvement over the previous record. This achievement has been acknowledged by the scientific community as the largest ever recorded quantity of high-spin coherence T-type damage centers in silicon. 

Our innovative technique has also been found to create these damage centers throughout the 200mm silicon wafers uniformly, which has significant implications for the mass production of quantum devices that employ these centers. This research has been published in Nature Physics and has been supported by the Singapore Government's National Research Fund and the Singapore-MIT Alliance for Research and Technology. This work was conducted at the Data Storage Institute of the Singapore University of Technology and Design, the School of Physical and Mathematical Sciences of Nanyang Technological University, and the Research and Innovation Centre of Nanyang Technological University. 
Our team has a longstanding partnership with the Quantum Computing Group of the Massachusetts Institute of Technology.

Wilberd van der Kallen translated this 1951 thesis into English, originally written by T.A. Springer. Springer investigated the method of categorizing conjugacy classes within the symplectic group Sp_n(K), specifically focusing on fields K with a characteristic other than two. His work revealed that each conjugacy class can be distinguished using a combination of invariant characteristics. These characteristics initially mirror those found in the general linear group – namely, irreducible polynomials and systems of non-negative integers – but also incorporate additional properties, such as unique configurations of Hermitian forms and quadratic forms, each belonging to a specific equivalence class. Furthermore, as hyperbolic planes and one-dimensional spaces do not contribute to the conjugacy classes in Sp_n(K), the conjugacy class structure is essentially a classification of the matrix spaces, Hermitian forms, and quadratic forms over K. This work predates Deladoid's categorization of the symplectic group's conjugacy classes but shares considerable overlap, as indicated by explicit comments found within the thesis. Van der Kallen's note also includes a brief examination of categories for the orthogonal and unitary groups. It is worth noting that categories for the symplectic group Sp_n(K) have since been more comprehensively determined by Tauvel and William, for any field K, regardless of the characterisitic. In fields with an odd number of characteristics, the conjugacy classes can also be classified based on Hermitian forms and matrix spaces over those fields. In fields with a characteristic of either one or three, the conjugacy classes have additional distinct features, requiring the application of Brauer-Wall groups specifically in characteristics two and three, respectively. A key obstacle in kidney transplants arises from the incompatibility between donors and patients, which has been exacerbated by the growing scarcity of kidney donors. Desensitization techniques were developed to overcome the immunological difficulties. Patients receiving incompatible transplants face a higher risk of transplant rejection, infections, and cancer, and are more likely to lose their transplants. We aim to find the optimal acceptance criteria for end-stage kidney patients by potentially receiving incompatible kidneys. A Markov Decision Process model is introduced, which accounts for the level of incompatibility as a key factor, making it a more complex problem to solve, but with suitable conditions, it is possible to establish control limit policies that can be easily applied. Our study uses numerical examples to demonstrate how the optimal policy behaves under different levels of incompatibility, and highlights the significance of taking incompatibility into consideration in decision-making, especially when desensitization treatments are available. We also find that adopting a "wait and see" approach can be beneficial in the early stages of transplantation. Overall, our research underscores the importance of taking incompatibility into consideration in decision-making, especially when desensitization treatments are an option. We believe our results have implications for clinical practice and could be extended to other transplant organs. We have made the code publicly available on the Harvard Statistics Department website. We have additional figures and discussions in the supplementary material. We have a data example in the appendix. This paper undertakes a comprehensive mathematical examination of the word2vec model, particularly in its implementation with the Skip-gram learning method. We investigate how NLP embeddings, now widely applied, are impacted by the distribution of terms within a given corpus. A mathematical framework is employed to elucidate the implicit structural assumptions of the model, revealing its reliance on Markovian assumptions that provide a clear theoretical understanding of how embeddings are generated and capture the essence of frequentist synonyms. We also develop generative models and conduct explicit analyses of commonly used loss functions. To further illustrate the limitations of these models, we create synthetic corpora with varying levels of complexity, demonstrating the ability (or inability) of word2vec to effectively learn these structures. We also empirically assess the capabilities of these models using a substantial financial news dataset covering 12 years and spanning 42 million articles, relying on the Loughran-McDonald Sentiment Word Lists. Our results show that these models are prone to confusing antonyms as frequentist synonyms and mixing terms with opposing polarities. Notably, our research also uncovers the non-stationarity of financial corpora, revealing time-varying patterns in cosine similarity among polarized words or company names. Our analysis highlights the entangled mixture of semantic and co-occurring word distributions that these models are capturing, posing challenges for their disentanglement. Our work contributes to a deeper comprehension of the theoretical foundations of these popular NLP methods and highlights the potential risks and limitations of relying solely on these models. This research introduces a new method to model the interaction of fluids with changing phases, combining level-set and embedded boundary techniques. By leveraging the strengths of these approaches, we've developed a numerical strategy utilizing Cartesian grids to efficiently handle complex boundary transformations and high-resolution interface representation. This method enables a second-order conservative numerical scheme and has been effectively applied to solve various problems, including Stefan problems, dendrite growth, and Rayleigh--B\'enard instabilities, even in the presence of melting boundaries. Furthermore, we've developed this method further to incorporate temperature and composition variables, thereby broadening its applicability to a wider range of melt flow phenomena. A key improvement over existing level-set methods is the elimination of the need for the reinitialization equation, which we've found to be unnecessary and even counterproductive. We've tested this approach using both structured and unstructured grids and have included results from these grid independence tests. This numerical method has the potential to be an valuable tool in the study of earth science, particularly in the investigation of melt flow. In multiagent learning settings beyond finding equilibria, learning rationalizable behavior that steers clear of dominated actions is another key goal. However, existing algorithms in the general multiplayer games scenario require an exponentially large number of samples relative to the number of players to determine rationalizable equilibria when working under bandit feedback. This research develops an initial suite of efficient algorithms to learn both Coarse Correlated Equilibria (CCE) and Correlated Equilibria (CE) that achieve polynomial sample complexities in line with problem parameters including the number of players. It also includes an enhanced approach for identifying a rationalizable action profile with a significantly improved sample requirement, exceeding the current benchmark established in 2021. Our innovative solutions involve the integration of multiple cutting-edge techniques that concurrently ensure the rationalizability and absence of (swap-)regret through correlated exploration and dynamic learning rate adjustments, offering potential value as standalone contributions. Moreover, our results are complemented by a sample complexity lower bound, underscoring the precision of the devised guarantees. This research was inspired by the challenges encountered in attempting to solve a problem of significant interest in the field of multiagent learning known as Stackelberg mean-field games. It builds upon the foundational work established in 2021, an year in which the first algorithm capable of learning a rationalizable equilibria in single-agent settings with polynomial sample complexity was first reported. It is worth noting that learning (CE) or (CCE) is significantly more challenging than finding a rationalizable action profile, as demonstrated by an unachievable sample complexity for the former relative to the latter in the present research. This achievement is made possible by an recently introduced specification of rationalizability that is more suitable for learning in multiagent settings, also known as the strong RRE property. This research has far-reaching implications, given the interconnection between multiagent learning and single-agent learning, as evidenced by the coexistence of tasks such as learning a Stackelberg equilibrium in multiplayer games and learning a single agent's rationalizable equilibria. This work has the distinction of being the first to achieve a polynomial sample complexity in the largest possible multiagent learning setting known to date, a level of complexity that has not been previously reached until this research was conducted. Integrating diverse datasets, stemming from data and theoretical sources, is a prerequisite for accurately fitting probability density functions. While aligning the format of experimental data is a straightforward process, reconciling disparate theoretical predictions is a more complex task. Given the numerous contributors to different physical processes, with various inputs and outputs, incorporating the predictions requires significant integration efforts. Furthermore, since processes are often measured across a wide range of scales, evolution equations such as DGLAP need to be applied to PDF candidates or already precomputed in the outputs, necessitating a unified framework that can automate this process for the benefit of research groups working on PDF fitting and potential phenomenological studies. To address this challenge, we present a basic framework called ``PDF Integrator'' that can effortlessly combine diverse sets of PDF predictions by tackling both technical and logistical difficulties. This framework, which can be executed locally or within a grid environment, incorporates a range of features that make it suitable for large-scale scientific collaborations, including data and PDF management, process-specific integration tasks, evolution equations, and NLO corrections through fast NLO libraries or alternative implementations. As an example of its capabilities, we successfully integrate a set of theoretical predictions for top quark production in deep inelastic scattering and proton-proton collisions, demonstrating the flexibility and scalability of this framework. This development is valuable for ongoing and future PDF fitting efforts and similar phenomenological studies that rely on the combination of theoretical predictions. As the field continues to evolve, we believe that this framework will facilitate the seamless integration of diverse datasets, even those emerging in the future. To ensure broad accessibility, the PDF Integrator is openly available at https://github.com/pdfintegrator/PDFIntegrator. To facilitate smooth operation, we also provide detailed documentation on how to use the framework, as well as guidance for researchers who wish to adapt it for their own needs. Furthermore, we outline potential future developments that could enhance the framework's capabilities, such as incorporation of advanced PDF fitting codes and machine learning models. We plan to continuously improve the framework and encourage feedback from the scientific community that uses it. We have already successfully applied this framework in a real-world context, having used it in recent analyses conducted by the ATLAS collaboration. We detail these specific experiences in dedicated appendices. We believe that this development will significantly streamline the process of combining theoretical predictions, thereby expediting the progress of PDF fitting efforts and similar phenomenological studies that rely on such combinations. To accelerate policy optimization in complex, dynamic systems with multiple influencing factors, reinforcement learning agents can effectively utilize previously collected historical data. Standard experience replay enables agents to retain information from prior iterations. However, the current approach equally values all collected observations, neglecting their varying significance. A more adaptive method, the variance reduction based experience replay framework, selectively leverages the most informative historical data. This approach prioritizes past observations more likely to represent the current target distribution. Theoretical and practical results demonstrate that this method accelerates optimal policy discovery and boosts the effectiveness of state-of-the-art policy optimization methods. Experimentally, variance reduction based experience replay leads to policy improvements in multiple complex systems and scenarios. The code is available at https://github.com/ikostrikis/VarREDR Lal. complex theory of mind problem that necessitates controlled text generation

Miller and Sheffield introduced the concept of an imaginary surface as a pairing of subdomains of the complex plane and associated Gaussian free fields under conformal equivalence. Specifically, they considered the relationship between these pairings and chordal Schramm-Loewner evolution. This paper develops Gaussian free field-valued processes in the upper half-plane and the first orthant of the complex plane, establishing their connection to multiple SLE evolving in time on these domains. We demonstrate that such connections can be made locally by driving multiple SLE with the Dyson model on the real line and the Bru-Wishart process on the positive reals, respectively. Ultimately, these pairings yield domains that evolve in time and associated Gaussian free fields. We refer to these as multiple field records. We study their properties and derive formulas for associated harmonic functions, demonstrating they form a Markov process and have a stationary distribution. Furthermore, we examine the relationship between multiple field records and multiple SLE evolving in time, obtaining an explicit formula for the radial Trubek-Wishart process as a limit of multiple SLE on the unit disk. This leads to a description of the domains evolving in time and their associated Gaussian free fields, giving us the multiple field records on the unit disk as a combination of the radial Trubek-Wishart process and the polar map. This formulation enables us to determine the probability of the radial Trubek-Wishart process remaining within a specified boundary, which we illustrate by investigating the ring process as an instance of multiple field records. This ring process represents the probability of a particle diffusing in the upper half-plane becoming trapped within a certain distance from the real axis before infinite time. We derive an explicit formula for this probability, confirming our result mathematically and validating our previous heuristic approach. This paper's results also pertain to the Schramm-Loewner evolution evolving in the upper half-plane and the first orthant of the complex plane. We demonstrate that a particle starting at a point in the complex plane has a positive probability of being trapped within a certain distance from the real axis as time approaches infinity, even if the SLE evolves in the entire complex plane. We establish a connection between this event and the radial Trubek-Wishart process. We refer to this event as the ring process. We derive an explicit formula for the ring process, giving us an exact probability of a particle diffusing in the upper half-plane becoming trapped within a specified boundary as time approaches infinity. This study undertakes a linear analysis of a methane-air jet flame experiencing turbulence to determine its response to acoustic vibrations emitted from upstream, while factoring in temperature fluctuations that can cause instability in flames. To accurately predict flame behavior in a linearized model, it is crucial to account for heat released from the flame's fluctuations. Unlike previous studies, the current work utilizes an active flame approach that considers how heat released from the flame's fluctuations respond to acoustic vibrations. To apply this approach in a linear framework, combustion models must be linearized, which is shown to be challenging using existing models such as LES and DNS. Nevertheless, RANS models prove to be effective alternatives due to their ability to avoid closure issues. To apply these models, the researchers used LES to obtain the average flow conditions of the jet flame. Furthermore, the results from the model matched the outcomes from the LES simulations, confirming its effectiveness. Finally, the reaction rate model was integrated into an acoustic wave equation that was solved using a numerical method, with the results confirming that heat released from the flame's fluctuations play a significant role in flame instability, particularly in the outer regions of the jet flame. Understanding how genomic elements affect specific traits through genome-wide association studies remains complex due to the sheer number of available annotations. We've developed a statistical approach to pinpoint relevant genomic elements, based on associations across the entire genome, by identifying patterns of influence in trait-associated SNPs. This approach can incorporate multiple annotation types and has been successfully applied to eighteen human traits such as blood, platelet counts, metabolism-related disorders, height, obesity and a bowel disease, by examining 450 distinct genomic features across one hundred plus tissues and cells types. Our results show that protein-coding regions influence traits to a degree of up to twenty percent, in comparison with two percent, in a wide range of cases and demonstrate specific patterns of depleted and enriched regions associated with different traits and SNPs that target repressed or accessible regions specifically within certain cell types. Furthermore, by re-ranking associations based on functional genomics, we have increased confidence in a significant portion of associated SNPs with an estimated 5%. Additionally, our approach has been applied to identify probable target genes for a substantial portion of SNPs associated with certain traits, as well as those linked to microRNA regulation, with notable results. Our methodology is readily available online for the analysis of genome-wide association studies. 

In a large-scale European population studied for 500,000 SNPs, our approach successfully mapped the genomic landscape associated with 150 traits and conditions, revealing a significant portion of unexplained genetic variation - an estimated 30 to 50% of the total. This unexplained variation was found to be linked to repetitive regions, centromeres, and around centromere-proximal regions on chromosomes. By examining this population's genomic landscape through the lens of centromere-associated epigenetics, we were able to identify specific centromere patterns linked to 20 traits and conditions such as schizophrenia, bipolar disorder, type two diabetes, obesity, and certain cancers like breast, colon, and prostate cancer. Our study highlights the critical role centromere epigenetics plays in understanding human genetics and provides a foundation for further research into this uncharted area. 

Our approach has been successfully applied to non-European populations as well, using genome-wide association study data for 500,000 SNPs in an African, Asian, and Latino population, and has revealed similar patterns of linked centromere variation across these populations, despite geographical differences. This suggests that centromere epigenetics could serve as a universal factor that influences specific human traits and conditions, regardless of geographical origin.

Bipartite graphs depicting connections between distinct groups of objects have numerous practical applications, and their visualization often takes the form of a 2-tier layout where corresponding entities are aligned horizontally across two parallel lines, connected by lines representing relationships between them. The task of reducing edge crossings within these visualizations can be computationally intensive, yet might not always guarantee sufficiently low crossings levels to maintain the visualization's clarity. In contrast, an approach has been developed to remove edge crossings by splitting specific nodes, targeting the minimum number required to yield an edge-free (planar) drawing. The question of determining if an edge-free representation exists after breaking at most a specified number of nodes remains tractable in relation to that number. In this paper, an algorithm is presented that can handle such a task efficiently and provides an illustration of the approach through an example application to co-authorship analyses. The algorithm and the results of the experiments conducted indicate that even in situations where node splits are not feasible in polynomial time, the approach can still be valuable by offering an acceptable compromise between node splits and other desirable visualization characteristics. The purpose of the feedback loop was to adjust the thruster settings to account for unexpected disturbances. To control the robot's position and velocity, we used a closed-loop system with a constant gain. Moreover, we incorporated a thruster shutdown mechanism to prevent the thrusters from being overpowered. To test our approach, we conducted simulations using two different robot models. In this context, we explore a privacy-preserving approach called federated learning that enables several entities to train a robust machine learning model jointly, without exchanging sensitive information about their data. Based on how entities cooperate, FL can be categorized into two primary forms - horizontal and vertical FL. The former involves participants who collaborate using identical data attributes, while in the latter, entities with overlapping sample IDs collaborate using different features. Given its versatility, vertical FL is deemed particularly suitable for collaborative training by major enterprises. Here we concentrate on FL and delve into possible privacy breaches in actual VFL implementations. Two applicable attacks were created by us - one is called a reverse multiplication attack designed to circumvent logistic regression, while the other, known as a reverse sum attack, targets XGBoost protocols. Our empirical study validates that both attacks are successful, effective, evasive, and straightforward - they do not diverge from the predefined protocol, nor do they lower the model's accuracy; even with data encrypted. Additionally, we found out the stolen information can train a new machine learning classifier which is just as accurate as the one trained using actual data, without knowing beforehand much about the target user. Our analysis highlights potential preventive strategies, while revealing challenges that might give rise to several exciting research opportunities. Our code is available at: \url{https://github.com/yingtuo1998/VFLAttack}.

Kernel methods have proven highly effective in various machine learning applications, yet their scalability to large datasets is severely limited due to the computationally expensive nature of pairwise evaluations. In response, Random Fourier Features were proposed to approximate kernel functions using randomized transformations, thereby enabling the use of kernel methods on larger data sets. While widely adopted, this method has significant drawbacks, notably requiring an unnecessarily large number of features, directly proportional to the size of the dataset, in order to achieve satisfactory results comparable to traditional kernel-based methods. In order to circumvent these limitations and efficiently process large datasets, this paper introduces an alternative method of kernel approximation that leverages insights specific to the underlying data and offers both feature dimensionality reduction and performance enhancements. We test and evaluate this novel method against a range of competitors, including RFF, orthogonal random features, and the Nyström method. In multiple assessments, our approach is found to consistently outperform existing methods in both accuracy and efficiency when applied to kernel-based classifiers and support vector machines. This research focuses on creating resilient Molmer-Sorensen gates using trapped ions arranged in a line, incorporating Gaussian amplitude modulation and a consistent laser frequency. We chose a frequency that maintains balanced entanglement accumulation across all motion modes to provide a significant degree of protection against frequency errors, particularly for long chains of ions. A demonstration of this method is performed on a chain of three ions, achieving an average reduction of under one percent from peak precision within a twenty kilohertz range of frequency deviation, and the efficiency of this gate design is examined through numerical simulations on chains consisting of two to thirty-three ions. We found that this technique can lead to nearly uniform entanglement generation across all motion modes, resulting in a high degree of frequency tolerance. This robust Molmer-Sorensen gate design can be executed using existing trapped ion setups and has the potential to significantly enhance the reliability of quantum computations involving large numbers of ions. This technique's effectiveness is demonstrated through successful execution of both quantum Fourier transforms and Shor's algorithm on up to eleven qubits. This robust gate design can be combined with other frequency-insensitive implementations, further enhancing the reliability of quantum computations. This method's efficiency and frequency robustness can be traded off by adjusting the duration of entanglement generation, and this robust implementation has been successfully applied in multiple-use scenarios. Building upon this discovery, we developed a neural model that learns from the remaining knowledge between $n$-gram models and the true language distribution, allowing for both a deeper grasp of language and the flexibility to adjust models through the $n$-gram base without altering the neural model.
