Reconstructing three-dimensional faces in complex real-world scenarios poses significant difficulties due to frequently missing or occluded facial details, particularly in images depicting large head orientations. This challenging problem is compounded by the extensive variability of head poses, which significantly expands the potential solution space and complicates modeling efforts. To break down this complex task into more manageable components, our approach focuses on modeling both pose and occlusion. In this regard, we introduce an end-to-end framework called SADRNet, which produces a face that varies based on the orientation and another face that remains invariant, then fuses these faces via a self-alignment mechanism informed by occlusion. Exhaustive testing of our proposed technique on the widely used AFLW2000-3D and Florence datasets shows substantial performance enhancements over existing top-ranking methods. Moreover, our approach provides interpretable results, with visually plausible output facing different head orientations and occlusions. Our code is available at this link: https://github.com/SleepsBest/SADRNet.

In an inflationary model, with a specific type of $\alpha$-attractor potential, we examine the behavior in the high-$k$ regime, where cosmological perturbations exhibit excessive growth and negative values of the Bardeen potential. This regime is found to be conducive to the formation of primordial black holes (PBHs). Our calculations were carried out within a spatially flat gauge with a non-zero fluctuation in the inflaton field and its impact on the background gravitational field. We determined the scalar density fluctuations ($\sigma$), asymmetry ($\beta$), and PBH mass fraction ($f_\mathrm{PBH}$) in relation to specific mass scales. Our results reveal that a considerable fraction of the early universe could be converted into PBHs under certain conditions, with estimates suggesting that the PBH density peaks at $10^{-5.5}$ geV per cm$^3$ in a particular parameter range. This leads to an estimated total PBH mass of $10^{50}$ to $10^{51}$ dollars, with a corresponding optically thick PBH collapse rate into heavy-element abundances via primordial black hole nucleosynthesis (PBNN). Our study predicts specific spectral lines in the cosmic microwave background and offers an explanation for heavy-element abundances observed in very metal-poor stars. Furthermore, we outline the methods for detecting PBHs and the PBNN signature in future astronomical observations. This includes the use of high-resolution spectroscopy in searches for certain element signatures in the spectra of very metal-poor stars, while larger PBHs would result in gravitational waves compatible with current and future detectors, and an enhanced anti-lepton flux from PBHs annihilating with antineutrinos from the sun and the Earth. This could potentially be confirmed via the detection of specific lines in the spectra of very metal-poor stars, a notion we refer to as Primordial Nucleosynthesis from the Very Early Universe (PNVEU). A key factor for maintaining stability in future low-carbon power grids is expected to be energy storage systems. Studies examining past experiences reveal a common issue with storage units - they frequently fail to take advantage of high-price signals during periods of low energy supply. This behavior has been often attributed to inaccurate forecasting, operational issues, or market manipulation. However, our research suggests a more plausible explanation is rooted in risk management practices. By utilizing a stochastic self-scheduling approach and an empirical storage unit risk preference, our findings show that risk-conscious storage units tend to take part in short-term energy trading, but only during times of extreme price volatility. This allows them to minimize potential losses and capitalize on opportunities, thus managing their risks more effectively. As the energy mix becomes increasingly reliant on storage, understanding and accommodating the risk-taking propensities of these systems will be crucial for developing healthy electricity markets. 

This report focuses on a specific aspect of storage unit behavior - their ability to engage in peer-to-peer energy trading. These findings are valuable for market designers and operators, as they highlight the significance of considering storage unit risk management in markets that include peer-to-peer trading. Furthermore, our model can be easily adapted for use in other electricity markets around the world.

In Dynamic Time-Division Duplexing (TDD), individual cells can schedule uplink and downlink modes independently, depending on local traffic conditions, but this causes interference between neighboring cells, turning a critical problem into an NP-hard mixed-integer non-convex challenge. We've developed an efficient and localized solution, separating power allocation and scheduling processes, first assigning power independently to cells, followed by a non-cooperative game determining scheduling modes, with payoffs calculated according to the level of interference and required cell communication. Simulations, set in an outdoor scenario with multiple small cells, reveal our method outperforms static TDD solutions. Furthermore, we found that our algorithm adapts well to various network configurations and demands, despite some cells often being excluded from optimal solutions. We also observed that our method performs best when cells are powered equally, but other power allocation strategies are explored in the paper as well. Finally, we discovered that our algorithm can handle large scales, albeit with a substantial computational requirement, an issue we aim to address in the future by considering tighter stopping criteria for the end of the algorithm, as well as other optimization strategies. We've also looked into variants of our algorithm, including one that reduces computational needs by half, according to our results. We've tested our algorithm using real-world data, including an outdoor scenario with 24 small cells, over a 24-hour period. We've published our data and code online, to help others in the field with their own variations of our algorithm. Researchers have successfully used hydrodynamic theories to simulate complex dynamics of quantum many-body systems, and in this work, we've developed a novel stochastic hydrodynamic approach for describing interacting Bose gases within a specific phase-space framework. This method extends previous hydrodynamic methods, enabling the simulation of a system's full quantum dynamics and allowing for the calculation of non-equilibrium correlations, even for short-wavelength phenomena. Building upon this description, we derived a linearized stochastic hydrodynamic model that simulates long-lasting non-equilibrium situations while sacrificing a more precise quantum fluctuation treatment, and found it to be directly connected with the established Bogoliubov approach. Furthermore, we applied and validated our method by investigating a quantum shock wave scenario and a rotating Bose-Joseim-Hubbard system, and it holds promise for tackling more intricate, albeit somewhat modified, configurations. All numerical results are compared with existing data and demonstrate a clear agreement. All code associated with this research is available on open-source platforms, and researchers can utilize it to tackle similar problems involving multibody quantum systems. 

A particular focus of this work is a novel stochastic hydrodynamic model, which was discovered to be equivalent to the Bogoliubov approach in situations of long-lasting non-equilibrium conditions, and this equivalent representation was found to consist of an analytical expression of the Wigner function, which is otherwise challenging to obtain directly from the original stochastic hydrodynamic equations. This representation provides a clear explanation of the positive-P phase-space formalism's ability to successfully simulate interacting Bose gases, even when considering the breakdown of the hydrodynamic approximation, as seen in shock wave configurations. All numerical results generated in this research were obtained using the hydrodynamic model, the linearized model, and the stochastic Gross-Pitaevskii equation as reference points of increasing accuracy. All numerical code associated with this research is open-source and can be found on the GitHub platform. 

Finally, this research demonstrated the capability of the positive-P phase-space formalism to successfully simulate full quantum dynamics even in non-equilibrium situations, and has provided a novel approach to describing interacting Bose gases within a hydrodynamic framework, which was discovered to be equivalent to the Bogoliubov approach. A direct connection between the positive-P phase-space formalism and the hydrodynamic model, as well as the linearized model, has been established, and both the stochastic hydrodynamic model and the linearized model were found to be connected with the established Bogoliubov approach in situations of long-lasting non-equilibrium conditions. Machine learning models often undergo performance assessment through k-fold cross-validation to facilitate model selection and parameter adjustment. Yet, due to the random partitioning inherent in CV, estimated model performance exhibits significant variability. This unpredictability makes effective parameter tuning challenging, as it introduces substantial uncertainty into the choice of parameters. Moreover, our study reveals that the optimal parameters obtained are excessively sensitive to the manner in which the data is divided, often resulting in suboptimal solutions and significant difficulties in achieving reproducibility. In contrast, our research suggests employing the reduced variance j-k fold CV method, which involves conducting multiple independent assessments across K subgroups within the training set J times. The aim is to prioritize the minimization of performance estimation variability over that of model generalizability, making our recommendation particularly suitable for applications where there is a substantial gap between the sizes of training and testing datasets. In such cases, our study demonstrates a marked improvement in the accuracy of model performance estimates and parameter robustness, as evidenced by our experiments based on real-world data. Our findings provide a clear understanding of the inherent challenges associated with CV and model selection, along with a concrete solution that can be applied to a wide range of existing algorithms, including support vector machines, gradient boosting, and neural networks. Our proposed approach has been made available as an open-source tool on GitHub, allowing for the convenient integration of j-k fold CV into existing machine learning workflows via popular software tools, thereby facilitating scalable and reliable parameter tuning for a broad spectrum of applications. Deep Neural Networks with vast parameters have faced challenges in real-time deployment, prompting the utilization of Teacher-Student architectures in knowledge distillation. Initially used to achieve comparable performance with smaller student networks, these architectures have now been applied in various knowledge learning applications such as knowledge distillation with multiple teachers, student network expansion, and knowledge consolidation across domains. Current methods primarily focus on assigning weights to input data, neglecting the potential benefits of weighing student network outputs when transferring knowledge. We discovered that by incorporating weights for the student network in Teacher-Student architecture, we could enhance the performance by up to 6.5% in certain cases. We further explored this idea by proposing a novel weighted knowledge distillation framework that considers both input and output weights for the student network. Experimental results showed significant improvements of 5.4% to 6.5% in certain cases when compared to traditional knowledge distillation methods. We also observed that weighted knowledge distillation can be applied to a wide range of datasets and networks. Notably, our proposed method outperformed the current state-of-the-art method by a margin of 2.4% in CIFAR-10 when using ResNet50 as the student network. We introduce a new efficient framework for representing functions in graphical models, which serves as a foundation for a variety of computational tasks. Our concise model then leverages this framework, specifically using deterministic finite state automata within a variable elimination approach known as Bucket Elimination. We dub this variant FABE, which we found significantly enhances Bucket Elimination by substantially reducing the computational time and memory usage. Our FABE approach compares favourably to the current state of the art methods, particularly recursive best-first and structured message passing for the most probable explanation, and structured memory management, especially in scenarios with large datasets and complex decision trees. Our findings are evident through various performance metrics in our comprehensive testing, which involved multiple real-world examples including a scientific case study. We have publicly available code to support these results. 

We outline the key steps for applying FABE to any given problem, which can be broadly categorized into the following steps: First, establish the underlying structure of the problem through a cyclic dependency view, followed by the construction of a set of rules that the problem adheres to, and finally, apply the FABE approach. We have successfully applied our approach to the analysis of three distinct domains: knowledge discovery in large ontological knowledge bases, the interpretation of astrological spectra, and the examination of X-ray binary star spectra based on specific characteristics. We have also incorporated the astrophysical features into the appropriate frames of reference in order to verify the validity of our findings. We have a public repository for our code and research on the following link: https://github.com/rami972/FABE. 

We highlight the primary advantages of using the cyclic dependency view, which we believe has significant potential for expansion, given the diverse range of domains where our approach has been applied successfully, despite the limited scope of our current research. We have observed in all our tested cases that the removal of parallel edges results in a significant decrease in the computational time required, which we attribute to the elimination of unnecessary reasoning about conflicting information. We have also observed the variety of ways that the removal of parallel edges can be beneficial, which we have categorized into the following: the reduction of the size of the search space, the removal of redundant reasoning, the removal of conflicting information, the enhancement of the efficiency of approximation methods, and the enhancement of the accuracy of approximation methods. We have a comprehensive list of acronyms for easy reference. We have a public repository for our code and research on the following link: https://github.com/rami972/FABE

We investigated the absorption of a single, monochromatic light beam at 689 nm as it passes through a cloud of ultracold $^{88}$Sr atoms. Due to the interaction, the absorption pattern deviates significantly, taking on an asymmetric shape as a result of a shift in frequency that is equivalent in magnitude to the natural width of a specific atomic transition in strontium. This effect becomes more pronounced under conditions of high saturation. Our research incorporated momentum transfers resulting from the absorption and emission of photons, as described by a modified version of the optical Bloch equations. We demonstrated that even a single-beam setup can illustrate photon recoil effects that have substantial implications for fields like saturation spectroscopy, Ramsey interferometry, and absorption imaging. Moreover, we highlighted the significance of accurately accounting for photon scattering when interpreting data obtained using ultracold atoms and other systems that involve slow, sensitive measurements. 

In addition to the absorption of a single-light beam, we examined a setup featuring two overlapping beams, one of which is copolarized with the atoms, to demonstrate how photon recoil can significantly alter distributions of orientation and polarization that result from interactions between light and ultracold atoms. This is particularly notable when the involved atomic transitions have non-zero angular momenta. Our findings also hold value for other systems of cold and trapped particles, including molecules and condensates of bosonic and fermionic atoms. 

Our research further shows that even a single-beam setup can exhibit large photon recoil effects, especially when using short-wavelength light on clouds of ultracold atoms, and we have tested our model using experimental data. Alternately, the same parameters used to generate the data can be employed to plan future experiments that are optimized for detecting these photon recoil effects. 

Finally, we explored the behavior of a specific two-beam interaction setup that is commonly used in Ramsey interferometry, to demonstrate how photon recoil can shift the absorption pattern at 680 nm by as much as 10 times the width of a natural atomic linewidth, thus indicating that this effect needs to be accounted for when using strontium clouds. This is particularly true when attempting to measure small frequencies of shift that are equivalent to the natural width of a spectral line, as is the case when searching for tiny environmental effects that might be influenced by ultracold atoms.

When subjected to high stresses, the vast majority of dense mixtures undergo a sudden and extreme thickening, characterized by a transition from fluid-like behavior to rigidity. Researchers propose that abrupt shear thickening serves as an initial indicator of a state transition, developing a comprehensive framework for interpreting viscosity through a universal function that bridges the frictionless point of jamming and a state of rigidity influenced by friction, anisotropy, and shear. Studies involving cornstarch in glycerol and silica spheres in glycerol found that for these two systems, viscosity can be condensed into a singular, stress- and volume fraction-independent curve, revealing distinct scaling regimes that reflect different universality classes and implying that isotropic and anisotropic shear jamming have unique characteristics. Furthermore, by integrating the effects of microscale interactions into a dimensionless variable that gauges the distance from shear jamming, scientists have paved the way for applying theories developed for equilibrium phenomena to better understand the physics governing the shear thickening transition. While the rigidity induced by shear stress ultimately leads to a logarithmic fracture viscosity, the research highlights the significant role that the point of shear jamming plays in defining the stress and volume fraction limits within the state of chaos that precedes rigidity. Ultimately, the findings provide a foundation for further investigation into the dynamics of chaos and the creation of fractures, offering insights that can be applied across various fields of study, including geophysics, materials science, and physiology. The proposed framework can also be used to address critical concerns, such as the generation of turbulence during the transition from laminar flow and the capabilities of suspensions to withstand impacts before being damaged. The study has been recognized for its significance, being awarded the 2023 IOP Institute Physics prize for Outstanding Ph.D. Research. The research builds upon a paper published in Nature Physics, with the full study drawing upon data and insights derived from numerous experiments, simulations, and theoretical analyses conducted within the fields of condensed matter and fluid mechanics. The associated data has been made publicly available, with the aim of fostering open science and encouraging further research among the academic community. The research has been conducted within the Department of Physics at the Australian National University, under the guidance of Dr. Trushar Hanspal and A/Prof. Thomas Salez. Recently introduced is a higher rank algebra known as the Racah algebra $R(n)$. A special variant, termed the special Racah algebra $sR(n)$, is then defined as a quotient of the Racah algebra by its central elements. It is then demonstrated that this $sR(n)$ algebra is equivalent to the centralizer $Z_{n}(\mathfrak{sl}_2)$ through application of classical invariant theory, particularly with respect to a specific embedding of the Lie algebra $U(\mathfrak{sl}_2)$ within a tensor product. As a result, the centralizer $Z_{n}(\mathfrak{sl}_2)$ can be presented through generators and defining relations, offering an innovative perspective on its structure. Additionally, the series known as the Hilbert-Poincar\'e series of the centralizer $Z_{n}(\mathfrak{sl}_2)$ can be computed explicitly. The research discussed also extends towards the special Askey-Wilson algebra as well as the continuous version of the latter, for both of which the centralizer $Z_{n}(\mathfrak{sl}_2)$ can be determined as the coalgebra whose dual becomes the centralizer $Z_{n}(\mathfrak{sl}_2)^{\vee}$ within the dual space of the ring of polynomials $\mathbb{C}[x_{1}^{±1}, \ldots, x_{n}^{±1}]$. Furthermore, the application of the latter case leads to a formula for the Hilbert-Poincar\'e series of $Z_{n}(\mathfrak{sl}_2)$ as $\frac{(1-x^{n+1})\cdot(1-x^{n-1})}{(1-x)^{2}}$. An area where Web search personalisation's effect on professional work has been inadequately studied is that of professional knowledge work on the Web. This study examines public sector officials' reliance on Google's Web search engine for their assessment, their knowledge of potential biases in search algorithms and the influence they have on retrieving all relevant information. The study's results show that a substantial number of the participants are unaware of potential biases in search algorithms and the possible strategies to prevent them from overlooking essential information. Notably, our data reveal that as much as 20% of the necessary information may go undetected due to the influence of Web search personalisation. This study's findings highlight the significance of Web search for public sector professionals, suggesting the necessity for training on search algorithms' potential biases that can shape judgments and decisions. In addition, it is crucial that these professionals are provided with guidelines to reduce the likelihood of missing relevant information. This study's contributions are reflected in its policy recommendations and potential avenues for future research in this underexplored domain. In particular, it is essential to study Web search personalisation's effects on professionals in other fields such as business, medicine and law, and even non-professionals, with a view to possible corrective measures. A novel approach is proposed to create and assess a respiratory motion-compensated four-dimensional T2-weighted MRI sequence, which is crucial in radiology and radiotherapy treatments guided by MRI. Data acquisition is continuous via a spiral acquisition method with reordering of Cartesian sampling points (rCASPR) that ensures matching image contrast and sorts data into respiratory phases. Initial 4D images are reconstructed using a compressed sensing technique and deformation fields are estimated for compensation in subsequent images. Experiments with phantom and human subjects compared sampling methods, including in silico trials. Parameters for low-resolution reconstruction, including resolution and regularization, were optimally selected through a grid search method. Motion compensation in rCASPR was tested in eight subjects with results indicating better point-spread-function in rCASPR with little difference in contrast, thus making it feasible for direct application in radiology and radiotherapy treatments. Optimized 4D MRI reconstruction parameters were also determined with spatial resolution and temporal regularization set at $4.5mm^3$ and $10^{-4}$. A quantitative evaluation of image quality through the use of gradient entropy showed a score of 22.02 for motion-compensated rCASPR. Ultimately, this rCASPR-based method provides high-quality, free-breathing MRI images that minimize alterations in scan duration and image contrast, allowing direct application in radiology and radiotherapy treatments guided by MRI.

The paired-permutation test in NLP systems has long relied on testing the statistical significance of differences in performance. This test aims to verify that observed discrepancies aren't simply coincidental. Despite the importance of accurate results, a lack of suitable exact algorithms forces practitioners to use time-consuming Monte Carlo approximations to achieve this goal. In contrast, we've developed an efficient method for calculating paired-permutation test results exactly. This exact algorithm takes significantly less time to compute than Monte Carlo methods. In particular, we observed a 10 times speedup when using our exact algorithm versus the commonly employed Monte Carlo approximation on a representative dataset of 20000 samples. Moreover, our code can be used independently to perform paired-permutation tests exactly. We've tested this on numerous datasets and found it to be accurate and up to 100 times faster than Monte Carlo methods for large datasets. We've made our exact algorithm and associated code available to the community, hoping it will significantly reduce the time NLP researchers spend conducting paired-permutation tests. We've also included a simple command-line interface to make the integration process as seamless as possible. We propose using our exact algorithm as the standard method for paired-permutation tests in the field of NLP. This research investigates double Higgs boson production at future electron-positron colliders CLIC and ILC with TeV-scale energies within the framework of Effective Field Theories (EFTs), focusing on beyond-Standard Model Higgs physics. Initially, we consider the Higgs Effective Field Theory (HEFT) and then compare the predictions with the Standard Model Effective Field Theory (SMEFT). Our primary analysis concerns the double Higgs production process in the two EFTs through the dominant subprocess $WW \to HH$. We calculate the cross-section of this subprocess for all polarization channels and relevant effective operators at various energies, and demonstrate how in the HEFT case, the cross-section primarily depends on two leading coefficients at these TeV scales. We then establish the equivalence between the dominant coefficients of the HEFT and SMEFT at the level of the scattering amplitude for this subprocess. In the subsequent analysis, we explore the detectability of the two leading HEFT coefficients at the two planned colliders CLIC (operating at 3 TeV, 5 ab$^{-1}$) and ILC (operating at 1 TeV, 8 ab$^{-1}$), and identify the accessible parameter regions by studying the predicted rates for the characteristic four bottom jet signatures with missing energy in the $b \bar b b \bar b \nu \bar \nu$ final state. We find that the pole region of the HEFT is already excluded at the level of cross-section for the 13 TeV LHC, while at the future colliders: at the 95% confidence level, the coefficient values k $\Lambda \geq 1.6$ TeV for the CLIC and k $\Lambda \geq 0.26$ TeV for the ILC; furthermore, the expected limits also demonstrate the futures' prospects for discovering the double Higgs boson in the standard scenario, where the dominant subprocess $WW \to HH$ occurs mediated by the neutral vector boson self-energy correction, which is already well-restricted by the existing LEP and LHC data. We ultimately conclude that future electron-positron colliders with TeV-scale energies have a higher discovery potential for the double Higgs boson in the HEFT beyond the Standard Model, and that the main production process in the SMEFT at these energies is not accessible due to the constraints of the existing LEP and LHC data. We also outline the necessary improvements for the event simulation generators that will be utilized in the actual experiments

This anisotropy varied greatly with the speed at which the cylinder was moved, its length compared to its width, and whether the grains it was moving through had high friction or little friction. The ATLAS experiment at the Large Hadron Collider (LHC) has achieved precise measurements in two areas, namely neutral B meson mixing and CP violation, as well as in rare electroweak processes occurring in suppressed B-meson decays. This study concentrates on recent findings from the ATLAS collaboration, encompassing evaluations of rare occurrences like $B^0_s \to \mu^+\mu^-$ and $B^0 \to \mu^+\mu^-$ decays and the determination of CP-violating processes in $B^0_s \to J/\psi\phi$. The research utilizes data collected from 13 TeV proton-proton collisions, with the exception of $B^0_s \to J/\psi\phi$ measurements derived from 8 TeV and 7 TeV experiments. The results are compared to previous findings and are in line with predictions made by the Standard Model, with certain measurements showcasing enhanced precision. The effective lifetime of $B^0_s$ mesons and the weak phase angle $\phi_s$ have been determined to be $1.466 \pm 0.017$ ps and $0.017 \pm 0.006$ rad, respectively. Moreover, the effective CKM matrix element $S\beta^2_{slight}$ has been calculated to be $2.300 \pm 0.081$. The research has also led to the creation of upper limits for rare processes like $B^0 \to \mu^+\mu^-$ and $B^0_s \to J/\psi\phi$ at the levels of $6.9 \times 10^{-6}$ and $6.9 \times 10^{-5}$ decays per proton-proton collision, respectively. The findings have also been applied in deriving constraints on certain scenarios beyond the Standard Model. The precision of these measurements will be crucial in distinguishing between different theories that go beyond the established particle physics framework. The ATLAS collaboration has successfully demonstrated the capabilities of the LHC to study rare B-meson decays and has contributed significantly to the global understanding of CP violation and matter-antimatter asymmetry in the universe. The research has also highlighted the significance of collecting more data at the LHC to achieve greater precision in these measurements. For laparoscopic liver surgery, we integrate an organ model derived from preoperative CT scans with a partially reconstructed intraoperative surface from laparoscopic video footage. The complexity of this task arises from insufficient and inaccurate intraoperative data, real-time processing needs, and unknown variables, such as organ properties and boundary conditions. The liver's featureless surface and varied image modality noises also pose significant challenges. We addressed this challenge by training a single convolutional neural network to simultaneously identify surface correspondences and perform non-rigid registration. The network's training dataset includes realistic biomechanical simulations of randomly generated organ models undergoing deformation. This allows it to efficiently apply to novel patient organs without retraining, also enabling robust performance against noisy intraoperative surface inputs during testing. The trained network provides an optimal displacement field to map preoperative volume to the intraoperative surface, demonstrated by multiple experiments showing its applicability and efficiency with real-world data. Determining scene flow involves calculating the three-dimensional motion trajectories for specific points within an animated three-dimensional environment. Motion trajectory data has been found beneficial for downstream tasks like activity classification and obstacle detection. Nonetheless, obtaining precise data through LiDAR sensors and stereo cameras is laborious due to its computationally intensive annotation process. We address this issue by presenting a 3D scene flow benchmark alongside a novel self-supervised training framework for estimating scene flow. The benchmark comprises progressively complex datasets to study the estimation process, beginning from a singular object in motion to complex real-world environments. We introduce a unique method, Adversarial Metric Learning, for self-supervised flow estimation where two models work in tandem: one performs flow estimation and another derives a latent metric to differentiate the altered points from the target point cloud, achieved through a Multi-Scale Triplet loss calculation using intermediate feature vectors. We leverage our benchmark to gain insight into various models and our proposed framework, finding that our method successfully preserves spatial coherence and detailed geometric structures, whereas many self-supervised baselines fail in this aspect. Nonetheless, overcoming occlusions remains a significant challenge. We hope this research paves the way for improved estimation techniques and encourages others to contribute to this essential task. Code and datasets are available at: \url{https://github.com/Tong-Shuo/adversarial_metric_learning}.

A streamlined variation of the Rao-Blackwellized point mass filter predicts the density of unobserved targets, with their distribution approximated as Gaussian for initially detected targets. Contrary to conventional implementations, the method presented utilizes grid-based variations to represent unobserved target densities. The dynamics of soccer games mean even small moments can greatly impact the outcome, making players, coaches, and scouts intensely curious about how to act effectively in pivotal situations. In such moments, teams may lose possession of the ball or score, leading to a desire for an optimal course of action. To address this need, we propose a novel way to describe the game's state and a batch reinforcement learning method to train a strategic policy network. By analyzing the contextual aspects of situations, the network can provide the best action to increase the team's chances of scoring, drawing on real soccer data from InStat. In a large-scale experiment with 104 European soccer matches, we found our optimized strategy consistently outperformed the standard policy, and it even mimicked the behavior observed in real games. Notably, we observed situations where actions like committing a foul or kicking the ball out of bounds might be preferable to shooting, showcasing the importance of nuanced decision-making. Our model has been made available for open research at https://soccerrl.github.io/.

The model shows that an abrupt transition occurs as immigration intensity surpasses a critical point, causing the irreversible decline of the species with shorter dispersal range due to a cusp catastrophe leading to half loop dynamics. The model's behavior is examined through the lens of TM dynamics, Kimberling's formula, and the role of the lattice size. resolution on an uncorrected TEM. By examining various design features

Active galactic nuclei (AGNs), containing accreting black holes at their center, allow for the investigation of black hole mass and spin through the analysis of electromagnetic spectra. This research considers the electromagnetic spectra of a comprehensive dataset of AGNs, consisting of over 5000 radiation-banded objects, to determine the methods by which black hole characteristics can be identified. Based on the previous work of others, the key factors in achieving this identification are as follows. 

First, both optically thick and thin components of the electromagnetic spectra need to be determined to estimate the black hole mass and spin. The analysis of thin components is more reliable as they are less affected by uncertainties in the properties of the environment surrounding the black hole. 

Second, the effects of the direction in which the light is emitted and the motion of the source's material on the spectra need to be considered. This entails using a sophisticated model that takes into account the properties of the accretion disk around the black hole as well as the characteristics of the electron distribution. 

Third, both the spin and mass of the black hole need to be identified from the same set of spectra through the use of a technique called "degenerate fitting." This approach involves attempting to fit the spectra using a range of different spin and mass values before determining the most suitable ones based on the characteristics of the source. 

Fourth, both the spin and mass of the black holes need to be within physically plausible limits. This entails verifying that the calculated values align with those of other objects with similar properties and verifying that the calculated values for the same object vary by only a minor amount when different techniques are applied.

A distinctive feature of neural development is the rhythmic shifting of cell nuclei
between the upper and lower layers of the neuroepithelial tissue as interkinetic nuclear
migration (IKNM) unfolds. In this study, we utilize extended, high-speed lightsheet and two-photon imaging
techniques in live zebrafish retinas during initial development to gain a deeper understanding of the underlying mechanical
processes driving IKNM. Our high-resolution images permit us to precisely track individual cell nuclei as they
migrate across the tissue, revealing a complex, three-dimensional movement pattern that previous two-dimensional
studies have been unable to capture. We uncover a previously unobserved, overcast, layered configuration of cell
nuclei within the central region of the retina, surrounded by a outer rim of migrating nuclei. We also explore the
mechanisms propelling the movement of these nuclei and the interactions between them, uncovering a crucial role for
the upper layer in initiating movement that is then reinforced by the lower layer. We believe our current understanding
of the mechanical processes governing IKNM, combined with previous findings on the underlying cellular and
electrical processes, present a comprehensive neural development model that we term the "retinal roller" model. We
also examine the intricate relationship between the spatial and temporal movement patterns of these nuclei during
neural development, uncovering a repeating, rhythmic movement pattern that we term the "interkinetic wave" that
appears to be driven by a 4.5 hour cycle that is a fundamental time frame for retinal development. We theorize that
this "interkinetic wave" pattern could serve as a key time-keeping mechanism for the coordinated, balanced growth
of the retina. We believe our current findings open the door to a broader understanding of the intricate mechanisms
governing neural development and make them available to the scientific community for further scrutiny and possible
extension to the development of the brain as a whole. We also reflect on the wider implications of using zebrafish
as a model for studying human brain development, a topic we feel requires further discussion within the scientific
community. We have made the data and images used in this study available online for the benefit of the scientific
community. We have made the code we utilized for image analysis and modeling available online for the benefit of the

The Yarkovsky-O'Keefe-Radzievskii-Paddack effect significantly impacts the rotational states of small asteroids by exerting a net torque resulting from solar radiation reflected and re-emitted by the surface. As a consequence of this phenomenon, the rotation period of these asteroids gradually changes, which can be best measured through light curves as the phase shift accumulates over time in a quadratic manner. To study this effect in detail, researchers collected archived data and conducted new photometric observations for asteroids 1992 SK, Geographos, and Toro, before utilizing a light curve inversion method to match their shapes and rotation characteristics. By modeling the phase shift caused by the YORP effect, the researchers were able to determine the rotation period of these asteroids with high precision, which in the case of 1992 SK and Geographos, allowed the researchers to calculate the YORP acceleration and deceleration respectively, and thus, understand the fate of these asteroids which are either gaining or losing rotational energy. For the asteroid Toro, which showed an irregular light curve pattern, the researcher was unable to conclude how the YORP effect influences its rotation. Moreover, an increase in the rotation rate of 1992 SK and Geographos, which have different spin directions, was also observed, which the researchers believe could be as a result of triaxial shapes of these asteroids triggered by the YORP effect, or also as a result of triaxial shapes as a result of mass transfer caused by the Yarkovsky effect. The study of these asteroids through light curves also revealed their surface temperature ranges and suggested that future observations through thermal infrared spectroscopy could provide further information on their surface compositions. The research on the YORP effect for these specific asteroids is significant as they are notable for their large rotations rates and could serve as a link between small asteroids and planetary satellites. The YORP effect on these asteroids is so strong that it could eventually lead to a loss of rotational energy, resulting in a rotation period of approximately 80 hours, which would allow the researchers to study the link between the effect and triaxial shapes caused by tidal forces in satellite asteroids. The research also highlights the significance of future observations of these specific asteroids as well as other small asteroids with notable rotation rates. The combination of photometric and thermal infrared observations can provide a comprehensive understanding of these asteroids' surface compositions, shapes, and spin evolution. The study suggests that the YORP effect can be observed in asteroids as small as 100 meters in diameter

The underlying mechanisms of the ventral temporal cortex's animacy organization remain contentious, suggesting that animacy exists along a spectrum rather than a binary divide. Recent evidence suggests this continuum is influenced by the degree of presence or absence of distinct animal features or by how entities are perceived as social agents. In this study, a stimulus set with independent factors of visual categorizability and agency perception in animals was used to test these hypotheses through both computational neural networks and behavioral experiments. Utilizing functional magnetic resonance imaging, our findings showed that visual categorizability and agency perception separately explained independent components of the animacy spectrum in VTC. When combined, they fully captured the continuum, and our data highlighted a notable shift in animal perception towards prioritizing agency over categorizability. Moreover, an examination of pre- and post-lateralization VTC regions revealed that they respectively represent the spectrum's starting and endpoint. This research provides empirical evidence for the animacy spectrum hypothesis and highlights the importance of distinguishing between different animal perceptions within VTC. Furthermore, it highlights the utility of computational neural networks in guiding and interpreting VTC's animacy organization. This study's findings have implications for understanding the complex animal perception in the human brain and it also highlights the potential biases in training deep learning models on natural text. This is particularly evident when considering the influence of agency perception in animals as embodied in linguistic knowledge. This study's robust methodology and stimulating research questions make it relevant to fields including computer science, philosophy, and anthropology. It also provides a framework for the ongoing debate on the animacy spectrum hypothesis within the fields of neuroscience and linguistics. Secondly, it employs the Puck Covariance formula in conjunction with Selberg's delta-symbol method to derive an unfolded, convex 2-sided estimate for the Laplacian operator on the unipotent orbits within GL_2 over a specific Hilbert space, from which it deduces the nonexistence of Landau-Siegel zeros. The study also mentions the broader implications of its findings, including the fact that its methods can be extended to address the Landau-Siegel zero issue in contexts more broadly defined, as well as its support for quantum unique ergodicity for GL_2 Hecke-Maass newforms through the application of prominent results from the works of Snider, Miller, and Kowalski-Vladimirov. The study's results can be viewed as an expansion upon the earlier, more constrained theorem regarding the nonexistence of Landau-Siegel zeros proved by Conrey, Goldstein, and Papanou in 1981, given its wider scope of generalizability to Dirichlet L-function zeros. The research was motivated by the broader issue of zero avoidance off the s=1 axis, and it is further related to the significant question of whether the distribution of automorphic L-function zeros at s=1 is consistent with the GUE distribution predicted by the Random Matrix Theory. To achieve this, we have also established a connection between the input and output relationships of Shor's algorithm and those of its component programs, which involves both classical and quantum programs, and involves both shared and separate memory models. To facilitate the verification of our extension, we have also established the soundness and completeness of our approach with respect to the original proposal of the quantum relational Hoare logic in (Unruh, POPL 2019), which provides a set of conditions for defining preconditions and postconditions that are equivalent to those defined by Unruh. To put our work into perspective, we have examined the relationship between our approach and the earlier proposals of the quantum Hoare logic without relations as well as the probabilistic Hoare logic without relations, which have been verified to be sub-theories of our approach. To further explore the capabilities of our extension, we have also investigated the comparison of different implementations of the same algorithm, which has been found to be inseparable from the comparison of programs that involve shared memory in both classical and quantum settings, which has been found to be a non-trivial task that requires the extension of our approach to deal with concurrency

By leveraging previously acquired skills and adapting them to unfamiliar tasks without explicit guidance, humans demonstrate impressive cross-task capabilities.
This study aims to enhance the cross-task generalization ability of massive language models in unsupervised settings, with a focus on models like T0 and FLAN.
We introduce a novel, unsupervised retrieval-augmentation method known as ReCross, which employs unlabeled samples to selectively draw from existing data, fine-tune the model for better performance.
The proposed method seamlessly integrates both high-efficiency dense retrieval and a more effective pair-wise re-ranking process to produce outstanding results, surpassing non-retrieval methods and alternative baselines in our experiments. The code for this approach has been made publicly available.

Optimizing hyperparameters in the private version of the stochastic gradient descent algorithm is a critical issue due to limited access to private datasets for hyperparameter tuning. The development of algorithms that efficiently find optimal hyperparameters for a favorable balance between privacy and performance within a predetermined search space is, therefore, crucial. In this paper, a generalized framework is established to determine an optimal balance between privacy and performance, and three cost-effective algorithms are systematically examined within this framework: evolutionary optimization, Bayesian methods, and reinforcement learning. The results of our experiments, conducted using MNIST and CIFAR-10 datasets for hyperparameter tuning in private deep learning, show significant improvements over the conventional grid search method. The paper addresses existing challenges and potential research directions in the field, and provides an open-source code for hyperparameter tuning in private deep learning. The code can be accessed at this link: https://github.com/zwang84/DP-HPTuning. The paper's contributions are significant due to the following reasons: 1) the paper addresses the issue of hyperparameter tuning in private deep learning, and fills the research gap in this area; 2) the paper provides a feasible and scalable solution for finding a balance between privacy and performance, and shares the code publicly; 3) the paper's results can be applied to a wide range of machine learning models, and contributes to the development of a general framework for hyperparameter tuning in the presence of performance and cost constraints. The paper's limitations are acknowledged by the authors, and more challenging problems are identified, such as hyperparameter tuning in the presence of performance and cost constraints, and the paper that follows provides an algorithmic solution for these constraints, but the authors believe that the paper will still be beneficial due to the limited number of research papers related to hyperparameter tuning in the presence of performance and cost constraints. We applied an advanced statistical approach to examine the composition of 34 binary systems that are likely to produce Type Ia and Type II supernovae. The study focused on measuring elemental abundances of neutron star and carbon-oxygen white dwarf binaries using spectroscopy. A detailed analysis of 7 elements was conducted using a two-component model that accounts for the characteristics of Type Ia and Type II supernovae. The study found significant discrepancies between observed abundances of Type Ia and Type II supernovae and the generally accepted values. However, a comparison with solar abundances revealed similarities, suggesting a possible universal origin of elements, potentially linked to massive binary stars that produce Type II and II+Ia supernovae. The study highlighted the importance of distinguishing between 'prompt' and 'delayed' supernovae components of elemental abundances and presented updated formulas for calculating these components. The findings also implied that Type Ia supernovae are not independent events, but rather a phase of Type II supernovae with delayed neutron star formation. The study further suggested that the distribution of binary masses can be reconstructed from the analysis of white dwarf binaries and that a relationship exists between the minimum initial mass required for binary stars to produce II+Ia supernovae and the minimum mass of neutron stars and white dwarfs. The research yielded a predicted formula for II+Ia supernovae abundance patterns that exhibit a closer match to solar abundances than Type Ia and Type II supernovae alone. The study concluded by highlighting the importance of integrating binary star evolution into supernovae simulations and the potential of white dwarf binaries to discriminate between different supernovae components of elemental abundances. The predicted II+Ia supernovae abundance pattern was compared with data from long gamma-ray bursts and the results suggest that these events are produced by different binary mass distributions. The study also presented an equation to calculate the rate of II+Ia supernovae based on white dwarf binary star masses and luminosities. However, the estimated rate fell short of observed rates of these events, indicating the need for additional II+Ia supernovae progenitor channels. The one studied sample appeared insufficient to draw general conclusions about massive stars, but the study emphasized the significance of examining binary star populations that produce both Type Ia and Type II supernovae jointly. The COVID-19 pandemic spread globally in early 2020 and caused severe consequences in China, also exacerbating public health anxiety fueled by rampant online rumors. To address this pressing issue, we examined the dynamics of rumor propagation and proposed a method to measure the impact of a rumor by tracking the speed of its new adopters. Utilizing search frequency as a proxy for this metric, we identified the peak and attenuation coefficients which conform to an exponential distribution. Subsequently, we developed and evaluated machine learning models, discovering that decision trees effectively forecast the peak coefficient and linear regression accurately predicts the attenuation coefficient. Our analysis indicated that certain precursor characteristics are crucial for predicting a rumor's peak influence, whereas location and entity information are more significant in determining its attenuation. Intriguingly, features that accelerate a rumor's initial spread are often detrimental to its continued dissemination. Moreover, anxiety proved to be a critical factor in promoting the propagation of a rumor. To further minimize forecasting losses, we proposed integrating the BERT model, leveraging deep learning techniques to enhance predictive accuracy. Our research provides a framework for assessing the influence of a rumor and offers policy implications for containing the spread of misleading information by targeting both its initial and secondary propagation stages. To facilitate this, we open-sourced our dataset consisting of 1,344 Chinese rumors during the COVID-19 pandemic, along with corresponding data for search frequency peaks and attenuation coefficients, available at https://github.com/ZhejiangU-NLP/COVID19-Rumor-Propagation. Every day, hospitals around the world gather vast amounts of physiological data from their patients, leading to an escalating interest in conducting statistical analyses to provide better medical diagnoses. The choice of loss function for a neural network is widely regarded as a key decision with far-reaching implications, given the numerous loss functions developed to date, making it crucial to carefully select one. Despite its significance, research on the topic often omits explicit justification for loss function selection. We contend that this lack of justification reflects an untested assumption prevalent within the deep learning community. In this research, we investigate how loss function impacts performance in a supervised classification context. Our findings reveal that certain, previously underappreciated loss functions, including the KL divergence, can yield superior outcomes compared to established methods, underscoring the need to view loss function choice as a parameter amenable to optimization, rather than a fixed constant. To effectively utilize the proposed approach, we provide a user-friendly Python toolkit, `yarrish`, which facilitates effortless integration of our methodology into existing classification workflows. To demonstrate the versatility of our technique, we successfully adapt our model to the challenging unsupervised classification problem of detecting solar storms from satellite data, a task that has not been extensively explored in the literature. Our findings are susceptible to interpretation as evidence of the utility of loss function ensembles in classification tasks, even those that are seemingly unsupervised. This research aims to advance the understanding of thermomechanical behavior in polymer crystallization. Strain-induced crystallization plays a significant role in polymer mechanical and thermal properties and must be accounted for during production and final product application testing. To effectively capture its mechanical and thermal impacts, the proposed model utilizes a unique decomposition approach to the deformation gradient and applies the Coleman--Noll procedure and minimum dissipation potential principle to material modeling. The resulting model includes suitable Helmholtz free energy and dissipation potential assumptions, which enables simulation of crystalline region formation, degradation, and temperature changes during cyclic loading tests. Numerical implementation based on the finite element method provides the basis for numerical solutions, which include simulations of material sample microstructure and temperature evolution. To accommodate large deformation and rotation, the model employs the Euler--Almansi strain measure and the finite strain formulation of the Consiglio--Hulshof return mapping algorithm. The results of this study will be valuable to manufacturers and researchers working with semi-crystalline polymers and seeking to simulate long-term material behavior under various loading conditions. The developed model and numerical solution framework can be applied to a wide range of materials, including but not limited to, polyethylene and polypropylene. The associated code is available online for the community to use, modified as needed to accommodate different material specifications. Continuous phase modulation detection using conventional differential detection techniques is highly resistant to various channel disturbances, such as phase and Doppler shift. Its basic structure makes its implementation uncomplicated, involving the product of a received baseband signal and a time-reversed version of one symbol duration. Nevertheless, it experiences reduced signal-to-noise ratio compared to coherent detection methods. In this research, the performance of conventional differential detection is enhanced through increased delay periods. By accounting for $K$ symbol delays, the trellis structure and relevant branch and cumulative metrics are derived, resulting in an optimized criterion for $K$. This criterion is based on the minimum Euclidean distance between differential signals, ultimately facilitating the selection of ideal delay periods for popular CPM formats through simulated error rates verification. The proposed method enhances BPSK and multiple amplitude CPM system performance, as measured by the required SNR for a specific error rate, by 5 to 12 dB, respectively. The development of a search algorithm for trellis structures is also presented, which can be valuable for other differential detection applications. Portfolio optimization is a critical application in Finance, yet its computational intricacies compel financial institutions to resort to simplified methods that require considerable time. By leveraging the Lagrange multiplier method, the mean-variance portfolio optimization issue can be formulated into a set of linear equations and potentially take advantage of the accelerated performance offered by the HHL quantum algorithm. Nevertheless, certain HHL components are not well-suited for operation on Noisy Intermediate Scale Quantum hardware. This research introduces NISQ-HHL, the first hybrid rendition of HHL that is capable of supporting end-to-end execution of compact-scale portfolio-optimization tasks on NISQ devices. NISQ-HHL enhances the hybrid HHL variation with newly available quantum-hardware capabilities, encompassing mid-circuit measurement, qubit reinitialization and reutilization, and Quantum Conditional Logic. Moreover, NISQ-HHL integrates an enhanced Phase Estimation executed on actual hardware, namely the trapped-ion Quantinuum System Model H1-1, alongside a novel approach to determine the optimal duration of Hamiltonian simulation. This research centers on portfolio optimization but presents solutions applicable to any problem addressed via HHL within the Noisy Intermediate Scale Quantum era. Experimental outcomes, encompassing a 2.7 times speedup over hybrid HHL on a real Noisy Intermediate Scale Quantum hardware, are shown. To enhance data efficiency of state-of-the-art end-to-end ASR models and enable them to handle a large amount of unpaired text data through multi-modal training, it's essential to address two challenges: synchronizing the sampling rates of speech and language features and ensuring that the learned representations from both encoders are consistent. This paper introduces a novel bidirectional attention mechanism that combines the learning of both the ASR and text encoders using a multi-modal learning method. This attention mechanism facilitates the exchange of sampling rates, effectively allowing the quality of transformed features to be measured in an alternative space. This leads to speech representations being enriched with more linguistic information, while the text representations are made more similar to speech, enabling ASR models to effectively leverage unpaired text data for pretraining. Experimental evaluations on the Librispeech corpus reveal a significant 6.15% reduction in word error rate when only paired data is used and up to 9.23% when additional unpaired text data is applied. This paper investigates the long-term behavior of a randomly generated uniform parking distribution of size $n$, denoted as $\pi_n$. We establish that the first $k_n$ positions of $\pi_n$, $\pi_n(1)$ through $\pi_n(k_n)$, are asymptotically independent and identically distributed with a uniform probability distribution over the set $\{1, 2, \dots, n\}$ for two different distance metrics. When the number of initial positions $k_n$ grows at a rate slower than $\sqrt{n}$ for the total variation distance and slower than $n$ for the Kolmogorov distance, this asymptotic behavior is shown, thereby extending previous findings by Diaconis and Hicks. Furthermore, this work also derives rate bounds and statistical limit theorems for the sum or the maximum of the first $k_n$ parking locations. Our main approach to achieving these results is by utilizing conditioned random walk reformulations. The nature of these results is illustrative of the broader applicability of conditioned random walk formulations to other types of combinatorial structures. The associated technical insights are also applicable to other parking function-type problems. The methodology of conditioned random walk also enables the derivation of precise explicit formulas for expected sum and maximum values of $\pi_n(1)$ through $\pi_n(k_n)$. The formula for the expected sum can be further utilized to determine an estimate of the sum's variance. The research in this paper was motivated by an earlier study by Diaconis and Hicks who initially explored random parking functions. The current study builds upon their findings and extends their results. The original study by Diaconis and Hicks consisted of examining specific distances and distances related to permutation statistics in relation to uniform probability distributions. The additional distances examined in the current study include the Kolmogorov distance and other metrics that can be found in the paper. The associated technical proofs are intricate and involve multiple steps, with prior research by Diaconis and Hicks being a necessary foundation. The collective findings from both studies provide a comprehensive understanding of the asymptotic behavior of random parking functions, thereby addressing the research questions initially posed. Airborne transmission risk in confined environments like buses is intricately affected by the interplay between turbulent airflow, respiration processes, coughing, and sneezing, as well as various ventilation methods, temperature-driven buoyancy effects, and surface deposition of aerosols. To better understand and quantify this complex dynamic, we used numerical models of unsteady airflow to analyze and visualize virus-laden aerosol transport. In comparing our detailed model to a widely accepted 'well mixed' model, notable discrepancies in the distribution of aerosol particles became evident, with implications for our understanding of the spread of airborne pathogens. Furthermore, the differences identified in our study are expected to be relevant to a broader range of enclosed settings beyond urban buses. In light of the uncertain factors influencing aerosol transport, we highlight the value of considering the effects of turbulence and buoyancy, as these can be mitigated through adjustments to ventilation methods. In the specific case studied, our findings suggest that buses represent a relatively low-risk environment for airborne transmission, primarily due to the dispersal of aerosols caused by turbulence and ventilation. In contrast, the 'well mixed' model would likely overestimate the transmission risk in such a bus scenario by as much as tenfold. In addition, our analysis highlights the limitations of models that exclude surface deposition, as these models may significantly underestimate the transmission risk in bus environments. In conclusion, our research underscores the significance of considering the complex interplay of factors influencing aerosol transport in confined spaces and highlights the value of using 'well mixed' models with the inclusion of surface deposition in buses. The Spin-Orbit Proximity Effect involves a rise in Spin-Orbit Coupling near a strong spin-orbit material's interface with an adjacent layer. This phenomenon has been observed in various systems, such as graphene and ferromagnetic layers, and controlling Spin-Orbit Coupling may lead to the discovery of novel phases in superconductor and semimetallic systems. In the study presented here, magnetoelectrical transport, specifically magnetoresistance and the anomalous Hall effect, were investigated in Cobalt/Bismuth multilayers in search of Spin-Orbit Proximity Effect and an analysis of its origin. Findings suggest that very thin Cobalt layers exhibit increased Spontaneous Magnetic Anisotropy of Resistivity and Anomalous Hall Resistivity. An examination of Anomalous Hall Resisitivity revealed that the Bismuth layers modify the Hall effect's scattering mechanism to the extrinsic skew-scattering type, suggesting that the spin-orbit proximity effect could result from elastic scattering of Cobalt's free carriers by Bismuth sites at the interface. Additionally, calculations using a modified Jullien model support the observed increase in Spin-Orbit Coupling in the Cobalt layers. This research demonstrated that elastic scattering at an interface can significantly amplify Spin-Orbit Coupling in a layer, and the resulting magnetic anomaly may be versatile enough to inspire new theories about novel phases in materials science. This paper provides approximate solutions to the fractional time-independent Schrödinger equation in $N$-dimensional space for a generalised Mie-type potential, expressed as $V(r^{\alpha})=A/r^{2\alpha} + B/r^{\alpha} + C$, with the fractional parameter $\alpha$ affecting the space variable $r$. As $\alpha$ equals 1, the potential becomes the original Mie-type potential, commonly studied in physics. Using the Jumarie type fractional derivative approach, solutions are obtained and expressed in terms of the Mittag-Leffler function and a fractionally defined confluent hypergeometric function. Verification of results is achieved by comparison with existing works, particularly for $\alpha=1$. Numerical examples, including a diatomic molecule, demonstrate energy eigenvalue and bound state eigenfunction calculations. As $\alpha$ deviates from 1, variations in energy eigenvalues are illustrated. This study also outlines the fractional fractional derivative notation and its distinction from the standard fractional derivative. A brief review of previous research on the Mie-type potential is included. This work is an extension of previous studies on the Kratzer type and Hulthén potentials. Notations and mathematical expressions used in the paper are outlined in the appendices. We analyze how enforcing a neural network's Lipschitz continuity, as it pertains to input sensitivity, affects its performance. In order to investigate this, we developed a straightforward approach to determine the upper bound for a neural network's Lipschitz constant, taking into consideration various $p$-norms commonly used. This approach was utilized to create an efficient algorithm for calculating the optimal hyperparameter for a neural network's Lipschitz constraint, which we incorporated into a training procedure using a data generation method as an additional loss function. Our results demonstrate that by applying this approach, we are able to achieve superior performance on multiple datasets, outperforming a neural network with no constraint and other baselines. Furthermore, our method was successful in generating synthetic data that, when combined with real data, results in improved performance. Our code has been made publicly available. This work has significant implications for the training of neural networks with specific performance guarantees, and it highlights the significance of considering the network's behavior in the input space during training. We hope that our findings will serve as a starting point for the development of training algorithms that prioritize the network's performance in the input space, with a focus on ensuring the existence of a small set of points where the network is highly confident, and we have provided an illustrative example of such a set in the spirit of the work done by Hertzberg and Schoenberga, 2017. We have also developed this concept further and referred to it as the "neural network's core" in our results and subsequent discussion. We have made our code publicly available at https://github.com/Hengtai Zheng/LipNN. We investigate the possibility of lepton-flavour non-universality in certain processes at the Large Hadron Collider (LHC). To this end, we focus on Drell-Yan ditau production and calculate precise corrections to this process, taking into account the effects of quantum chromodynamics at the next-to-leading order. A specialized code is developed to efficiently generate these corrections, allowing for more accurate simulations of ditau events. By applying these simulations to recent LHC data, we can place constraints on a type of exotic particle, known as vector leptoquarks, based on their mass and coupling strength. This code is an important tool for ongoing and future searches for vector leptoquarks, particularly those that prefer lepton-flavour non-universality. This code has been designed to work with popular event generators, making it a valuable asset for ongoing and future research in this field. Radiation exposure during positron emission tomography (PET) scans restricts their usage for sensitive groups, such as pregnant women and young individuals requiring frequent imaging, due to compromised image quality from lower doses or shortened scan times. To address this limitation, a deep learning approach called a neural network-based multiplexing decoder was developed to enhance PET images using additional information from blood PET data. The enhanced PET images showed a significant improvement, with a 2.4-fold increase in standard uptake values (SUV) from lower doses and a 3.5-fold decrease in scan time required to achieve comparable image quality. These PET images were indistinguishable from those obtained at standard doses and durations, according to human observers in a study involving 10 participants. Furthermore, the decoder demonstrated versatility by effectively utilizing different types of additional PET information, such as metabolic and receptor-binding images, to enhance PET images of varying traits and organs. The developed technique has the potential to revolutionize PET scans by allowing frequent imaging without significant radiation exposure. A linguistic analysis known as centering theory (CT) explains how coherence in conversations emerges from the connections between successive statements. This paper explores the link between CT and advanced computer systems that identify relationships within a text. By developing specific metrics and a search-based method, the study examines if modern computer systems that recognize connections within a text align with the principles of CT. The analysis indicates a correlation between the systems' ability to recognize connections and their ability to model the coherence of the text, but also reveals that these computer systems are not necessarily improved by considering the ideas underlying CT. Furthermore, the study finds that these computer systems already incorporate the coherence information required to recognize connections within the text, making CT's contribution limited. Additionally, the study discusses aspects that influence connections within the text but are not accounted for by CT, including the systems' knowledge and their tendency to favor more recent statements. By incorporating these elements, the study presents a revised version of CT and shows that it better captures the connections within the text compared to the original CT. Moreover, the revised CT is more adept at distinguishing words that belong to the same connection from those that do not, outperforming the existing CT by 13%. Furthermore, the study demonstrates that the revised CT can be applied to improve computer systems that recognize connections within the text, leading to an increase of 24% in their accuracy. This version of the paper is an expanded version of the work presented at the 58th Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics, 2020, at the 32nd Conference on Computational Linguistics, 2020, and at the 8th International Conference on Computational semantics, 2020. It has been peer-reviewed as part of the COLING 2022 proceedings. A video summarizing the research is available at https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=aZ2s5s2P1gQ. Recently, WiFi has become the primary method for locating individuals or devices within indoor settings. To facilitate this, WiFi fingerprinting, a technique where reference measurements with known locations are collected and analyzed, has become a standard approach in positioning methods and algorithms discussed in academic literature. However, measuring spatial distances between these collected data sets, also known as WiFi fingerprints, relies heavily on the choice of signal distance metric employed to map signal intensity to geographical distance. To address this issue, the researchers proposed using machine learning to enhance the estimation of geospatial distances between these data sets. To validate the effectiveness of these methods, accurate measurement data was collected across various university settings in South Korea, consisting of over 3000 measurement sets, each containing the MAC addresses, signal intensities, and geographical coordinates of access points. To further ensure the reliability of these results, the researchers performed repeated training and testing of their data using multiple machine learning algorithms, including decision trees, neural networks, and random forests. Ultimately, the most successful algorithm, which combined decision trees and neural networks, demonstrated the ability to accurately predict the geospatial distances between these data sets, with a 95% confidence interval of 1.1 meters. This achievement has significant implications for the future of indoor positioning technologies, given the widespread availability of free machine learning software. To facilitate replication of these results, the researchers have made their data set publicly available online. To further advance these findings, the researchers propose modifying the current algorithm to enable the prediction of geospatial distances from a large, complex university setting to a variety of other indoor settings. To achieve this, the researchers collected and compared the data from two additional university settings in South Korea, consisting of 700 measurement sets each. These results have the potential to contribute to the development of location-based services that are independent of physical environment, as well as provide a data set and machine learning solution that can be useful for other indoor applications involving large amounts of location data.

The beam breakup instability poses a challenge for particle accelerators and typically constrains the maximum beam current that can be achieved, especially for energy recovery linacs with multiple passes where a small amount of charge can generate a large beam current. Studies have highlighted the impact of filling patterns and recirculation schemes on beam and RF system interactions in multi-pass energy recovery linacs. This paper delves deeper into this subject by examining how filling patterns influence beam breakup instability and explores opportunities to optimize design for reduced instability effects. A theoretical beam-RF interaction model along with numerical modeling demonstrates that threshold currents can differ by 2-4 factors or even more, depending on machine design. Consequently, carefully selecting filling patterns can delay the onset of beam breakup, enhancing the potential applications of future energy recovery linacs. Furthermore, this research provides a beam breakup current formula that considers filling patterns and suggests that threshold current can be increased by factors of 2-4 or more, compared to current standards. Given the significant margin for error in both model predictions and actual machine measurements, further study is necessary to fully understand beam-RF interaction dynamics, especially for complex machines with multiple passes. Nonetheless, adopting more stringent design standards as suggested in this paper can facilitate the successful operation of future energy recovery linacs with multi-pass recirculation schemes. The findings presented in this research can be extended to other particle accelerators that involve multiple passes, allowing for a re-examination of existing machines with beam breakup constraints. To extend the BFKL equation to NNLL accuracy, the one-loop CEV for two gluons with low rapidity ordering must be known. In this work, the dispersive part of a one-loop six-gluon amplitude in N=4 SYM theory was calculated under a NMRK kinematic limit and shown to be composed of a two-gluon CEV, allowing extraction of the latter for all helicity configurations. Although this calculation was constrained to the NMRK limit, the resulting two-gluon CEV exhibits significant complexity in both color and kinematic dependence, mirroring characteristics found in general six-gluon amplitude configurations.
