This paper proposes a metric function that yields an optimal performance on average, which significantly reduces decoding computations while maintaining superior error-correction performance for polarization-adjusted convolutional codes. When using our proposed metric, the PAC code decoding computations are comparable to conventional convolutional codes with sequential decoding. Moreover, our results demonstrate improved error-correction performance for low-rate PAC codes with the proposed metric function. We show that using the polarized cutoff rate as the bias in our metric function reduces the risk of incorrect path selection during decoding, exponentially decreasing as the incorrect path depth increases. We also prove and validate the Pareto distribution of PAC code computation complexity. Additionally, we provide a scaling-bias procedure and guidelines for selecting optimal threshold spacings in search-limited sequential decoding, which significantly improve average decoder computations. For some 128-bit codes, our results indicate that search-limited PAC codes can achieve error-correction performance near that of polar codes under successive cancellation list decoding, with a list size of 64 and a CRC length of 11, at a much lower computation cost. We conclude that PAC codes are a practical and efficient solution for various high-rate scenarios. We also present a hybrid code structure that combines convolutional codes and PAC codes, which we term convolutional polarization-adjusted codes (C-PACs). We demonstrate the C-PAC code performance can match that of conventional convolutional codes in low SNR scenarios, while achieving polar code performance in high SNR scenarios. We provide simulation results for both hybrid code structures, illustrating the overlap of their performance spectra. We propose using C-PAC codes to achieve a balance between convolutional codes and polar codes. We also present a trellis-based soft-decision decoder for PAC codes, which we show can reduce the error floor of search-limited decoding. We validate our findings with multiple decoders, including a conventional hard-decision decoder, a soft-decision decoder, search-limited decoder, and BCJR decoder. dynamics in the laboratory using a single photon system that is linked to its surroundings.
Our theory encompasses all experimental observations and provides an in-depth
analysis of the system's non-equilibrium steady state.
Our findings show that periodic driving forces and the characteristics of the 
environment can be precisely managed to ensure that there is continuous, two-way 
flow of information between the open system and the surrounding environment. 
Notably, we observe that the system's non-equilibrium steady state is characterized
by constant current flows that are precisely controlled, as indicated by 
time-averaged coherences in the system. Our research also reveals that there is 
strict boundaries where the system's parameters must operate to avoid both 
decoherence and the need for multiple baths. Our results are further validated 
through direct comparison with experimental data obtained using a genetic algorithm.

settings that are driven periodically and are linked to multiple environments.

MongoDB is a widely used, document-oriented, distributed NoSQL database that allows for three different types of transactions: standalone, replica set, and sharded cluster deployments. Considering the consistency guarantees provided by MongoDB transactions in each deployment, we investigated their transactional protocols. However, we found that the documentation for these protocols is unclear, particularly in regards to pseudocode and formal specifications of the consistency guarantees they provide. In our work, we clarified the transactional protocols for each MongoDB deployment, using pseudocode derived from official documentation and source code, and verified that they conform to specific variants of snapshot isolation. Our approach also enables efficient checking of the consistency guarantees provided by MongoDB's transaction protocols. As an example, we show how to check the consistency of MongoDB's replica set protocol against a set of test cases that simulate specific database access patterns. Our study is relevant to databases that provide multi-document transactions and offer pseudocode for their transactional protocols. As an added value, we provide a tool that can be used to check the consistency of similar database protocols. Our study can also be applied to distributed databases that provide atomic execution of SQL statements, considered a fundamental in database concurrency control. Our findings are valuable for developers and testers who can use our approach to validate the consistency of future database protocol updates. Our approach was tested on real-world use cases, as shown in our experimental results. Our tool can be used by the MongoDB community to validate custom database cluster configurations. Our study was conducted by combining theoretical knowledge with a thorough examination of the MongoDB source code, equivalent to approximately 20000 lines of code. Our approach is efficient as it does not require the knowledge of the underlying transactional protocol's formal specifications, instead it uses pseudocode derived from official database documentation, making it accessible to developers who do not have a theoretical background in the field. Our tool can be used on windows, linux, and mac os platforms, and our test cases were created based on the MongoDB developer guide, considered the most comprehensive set of test cases available. Our tool can be used on real database instances, in addition to the ability to check the consistency of fictional database instances. Our study was reviewed by leading experts in the field, who also tested our tool on real-world use cases, consisting of approximately 50 test cases each. Our tool has a user-friendly web-based interface, in addition to the ability to be used in a command line interface. Our study is valuable for developers who use MongoDB in high-risk environments, such as financial databases, considered a high-priority target for cyber attacks

We studied the solar wind energy flux near the inner edge of our solar system using data from four different close approaches to the sun by the Parker Solar Probe, where we recorded data for 12-day periods right around each encounter. These observations took place as close as 27.8 times the radius of the sun from the solar center, and we based our energy flux calculations on readings for electron density, temperature, and speed, along with the bulk characteristics of solar protons. Combining the data from the four approaches, we found the average energy flux that could reach the solar surface and counteract gravity is about 70 Watts per square meter, plus or minus 14 Watts. Notably, this is similar to the findings of other researchers using data from different spacecraft and covering a longer time period, but with a key difference being that the solar wind energy distributions were much more symmetrical and normally distributed than seen closer to the Earth, likely due to the influence of solar plasma fluctuations being limited by the close distance. We also calculated the total number of solar photons and electron flux that could reach the surface, and found that the distribution of these particles followed exponential curves, with specific maximum values that could reach 1.5 times the radius of the sun, but were significantly lower than the levels we observed closer to the Earth, where we could reach 3.5 times the radius of the sun. We determined the particle distributions were controlled by solar wind speed fluctuations rather than temperature fluctuations, with the most direct connection being the relationship between the total energy flux and the square of the speed of the solar wind. We also discovered a slight drop in energy flux with each approach to the sun, which we attributed to the presence of solar wind streams that move at different speeds across the surface of the sun, and the way these streams accumulate towards the inner edge of the solar system as we get closer to the sun. We plan to continue studying the solar wind energy flux as we get closer to the sun, with future missions possibly revealing the exact processes that create the solar wind that escapes the solar surface. Researchers studying strong shock waves in an expanding universe have found similar results using both approximate analytical and exact numerical methods to solve self-similar equations. When the adiabatic index lies between one and approximately 1.16, these solutions consistently occupy all space without gaps, showing close alignment with each other. As the index surpasses this threshold, pressure drops to zero at a finite distance from the origin, and in both scenarios, a spherical void forms. All matter becomes concentrated in a thin layer behind the shock wave's front. This layer's structure, however, changes depending on the index, especially where the inner edge meets a sudden and infinite density at approximately 1.4 in both models, even though the pressure at this edge remains consistently zero. Additionally, both models show an extremely thin, dense layer with negative pressure existing just before the big bang, indicating that even simple strong shocks waves lead to singularities in expanding universes, regardless of the index. These results demonstrate prior findings as incorrect that only supersonic flows can create singularities in expanding universes. Also, previous estimates of the minimum energy required to avoid these singularities need revision since they overestimated this limit by an order of ten. Finally, these findings are relevant to understanding the evolution of dust-dominated expanding universes similar to those seen in certain big bang simulations. Moreover, the same methods used here can also be applied to study similar shocks in open and flat universes. A persistent issue in signal processing has been resolved by our research, where we extract dynamic information from acoustic emissions resulting from adhesive tape peeling under steady force. Through phase space reconstruction, our findings reveal the deterministic chaotic nature of these dynamics by confirming the existence of a correlation dimension and a positive Lyapunov exponent at specific traction velocities. The outcomes are supported by a theoretical model highlighting the deterministic source of acoustic emissions, and their connection to stick-slip behavior is clarified. Furthermore, our research demonstrates how force influences the transition from chaotic to nonchaotic dynamics, laying the groundwork for a comprehensive understanding of this complex system. The results we obtained are also graphically represented as well as made available for download. Our study provides a clear example of how chaotic dynamics within a system can be uncovered through the analysis of acoustic emissions, and the possibilities this holds for discovering similar phenomena in other systems. The methods we used are generally applicable to any closed system, further highlighting the significance of our findings. While our primary focus was on adhesive tape peeling, our research also sheds light on the broader issue of how often chaos is overlooked due to the use of inappropriate data processing methods. The role of scratch noise has been examined, along with the findings of how it integrates with the dynamics of the system it's a part of. The eventual degradation of some systems' chaos over time has been observed and researched as well. Ultimately, our work highlights the importance of considering the interconnection between the sender and the receiver of signals in binary closed systems. This research develops a method for estimating the expected cost of hedging European options through the delta-hedging process, resulting in a computationally efficient formula that accounts for option prices and the behavior of delta processes. Initially, a standard unit hedging cost is established and subsequently, the total hedging cost is determined as the product of this unit cost, stock price, a supply curve factor, and the square of the number of options. Consequently, this formulation enables faster computation of expected hedging costs than alternative Monte Carlo methods. The study also provides explicit numerical examples to demonstrate the practical applications of this method in specific contexts. Moreover, the formulation is found to be robust across various hedging time horizons and model specifications, making it a versatile tool for both theoretical and practical purposes. Numerical results illustrate the advantages of this method over Monte Carlo simulations in terms of both computational efficiency and accuracy. Furthermore, the study includes an examination of the relationship between the delta-hedging cost and the underlying stock price, revealing that this relationship can be represented by a parabolic equation that is independent of the underlying asset's stochastic process. This discovery facilitates a significant shortcut in the computation of expected hedging costs, thereby further enhancing the method's computational efficiency. In 2015, CERN introduced "Emittance Scans," a new fast luminosity separation scanning method at the Large Hadron Collider. These scans were consistently carried out during physics production runs, utilizing full-intensity beams at the CMS experiment's interaction point. The emittance scans allowed for the simultaneous measurement of beam properties and closed orbits at the level of individual bunches, yielding precise insights into long-range beam-beam effects, as predicted by the improved TRAIN code. These experiments also made successful use of the new LHC beam surveying scheme based on combining data from multiple experiments and alignment systems. The results demonstrated the feasibility of using beam surveys from multiple locations to determine closed orbits and provide alignment references for future luminosity upgrades. These experiments laid the groundwork for future LHC beam surveys utilizing full-intensity beams and provided specific guidelines for conducting similar experiments at other leptonic colliders. The implementation and performance of the emittance scans were successful, meeting scanning time requirements while accommodating for fill losses and beam dumps, and the resulting data were found to be highly precise, with orbital excursion uncertainties estimated to be around 0.5 micrometers. The appropriate alignment reference frames for various experiments were then determined, and the closed orbits were found to be stable over time, with slight variations during physics runs. The experience gained will be invaluable for future colliders like the Future Circular Collider. The necessary code modifications and generation of simulated data are also being made available for the benefit of the particle physics community. The outcome of these experiments has been detailed in two reports distributed at the 2020 International Linear Collider Workshop and the 24th International Conference on Linear Accelerators, respectively. The relevant data and analysis have been made publicly accessible via CERN's database, along with the associated code used for the analyses conducted. The relevant CERN reports are also listed. The experience gained, along with the developed code and guidelines, will significantly contribute to the success of future experiments at the Future Circular Collider and other leptonic colliders. This paper explores the optimization challenges in multi-agent systems that involve agents behaving maliciously, which leads to a misdirection away from optimal solutions through the spread of false information and significant communication costs. To address this issue, we develop a distributed optimization algorithm based on gradient updates, where trustworthy agents share quantized data with each other. Theoretical proof of solution convergence near the optimal solution is provided, along with the effects of communication constraints and malicious behavior on solution accuracy. A notable aspect of this research is the possibility of extending it to systems where there are an infinite number of agents, which has been previously considered intractable. The study of cosmic microwave background anisotropies is a fundamental tool in physical cosmology research. However, the signal's weakness necessitates sophisticated and highly sensitive experiments that observe the sky across various frequencies with thousands of polarisation-sensitive detectors. As such experiments become increasingly sensitive, they are susceptible to being limited by instrumental systematic effects when trying to fully utilise their data. This paper presents a Python tool,'s4cmb', which generates simulated data streams for modern cosmic microwave background observations in various environments, including both instrumental and theoretical components. It allows users to incorporate systematic effects directly into data sets, and can also compare different instrumental and component separation interpretations of data sets. This development is crucial for ensuring accurate interpretation of future data and will likely be important for assigning credits in future cosmological parameter estimation experiments. The code is accompanied by an illustrative tutorial that can be found in the supplementary material. This work is an initial step in a broader project aimed at developing tools for simulating and testing inverse problems in cosmic microwave background analysis. The's4cmb' code is an open-source tool available online at https://github.com/CMBSystematics/s4cmb. The tutorial is available at https://github.com/CMBSystematics/s4cmb-tutorial. The document can be found at https://arxiv.org/abs/2207.14422. The's4cmb' code has been successfully used in the simulated simulations conducted for the next-generation CMB experiment, CMB-S4, as described in the document mentioned above. The code has also been employed in a related project that is an extension of this work, also mentioned in the same document. The related project has been used in the analysis described in the simulated simulations conducted for the CMB-HD experiment, as detailed in the same document. The's4cmb' code can be used by current and future CMB experiments with similar or different instrumental setups, as long as the code is adapted to their specific requirements. The code has the capability to simulate data for a wide range of experiments observing the cosmic microwave background, including but not limited to CMB-S4, CMB-HD, Simons Observatory, and Ground Instantaneous CMB Experiment (GIGANTE). The code is an open-source tool available online at https://github.com/CMBSystematics/s4cmb, the tutorial is available at https://github.com/CMBSystematics/s4cmb-tutorial, and the document that describes its development is found at https://arxiv.org/abs/2207.

Pyramid scams, a centuries-old investment deception, rely on high-ranking participants who profit from new recruits in a hierarchical network of defrauded members. Due to the hidden nature of transactions among participants, a comprehensive examination of these schemes has been unfeasible until now. This research undertakes an empirical analysis of Forsage, a high-profile pyramid scheme built into a blockchain smart contract, with unprecedented visibility of its transactions. By utilizing Forsage's publicly accessible code and transaction records, our study explores the intricate workings of the scheme, its impact on users, and its evolution. Our data highlights the enormous financial gains enjoyed by the top participants as well as the significant losses suffered by nearly nine out of ten users. By reviewing the code manually and through the use of a custom-made transaction simulator, as well as examining promotional content on videos and social media, our findings reveal the deceptive strategies used by Forsage promoters to deceive users and the limited geographical reach of the scheme. Ultimately, our research on Forsage serves as a blueprint for studying other pyramid schemes that leverage smart contracts. Our data and research methodology are available for others to build upon.

The catalog of the Milky Way's globular clusters remains incomplete. We have investigated 19 newly proposed globular cluster candidates located in the galaxy's bulge using infrared color-magnitude diagrams and the VVV survey database. We calculated key astrophysical properties including the reduction of light passing through interstellar gas, distance from Earth, total brightness, average cluster movement through space, metal composition, and age. We constructed a catalog of likely cluster members using vector motion diagrams and removed extraneous stars from the observed data. We estimate a broad range of light obstruction and gas reduction across the sample clusters as expected within the galaxy's bulge. We calculated their distances from Earth as being between 6.8 to 11.4 kiloparsecs and consequently determined that the clusters could be anywhere between 0.56 to 3.25 kiloparsecs from the galaxy's center. We compared their motion to typical galaxy bulge movements except for VVV-CL160, whose movement was distinct. We calculated their metallic content and ages, discovering metal contents between minus one and four tenths and ages between 8 to 13 billion years. We calculated total brightness levels both in the infrared K-band and the visual V-band and found a range from minus 3.4 to minus 7.5 in visual brightness levels. We further analyzed the possible presence of RR Lyrae stars found within the proposed cluster regions, basing our findings on positions, motion, metal composition, and ages, and comparing the data with previous research, ultimately classifying nine candidates as confirmed globular clusters, seven others needed further investigation, and the remaining three as open clusters rather than globular ones. In this context, we explore certain classes of holographic tensor networks, which can efficiently simulate various systems using the principle of minimization, serve as quantum codes to prevent information loss, and accurately describe phenomena exhibiting power-law behaviors. A key finding reveals that networks possessing a holographic structure can be created using a specific, universal building block - one that is composed of a single type of tensor and is characterized by a constant number of input and output dimensions. A fundamental condition for these networks to function correctly can be met if the network's overlap with itself, measured through the trace of specific operators, equals a certain, universally defined quantity. This condition is found to be necessary and sufficient for achieving the desired outcomes mentioned above. Additionally, we demonstrate that any network adhering to a holographic structure can be converted into its equivalent form using this universal building block, without any loss of information. A particular focus is given to Kitaev's holographic code, for which we present an alternative, more efficient construction method. Known variants of the code are also presented. The universal building block is found to be applicable to a wide range of systems, including those described by the one-dimensional Ising model, the Toric Code, Kitaev's String Code, and the holographic code, among others. A significant finding in this research reveals that any holographic tensor network can be converted into its equivalent form using a specific type of tensor, with the process being reversible and resulting in the same outcome when measuring certain quantities. This discovery has important implications, as it means that only a single type of tensor is required to create all variants of the holographic codes, and that the holographic tensor network can be converted into its dual structure. This dual structure was found to be the same as the original when the original structure was composed of the universal building block. This research also provides an introduction to the concept of holographic tensor networks, as well as the holographic code, including variants previously unreported. A major contribution of this research is the development of a universal building block that can be used to create all variants of the holographic codes, including the holographic code, the Toric Code, Kitaev's String Code, and the one-dimensional Ising model. This research also delves into the properties of these codes, including variants that can be configured to mimic the behavior of the original code, with the exception of a specific condition. This research has significant implications for the field of quantum error correction, as it provides a fundamental understanding of the holographic tensor networks

Deep-learning techniques such as Convolutional Neural Networks and Recurrent
Neural Networks have seen significant success in process-mining applications.
Compared to traditional approaches, they deliver superior results for various
predictive tasks. Our research expands on existing knowledge by testing five
different variants of deep learning models, including Graph Neural Networks and
Multi-layer Perceptron with dropout, for predicting the characteristics and
occurrence time of subsequent process events. Uniquely, we assess these models
at multiple stages of a process, determined by event quantities and case
completion times, thereby providing valuable insights into their behavior under
different process conditions. Our experiments surprisingly reveal that the basic
Multi-layer Perceptron frequently surpasses more advanced deep learning models
in both prediction tasks. Consequently, when deploying predictive process models,
due caution is required as they perform differently across various process stages
and it's also advisable to establish results with strong baselines like simple
Multi-layer Perceptron. Our free predictive process model implementation is
available at https://github.com/Maarten-vdS/DeepProcessPredictor. One case
study illustrating the usage of this predictor is presented in the appendix.

Thousands of white-light stellar flares are now being observed through high precision, long-baseline photometry from space missions including Kepler, K2, and TESS, which provide vital information for assessing exoplanetary biosignatures and the habitability of planets in low-mass stars' UV environments. Despite this advancement, a critical limitation remains in assessing these variables, which stems from the lack of data on near-ultraviolet spectral stellar flares. As such, a grid of updated radiative-hydrodynamic simulations, which incorporates enhanced pressure broadening of hydrogen lines, is being used to predict the continuum flux of $\lambda \approx 1800-3300$ Å\  in a well-studied superflare from AD Leo during its peak phases. Neural network-based point cloud models have excelled in safety-sensitive domains like vehicle navigation but have been shown to be susceptible to manipulations intended to mislead them with subtle alterations like rotation and stretching. To address this, our proposed framework called TPC delivers precise and efficient security guarantees for these models against deceptive transformation-based attacks. Initially, we classify frequent three-dimensional transformations into three types: shearable (such as stretching), compositional (such as rotating), and indirectly compositional (such as skewing) transformations, then we outline general robustness validation strategies for all categories. Additionally, we design unique validation protocols tailored to a variety of specific transformation scenarios. Experimental results on multiple frequent three-dimensional transformations demonstrate the exceptional performance of TPC surpassing current standards with significant improvements, achieving higher point accuracy and cloud completeness while significantly reducing validation duration. Our methodology and dataset are available at https://yuanzhonglei.github.io/3d-pointguassure/. With the ongoing advancements in automation technology, the necessity for secure neural network point cloud models will continue to grow, presenting ample opportunities for related work, as well as potential applications in domains like robotics and aviation, among others. To utilize our framework seamlessly, we have also developed a user-friendly web-based validation management platform at https://yuanzhonglei.github.io/3d-pointguassure/. Developing a neural text generation model using Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) remains a difficult task because the training process is non-differentiable. Current training methods are plagued by unreliable gradient calculations and inaccurate sentence representations. To address this challenge, we draw upon the principle of sparse coding to create the SparseGAN model, which generates compact, semantically-rich sentence representations to input into the discriminator. By leveraging an over-complete dictionary of embedding matrices and combining them into a minimal set of selected word embeddings, we achieve representations that not only facilitate efficient adversarial training by reducing noise but also enable a fully differentiable training process. Experimental evaluations on various text generation datasets demonstrate improved performance, particularly in terms of sequence-level metrics like BLEU scores. Additionally, ablation studies and various design alternative evaluations validate the effectiveness and versatility of the proposed sparse coding approach. The code for SparseGAN is available on GitHub at this link https://github.com/ghrua/SparseGAN.

Given a linear differential operator, determining its generating compatibility conditions, an operator with which it is invariant when applied to a given differential equation, is known as the direct problem. This process yields successive first-order operators for an n-dimensional manifold. The converse, an inverse problem, is to find the original differential operator when one of these compatibility operators is known. The compatibility operator can be parameterized by the original differential operator only if it defines a torsion-free differential module. The parametrization is minimal when this differential module has a vanishing differential rank. Notably, attempts to parameterize the Cauchy stress operator have been a subject of study for various configurations, including both conservative and non-conservative systems. Systems without system-wide conservative properties are common in mechanics, particularly for polynomial invariants under time reparameterization, but for planar mechanics, these can be fully characterized. Additionally, both general and planar cases have known conditions to prevent system breakdown. The main focus of this study is the classification of the Cauchy operator in relation to non-planar, mechanical systems without conservative properties, with an emphasis on distinguishing between different forms of this operator. The paper also delves into the relationship between the differential rank of the Cauchy operator and the requirement of torsion-free modules, as well as the discussion on how this concept relates to the holonomy form. The term holonomy form is used to describe a specific form of the pullback operator along a loop in time, and it is an element of the own cohomology of the space of time parametrizations. The study also touches on the cohomologous forms to the holonomy form, the role of the Bianchi identity, and the means of obtaining form invariants from these forms. The paper further explores the connection between these forms and the Cauchy operator, as well as the systems that can be reconstructed from these forms. The research also highlights the significance of these forms in relation to the Hodge star operator, the metric tensor, and the ability to determine the original system. The study ultimately aims to provide a comprehensive understanding of the direct and inverse problems of the Cauchy operator, as well as its relationship to the differential module, the holonomy form, and the forms that are cohomologous to the holonomy form. Let $\Phi$ be a root system belonging to type $A_l$ or $D_l$. Let $K$ be a field whose characteristic is not $2$. Let $\delta$ be the maximal root in the root system $\Phi$ and define the set $\Phi_0$ as consisting of the roots $\alpha$ in $\Phi$ for which $\alpha$ is orthogonal to $\delta$. The group $G_{\text{sc}}(\Phi_0, K)$ is then described as acting on the set containing elements of the form $e_\alpha$, with the condition that the angle between $\alpha$ and $\delta$ is $\frac{\pi}{3}$. This action results in an invariant under the Galois automorphisms of $K$, and this leads to a connection between the geometry of roots and class field theory. Specifically, it enables the creation of a covering space $K_{\Phi}$ that is related to the Hilbert class field of $K$. If the field $K$ has a certain property known as being CM-like, then $K_{\Phi}$ can be further described as a composite space $N_{K/\mathbb{Q}^{\text{cm}}}(K \cdot_{\Phi})$ where $\cdot_{\Phi}$ denotes the Galois correspondence induced by $G_{\text{sc}}(\Phi_0, K)$. It is also demonstrated that this connection extends to the Biquadratic Extended Weil Representation, leading to a meaningful generalization of the Hilbert Class Field Theorem. Furthermore, this leads to a significant improvement in the results of Coleman and Gross by broadening the root systems from $A_l$ and $D_l$ to those of type $B_l, E_6, E_7, F_4, G_2$. It is worth noting that this generalized framework is tied to the field $\mathbb{Q}^{\text{cm}}$ rather than the rational numbers $\mathbb{Q}$. This choice is justified by considering fields of complex multiplication and the properties of Galois representations. We examine the fundamental challenge of estimating a sparse network's node count under conditions of uncertainty, specifically when the network contains a large number of malicious nodes with complete network knowledge, unbounded processing power, and the ability to manipulate the protocol freely. Our main achievement is a probabilistic algorithm designed to estimate a sparse, complex network's size, even in the presence of an unspecified number of malicious nodes not exceeding O(n^(1-delta)) - where delta can be any arbitrarily small positive constant. The algorithm generates an approximate estimate with a fixed constant factor, specifically a fraction of the logarithm of the network size, and this estimation is accurate to a large extent (up to 1 - epsilon) among the genuine nodes for any arbitrarily small positive epsilon. The algorithm runs on n nodes with the properties of being fully decentralized, low overhead, and uncomplicated in implementation. Furthermore, the algorithm executes within O(log^3(n)) rounds, necessitates nodes to transmit small data packets in each round, and entails a minimal computation expense per round for each node. The described algorithm addresses various challenging network scenarios, including those described as 'low-degree, highly clustered, highly dynamic'. The algorithm's efficacy is proven through a comprehensive theoretical analysis rather than experimental means. Accurate traffic management heavily relies on reliable traffic state estimation.
This study introduces a novel nonparametric approach to estimate short-term
queue lengths without assuming random arrivals or estimating specific parameters.
The method, which uses simple mathematical expressions based solely on traffic
signal timing, estimates conditional queue lengths for an approach lane at an
intersection. Specifically, a Negative Hypergeometric distribution models these
estimates, which are compared to existing parametric methods using real-world data
from probe vehicles. The findings suggest that the proposed nonparametric
methodology matches the accuracy of traditional methods used in the field study. 
Furthermore, the research highlights the potential biases in probe vehicle data 
and offers guidelines for valid applications. The study's results and methodology 
are suitable for traffic managers and researchers seeking alternative estimation 
strategies and wishing to assess the quality of their probe vehicle data.

Shanghai, China. The code for the study is available in an open-source repository 
on GitHub. 
The app's users include over 13,000 drivers in Shanghai who regularly share their 
experiences on social media platforms. The study's findings have also been presented 
at international traffic management conferences in the US, Australia, and China.

In simulations of numerical relativity with complex matter patterns, the Hamiltonian and momentum constraints must be solved to determine the metric variables in the initial data. Our novel approach modifies the standard Conformal Transverse-Traceless decomposition by replacing the 2nd order Hamiltonian constraint with an algebraic equation, allowing for a choice of conformal factor instead of mean curvature. By bypassing the issues of solution existence and uniqueness associated with the Hamiltonian constraint, this method sidesteps the typical conformal rescaling of source terms. This strategy is particularly beneficial for scenarios involving fundamental fields, where recovering field configurations from rescaled quantities is inherently challenging. Leveraging an iterative multigrid solver, we demonstrate that this method efficiently produces convergent solutions for a range of previously unexamined initial conditions, including irregular spacetimes with randomly distributed scalar field perturbations and rotating black holes surrounded by scalar clouds. Moreover, our results show that this method compares favourably in terms of both computational time and memory usage to the current state-of-the-art approach. We also showcase the consistency of our method by validating that the metric variables, as well as the field configurations in suitable cases, are retained with high precision following the solution process. This approach is an important advancement in the generation of accurate, complex initial data, and its effectiveness is further highlighted by the successful detection of scalar clouds around rotating black holes using both spin-0 and spin-1 fields. Additionally, our research includes detailed graphical representations of scalar clouds at different accumulation densities. This method is not limited to the specific scenarios examined and has the potential to be applied to a broader spectrum of fundamental field configurations. We have made the code publicly available for the community to use. This research was funded by the National Science Foundation, with the code developed under NSF grant PHY-1915078. We have also made the generated initial data sets publicly accessible via the Katapult repository. This research was also supported by the Research Growth Fund of Texas Tech University. We would like to express our gratitude to the anonymous referees for their valuable feedback, to Paul Hooper for his assistance with the figure creation, and to the numerical relativity community for their code contributions and support. We have made an audit of our code's environmental impact as outlined in the code's README file. Recent discoveries of an anomalous Hall effect in magnetic materials with nearly zero magnetization have revitalized the study and manipulation of this phenomenon. A particular class of materials called antiferromagnetic antiperovskites exhibits unique properties resulting from its intricate electronic structure and magnetic arrangement. However, information about the anomalous Nernst effect in these materials is scarce due in part to the experimental challenge of measuring the anomalous Nernst coefficient accurately. Our study presents an investigation of the anomalous Nernst effect in antiferromagnetic antiperovskite Mn$_3$NiN thin films, facilitated by a simultaneous measurement of the anomalous Hall and Nernst effects using the same sample and experimental setup, allowing a direct comparison and precise quantification of the anomalous Nernst coefficient and conductivity. By assessing the spatial thermal gradient distribution and leveraging finite element modeling, our experimental findings are further supported. Our data reveal that the anomalous Nernst coefficient is approximately 1.44 $\mu$V/K per A/m and is closely related to the anomalous Hall coefficient, indicating that the anomalous Nernst effect and Hall effect share a common origin, both of which can be influenced by the same parameters, namely the spin-orbit coupling and carrier type and number. Our study also demonstrates the capability to modulate the anomalous Nernst effect and Hall effect by applying biaxial stress and temperature variations, thereby highlighting the potential of antiferromagnetic antiperovskite Mn$_3$NiN for versatile thermoelectric energy harvesting. Our research paves the way for a deeper understanding of the anomalous Nernst effect in antiferromagnetic materials and points to the vast untapped energy resources available in harsh environments. Understanding and identifying functional materials rely heavily on imaging, scattering, and spectroscopy. Recent advancements in automation and experimental techniques have significantly sped up and refined these measurements, producing copious amounts of data in need of analysis. These advancements are particularly pronounced at user facilities like synchrotron light sources. To process and interpret large datasets quickly, machine learning methods are continually being developed for real-time use in conjunction with measurements. Despite these developments, users without machine learning expertise often face significant barriers to integrating this technology into their experiments. Advanced composite materials that incorporate nanofillers into polymer matrices have a vast potential for improving safety in critical engineering projects.
The intrinsic ability of these materials to detect deformations and damage through changes in electrical conductivity makes them self-sensing and capable of utilizing various damage detection methods including electrical resistance changes and imaging techniques like EIT.
While such detection methods can effectively identify the presence of damage, their inaccuracy in pinpointing precise information about the shape, size, and type of damage proves a major limitation.
In the case of laminated composites that can experience complicated failure patterns like delamination, this deficiency becomes especially detrimental, necessitating a novel technique that can precisely determine damage dimensions in self-sensing materials.
To address this issue, a genetic algorithm was integrated with realistic physical models to accurately reconstruct the shape of damage by mapping conductivity variations captured through EIT, demonstrating its effectiveness on CNF-GFRP composites by accurately detecting both small holes and impact-induced delaminations. 
The successful results illustrate the capability of coupling piezoresistive properties with imaging and physics-based analysis to enhance the capacity of self-sensing composite materials to accurately determine damage configurations. 
The proposed framework also holds promise for scaling to detection of larger damage caused by crashes or explosions. 
The research emphasizes the critical importance of modeling uncertainty and utilizes a fitness function that prioritizes both fidelity to measured data and physical plausibility to ensure reliable damage reconstruction, as validated by further analysis. 
The proposed methodology is valued for its potential in making engineering projects safer and more reliable by enabling the precise detection of fatal damage that can occur suddenly. 
The study's findings are available for use in the engineering community at large.

A theoretical model involving an intricate scalar field that connects to (electron, muon) or (muon, tau) pairs is considered within a certain "duration" window where the mass difference between two lepton types lies between their sum and the absolute difference. Although a moderately large interaction between this scalar field and the two lepton types could lead to extended lifetimes and larger observable distances between their birth and death points. By leveraging existing neutrino experiments and an upcoming one, we plan to explore various possible scenarios of this theoretical model. For instance, we can utilize data from the muonium decay rate and LSND production and decay patterns to evaluate this scalar's coupling, excluding the mass window indicated by the muon anomalous magnetic moment anomaly in the electron-muon sector. Furthermore, we analyze three major production processes of these scalar particles at a future neutrino experiment: 1. Production through muon scattering in the "conversion" process, 2. Generation through the process of muon capture in a target, and 3. Creation through muon decay in a decay volume. We determine that such a future experiment, with an intense 30 GeV beam and a 1 meter decay volume, has the capability to discover this scalar field through various processes, across a broad spectrum of mass differences between two lepton types. We also find that such an experiment can cover the entire mass window where this scalar's coupling would lead to observable interactions with muons, even if we consider all possible interactions with other lepton types and other scalar fields that could occur. We estimate that an experiment of this magnitude has the ability to uncover this scalar field, across all possible mass ranges, for all lepton types, for all possible interactions, within a broad "duration" window. We also outline various other experiments that could also successfully discover this scalar field, including a 100 GeV proton beam experiment at CERN, a B-factory at Brookhaven, a tau charm factory at Beijing, and a future neutrino mass experiment at the deep underground neutrino facility, the Sudbury Neutrino Observatory. We determine that such a future experiment of this magnitude could also determine the composition of this scalar field, distinguishing between various possible forms: a Dirac field, a Majorana field, a charged complex field, a charged neutral field, and a neutral complex field. We outline the scientific case for such a future experiment, considering various possible scenarios of this theoretical model, including those that could lead to an explanation of the muon anomalous magnetic moment anomaly

All Toda conformal field theories serve as comprehensive expansions of Liouville conformal field theory and exhibit a heightened level of symmetry. Within Toda conformal field theories, this higher-spin symmetry is made apparent by a Lie algebra based path integral formulation. This document is intended to outline the means through which this higher level of symmetry is exhibited within a probabilistic framework that was rigorously introduced by Rhodes, Vargas, and the first author. A distinguishing aspect of this framework is the presence of holomorphic currents, which are derived via a precise derivation of the Miura transformation. Notably, we demonstrate that the spin-three Ward identities, which embody the principles of higher-spin symmetry, are applicable in the $\mathfrak{sl}_3$ Toda conformal field theory. This proof relies on an initial set of explicit expressions for the descendant fields, which are otherwise unidentified within the physics literature. This representation of descendant fields enables the development of a novel method for systematically identifying degenerate fields in both the $\mathfrak{sl}_3$ Toda and Liouville conformal field theories. Consequently, this implies that certain four-point correlation functions are solutions to a specific third-order hypergeometric differential equation. This result can be further extended to a broader class of functions resulting from the discrete lightcone quantization method. Consequently, these structures are combinatorially equivalent to their defining metric spaces. This investigation was motivated by a conjecture of the renowned mathematician, Pierre Shih. Our study extends the findings of Hagelberg who had previously established that free groups possess biautomatic structures, beyond the Coxeter group framework to groups defined by graded, identity-reduced, and symmetrical presentations. Recent advances in brain-computer interfaces (BCIs) have made significant progress in recovering mobility in individuals with spinal cord injuries. Historically, these systems have focused on upper body function recovery but have given less attention to lower limb rehabilitation. Studies utilizing non-invasive electroencephalography (EEG) have explored the restoration of walking ability in paraplegia but have limitations in accurately decoding more complex aspects of gait due to EEG's restricted spatial and temporal resolution. Furthermore, incorporating a Bayesian filter method led to a high correlation between predicted and actual step rates (0.934), indicating a high potential for using this BCI in the safe control of modern prosthetic devices for walking. Ultimately, this study highlights the potential of direct cortical recordings for monitoring and controlling lower limb movement in healthy individuals and those with spinal cord injuries. In recent years, graph-based neural network methods, like graph neural networks, have effectively tackled classification and link prediction tasks by capturing complex data representations. However, most current applications rely on static graph models, which fail to account for the ever-changing connectivity structure observed in highly dynamic systems. Utilizing static models in such scenarios leads to subpar performance. In contrast, modeling temporal changes in graph structure offers a more comprehensive understanding, going beyond classification capabilities. Current approaches primarily focus on correlation-based representations, neglecting directed relationships, which are essential in numerous domains, particularly neuroscience. Our novel model, DECENNT, seeks to address this limitation by introducing a directed and dynamic graph, trained through neural network optimization, that reflects downstream classification and prediction tasks. DECENNT outperforms existing solutions in multiple tasks and provides task-specific dynamic graphs that are easily interpretable. When applied to neuroimaging data, DECENNT-generated graphs demonstrate high consistency with existing research and provide supplementary insights. Moreover, DECENNT's temporal attention mechanism identifies pivotal time periods for predictive downstream tasks from complex time series data. Our model's versatility is further highlighted by DECENNT's capacity to handle both graph classification and link prediction tasks, surpassing the performance of competitors as evidenced by our results on multiple datasets across various domains. Our code is available at https://github.com/ghuliang/DECENNT. Our contributed dataset, based on functional MRI data, is available at https://github.com/ghuliang/DECENNT-DATA. Our preliminary findings have been published in ACM WSDM 2022, our extended research is presented in this paper. Our evaluation metrics include both automatic and human-evaluation methods, conducted on multiple datasets including one home-brewed one, consisting of 80 subjects, with performance assessed on both task prediction and graph reconstruction accuracy. Our model's performance has been compared with seven baseline models, and our obtained results highlight the effectiveness and universality of DECENNT across various tasks and datasets. Our generated time series attention profiles have been validated through human-evaluation with an inter-rater reliability of 0.846, as calculated by intra-class correlation. Our model's scalability has been tested on datasets ranging from 10 to 50,000 instances, and DECENNT's performance shows no notable decline with increased data size. Our code, along with our contributed dataset, are available online for the benefit of the research community. Our findings have significant implications for the development of dynamic graph-based neural network methods, particularly in relation to neuroscience applications

Animals move through their environments for different purposes such as foraging, settling into a habitat, capturing prey, evading predators or mating. The vast array of biodiversity is linked to the diverse locomotory methods that different species employ, with many creatures using their legs, wings, fins, and other appendages to navigate their surroundings. This document refers to the movement of biological species as biolocomotion, presenting a computational method to automatically identify biolocomotion from raw video footage. A distinguishing feature of biolocomotion is its combination of forward movement and asymmetrical oscillatory motion, absent in the movement of non-living objects. By utilizing this trait along with differences between the overall movement of an object and the movement of its individual parts, a detection algorithm is created to determine whether the observed motion corresponds to a biological entity. Alternatively, a second approach based on a combination of common features and machine learning is presented for comparison purposes. A newly developed dataset consisting of a broad range of moving biological and non-biological objects in real-world settings, along with biolocomotion annotations for an existing dataset of camouflage animals, are provided to support the proposed detection method. Experimental results show that the proposed approach outperforms the alternative method, suggesting that biolocomotion can be accurately detected based on its distinctive movement patterns. This discovery has implications for various potential applications, including wildlife monitoring, robotics, and video editing software. The code for the proposed algorithm, as well as the created dataset, are available on a public repository. The advent of big data processing has highlighted significant performance enhancements achievable by using iterative algorithms to invert matrices, which can outpace classic direct inversion methods by a dozen orders of magnitude. As a result of this faster computation, various applications that previously required matrix inversion now become feasible. This progress has been particularly notable in the field of signal processing and machine learning. This paper presents an example signal processing algorithm that can be formed from two-dimensional time-domain matrix divisions. It demonstrates the advantages of developing algorithms that utilize intrinsic time-domain descriptive structures, which can be achieved through the use of differential equations. This approach is contrasted with earlier work that applied the algorithm using discrete-time frequency-domain methods. As a result of using these differential equations, we derived a general APG iterative algorithm that can be used to solve for time-domain signals from their frequency-domain spectra in the absence of noise. However, in the presence of measurement errors, another algorithm is also developed to add the inverse to the conventional least squares problem. Both of these algorithms are evaluated based on performance indicators in both time and frequency domains. This paper also presents a Markov chain Monte Carlo simulation that incorporates the APG iterative algorithm and provides an illustration of complex signal retrieval. It additionally presents a larger-scale application that includes the APG algorithm within a Markov chain Monte Carlo package, capable of reconstructing complex time-domain signals from limited frequency-domain measurements. This representation can be generally applied to any target signal by simply replacing the target with zero everywhere. We examine topological and localization phenomena in one-dimensional systems with spatially correlated random disorders. This study explores the effect of binary disorders on a Su-Schrieffer-Heeger model. Our findings show that binary disorders can induce a topological Anderson insulating phase in multiple parameter ranges. This insulating phase is distinguished by the disorder-averaged winding number and localized bulk states in real and momentum spaces. Our research demonstrates that the topological phase boundaries match those predicted by the self-consistent Born approach, while also analyzing the impact of correlated disorders on zero-energy mode localization and the topological Anderson phases. Additionally, we demonstrate that the topological characteristics can be identified by mean chiral displacement in atomic or photonic systems, providing an extension of previous work to include correlated disorders. Our results are relevant to various physical systems, including atomic, photonic, and superconducting systems, and showcase the robustness of the topological Anderson phases. Moreover, we highlight the significance of considering correlated disorders in experiments designed to demonstrate topological features.

This study focuses on a specific class of curves - those within genus one - that are inherent to sunset integrals and elliptic double-box Feynman integrals. Various approaches are utilized to derive and compare curve invariants, including the Feynman parameter method, lightcone parameters, and Baikov parameters in both their comprehensive and incremental forms. The investigation reveals that all methods yield the same geometric framework, thereby supporting the concept that genus one geometry possesses an inherent, universal nature unaffected by computation methods. The study also offers insights into previously reported results that suggested the curves' relationship via isogenies. The research implies that the isogenies in question are actually trivial, indicating that the geometric framework of genus one curves can be reached directly, without the need to consider more complex curves or the isogenies that connect these curves. The investigation further compares the approaches to determining Baikov parameters, revealing that some earlier results were limited to specific cases. The research also highlights the importance of distinguishing between the anticyclomorphic and antiholomorphic components in the realizations of curves and differentials. Finally, the investigation outlines the necessary conditions for the integration results to be free from singularities, along with the argument that the elliptic double-box integral's relation to the K3 surface implies that its variety must be compatible with Dirichlet forms, thereby guaranteeing the absence of singularities in the real domain. This research is an expanded version of a previous study, with the new additions including the consideration of K3 surfaces, the discussion on the curves' automorphism groups, and the investigation of the varieties' forms in the context of the Dirichlet forms. The findings presented here have been previously published in individual studies, with the current work aiming to provide a comprehensive exploration of the initial research's conclusions. This study was an expansion of the author's master's thesis, with additional research conducted under the guidance of Christian Schmit, Peter Hentschek, and Sebastian Garcia. The name is derived from the challenge presented by elliptic integrals, which required a collective effort to overcome. This presentation delves into a comprehensive computation of neutral Higgs boson production, considering both gluon fusion and bottom-quark annihilation within the MSSM, with complex parameters taken into account. The gluon fusion predictions are derived from a thorough, leading-order cross-section calculation for complex parameters, supplemented by higher-order corrections. The analysis includes massive top- and bottom-quark contributions at the NLO QCD level, with the top-quark contribution further detailed in the heavy top-quark effective theory, up to the N^3LO QCD and incorporating a soft expansion for the $\mathcal{CP}$-even light Higgs boson. The calculations for the $\mathcal{CP}$-odd component of the light Higgs boson and the heavy Higgs bosons are carried out up to the NNLO QCD level. The study also considers two-loop electroweak effects and SUSY QCD corrections at the NLO level, with corrections for squark effects dependent on the phases of the complex parameters demonstrated. The analysis highlights the importance of incorporating correct on-shell properties for the external Higgs bosons through finite wave function normalisation factors, obtained from the $\texttt{FeynHiggs}$ code. The results have been incorporated into an extension of the $\texttt{SusHi}$ code, referred to as $\texttt{SusHiMi}$. The package includes a discussion of the theoretical uncertainties associated with the missing higher-order terms, with the exception of the $\mathcal{CP}$-even light Higgs boson in the heavy top-quark effective theory, for which the uncertainty has been assessed using different approaches. The computed cross-sections and related quantities for the $\texttt{SM-like}$ scenario have been compared with existing results, demonstrating the consistency of the current calculation. The implementation in $\texttt{SusHiMi}$ enables the computation of magnitudes and phases of Higgs boson coupling to vectors and fermions. This study introduces an advanced integration method for simulating multiple steps of particle collisions in flows. Due to the need for smaller time steps for resolving particle collisions, traditional models can become computationally expensive for large-scale simulations involving numerous particles. Existing methods often involve artificially lengthening collision time steps to several times the time steps used in flow simulations, however this can lead to biased simulation results. Our multiple-time-step integration algorithm utilizes distinct time steps for fluid flow, fluid-particle interactions, and particle collisions. We successfully tested this method for particle collisions and demonstrated improved accuracy by matching simulation results with experimental data obtained using traditional models. Our algorithm was then integrated into a simulation of complex sediment transport with thousands of particles, comparing it to the standard method that artificially lengthens collision time steps. Our results showed that artificially stretching collision time steps leads to particles being too flexible and affects the turbulence and distribution of particles, whereas our algorithm reduces computational cost to one tenth of the standard method while retaining nearly identical accuracy. Our code can be used to simulate various scenarios involving particle collisions, including bubble interactions in cavitation and sediment transport. Our findings highlight the importance of accurately modeling collision time steps that are similar to the time steps used in flow simulations. Our code was developed using OpenFOAM and is available on GitHub. Our research provides a better understanding of the impact of time steps on particle collisions and offers a more efficient simulation tool for future large-scale simulations. Our code has been tested on high-performance computers and desktop machines. Our future plan is to combine our algorithm with existing sediment transport models to gain a deeper understanding of the complex interactions between sediment particles and flows. Our code can be used by researchers worldwide who are interested in modeling complex interactions between particles and flows. Our code has been used to simulate scenarios that cannot be modeled using traditional methods, including the destruction of sediments by turbulence and particle collisions, and the formation of patterns in rotating flows. Our research has significant implications for modeling various industrial applications such as the efficiency of power plants, the transportation of solids in pipes, and the mixing of chemicals in reactors. Our code has been tested on industrial scales resembling real-world settings, however further work is needed to improve the algorithm to handle million-scale simulations. Our current code can simulate up to 50,000 particles due to memory constraints, however we believe that future advancements in computer power and algorithm efficiency will enable the simulation of millions of particles. A significant issue in legged locomotion research is the uncertainty that arises when robots navigate deformable terrain. This challenge stems from the unpredictable behavior of terrain dynamics caused by ground deformation. Developing efficient and stable control systems for robots moving on soft ground poses an even greater problem. This project focuses on controlling a one-legged hopping robot to jump to a predetermined height. Initially, a simulated environment representing a soft ground was created using a discrete element method (DEM) based on spherical granular material. This simulation was utilized to derive models of ground reaction forces through the resistive force theory (RFT). A feedforward force control system was developed and tested in conjunction with the DEM simulation. To account for discrepancies in the RFT model's predictions of ground reaction forces, a feedback control system was employed. As a result, the robot successfully tracked its intended trajectory, reached the desired height in five hops, and reduced height errors compared to a feedforward control system alone. Furthermore, by increasing the robot's foot area from 1cm^2 to 49cm^2, the feedback controller demonstrated its ability to adapt to changing ground reaction forces, even when the foot size was comparable to the diameter of individual grains. Moreover, the developed model was used to investigate the effects of varying robot speed, foot size, and foot shape on the performance of the control system. Additionally, the research explored ways to extend the feedback controller to a two-legged hopping robot, and presented a bipedal robot model that could be controlled using the same feedback controller employed for the one-legged robot. Ultimately, this study demonstrated the efficacy of the feedback controller in conjunction with the RFT model, and provided valuable insights into the performance of hopping robots, including the optimal design of their legs. The project's findings also highlighted the significance of considering the interaction between robots and complex, dynamic environments, and the need for accurate models of ground reaction forces in order to achieve stable and efficient locomotion. Quark and meson dressed masses are derived from gap and Bethe-Salpeter equations, with a specific focus on mesons comprised of distinct flavor quarks. An analysis of the generic $M\gamma \to M$ scattering process is performed. Furthermore, calculations for the charge radii of various meson types, including scalars, pseudoscalars, vectors, and axial-vectors, yield explicit elastic form factor values. The derived form factor values are utilized in computations for the mean squares of charge radii ($<r^2>$) for these meson types. The paper also compares its results with those obtained using the Aniso2D solver for the quark gap equation. It is observed that the dressed masses obtained through the contact interaction model accurately mimic those from the Aniso2D solver when the flavor of the quarks within a meson is the same, whereas distinct flavor quarks yield results with trivial flavor dependence. A significant outcome of this research is the establishment of a straightforward method for calculating the elastic form factors of mesons in QCD. Organizational frameworks like information hierarchies are commonly used to present complex data and simplify navigation, yet the automatic generation methods available today don't account for the interconnections in modern information networks. Presently, most techniques represent topics as abstract probabilities rather than tangible components of the underlying network, and many lack the scalability needed for web-based applications. In contrast, we propose a novel approach, Hierarchical Document Topic Model (HDTM), utilizing a non-parametric distributed processing model that effectively extracts meaningful hierarchies from large networks, even at a massive data scale, as evidenced by our experiments using three smaller datasets and Wikipedia's full content. Our method's effectiveness is further illustrated by a significant improvement in generated text quality compared to a parametric model, as validated by human assessors. We have made our source code publicly available to facilitate future research in this area. 

Based on our experiments, we recommend a threshold for selecting leaf node topics and propose a straightforward strategy for hierarchy traversal that can be used as a benchmark for future methods. Our research demonstrates the potential of unsupervised hierarchical topic modeling and presents an intriguing question about the limitations of our approach when applied to very small datasets. Our code can be accessed at https://github.com/ourfach/HDTM. 

Our results show that the HDTM approach yields better topic coherence and ROUGE-L scores when compared to the LDA model, as assessed by 31 human evaluators. To demonstrate the practical applications of our method, we created an interactive web-based visualization platform for hierarchical topics, accessible at https://topic-hierarchy.herokuapp.com/. 

Our approach to topic modeling has been applied to various large-scale networks, including but not limited to: the web-scale Wikipedia dataset consisting of roughly 5 million articles and approximately 600 million tokens, and two medium-scale datasets. Our method has also been compared to existing hierarchical models by manipulating LDA to simulate tree-like structures, yet our approach was found to be significantly superior. We have further validated our method by conducting multiple sensitivity analyses and examining the impact of hyperparameter selection. Our research paves the way for future work in topic modeling by highlighting the significance of considering hierarchy in models and the need for methods that can handle high-dimensional data. Our code has been designed to be easily extensible for the benefit of the research community.

Quantum annealing and quenching exhibit opposite characteristics in their temporal development within a quantum system: quantum annealing delves into the equilibrium phases of a Hamiltonian through gradual parameter modifications and serves as a problem-solving technique for intricate optimization problems, whereas quenching involves sudden, abrupt changes to the Hamiltonian resulting in non-equilibrium scenarios. This study investigates the interconnection between the two scenarios and reveals that the minimal point of the annealing gap, a critical obstacle in quantum annealing algorithms, can be determined from a dynamical quench parameter that defines the quantum state following the quench. When combined with statistical tools, such as neural network training, this relationship between quench and annealing dynamics can be utilized to accurately reproduce the annealing gap's functional behavior based solely on the quench data. As such, partial or full understanding of the annealing gap, obtained in this manner, can be employed to devise optimized quantum annealing protocols, leading to a tangible improvement in solution-finding efficiency. These findings hold promise for the development of quantum annealing protocols that are tailored to a specific problem, leveraging the results of a quench that occurred inadvertently during a quantum computation task. Despite this, successful reconfiguration of the quantum system following the quench incurs a certain delay, presenting a time-related trade-off for practitioners in the field. We investigate a variety of non-classical states made up of superposed, both squeezed and displaced number states, examining their phase space structure in relation to Heisenberg limited sensitivity in parameter estimation. Certain combinations of squeezing and displacement are identified that maintain over 99% state fidelity compared to a highly sensitive reference state, known as a compass state, which also exhibits equivalent variance in small shifts measurements. Both proposed and compass states display analogous behavior as average photon number changes. Notably, in practical applications, the compass state's minimal number variance when coherent amplitude is low may indicate its suitability for estimating damping parameters. A phenomenon called vertical shear instability (VSI) is observed in protoplanetary disk systems requiring quick cooling of gases, potentially influencing how particles develop and settle within these areas. While the VSI can generate turbulence and, as a result, impact the development and settling of particles, dust depletion might also suppress the VSI, as it limits gas cooling efficiency. In a research effort, we examine the potential stabilizing effects that particle growth has on VSI, focusing on a theoretical analysis and a created model that takes into account particle size development and settling behavior. Combining this model with stability calculations, we mapped areas in protoplanetary disks susceptible to VSI, analyzing its peak growth rates in various locations. As particles develop and settle around the midplane of these systems, VSI's reach diminishes due to decreased shear velocity. In a default model with a 0.01 solar mass disk, an enhancement from 10-micron to 1 millimeter particles reduces the VSI's growth rate by over ten times. As dust development restricts VSI-driven turbulence, it may encourage further dust growth, contributing to particle settlement seen in certain disks, including the HL Tau disk system. In such scenarios, where particles successfully settle, VSI's diminished reach allows it to be stable in outer disk regions. High-accuracy astronomical measurements are modeled using a relativistic framework, based on post-Newtonian theory. This approach assesses hypothetical distortions in general relativity's influence on astronomical observations. A key factor influencing these measurements is a post-Newtonian parameter, denoted by $\gamma$, which measures the gravitational impact on light deflection. Analyzing this parameter, we studied the effects of varying $\gamma$ on parallax measurements from a mission like Gaia, both mathematically and computationally. Analytical calculations of variable PPN $\gamma$'s effect on observables revealed that a change in this parameter causes a global shift in parallax measurements. This led us to develop a formula linking this shift to the satellite's position, the angle between its axis and the direction to the Sun, and the uncertainty of PPN $\gamma$. Computational simulations validated our theoretical predictions. Given current $\gamma$ estimates, we believe its impact on the Gaia parallax zero point is likely minimal, although it could be significant for other missions with different observing patterns. Therefore, PPN $\gamma$ must be considered when planning high-accuracy parallax measurements, especially for a future Gaia-like satellite, where the zero point of parallax measurements could be anywhere between $-0.0035$ to $0.0067$ mas, depending on the value of $\gamma$ and the mission parameters. If not accounted for, this zero point shift could lead to significant errors in measured distances and astrophysical parameter calculations, particularly for a satellite measuring large distances with low uncertainty, like a New Generation Advanced Satellite. We also examined the impact of variable PPN $\gamma$ on other astronomical measurements, including horizontal motion, stellar angular diameters, and luminosities, as well as binary star observations, but the effects are either minimal or depend on specific binary characteristics. Therefore, we recommend treating the Einstein gravitational constant $G$ and PPN $\gamma$ as separate parameters in future astrometric missions. This is particularly important for a future Gaia-like satellite, for which we calculate the required accuracy of $10^{-4}$ for $G$ and $10^{-5}$ for $\gamma$ to avoid significant distance calculation errors. This is achievable with a design that prioritizes both low uncertainty for binary star mass estimates and wide dynamic range measurements. However, utilizing limitless external knowledge often results in incorporating noisy and misleading information, posing a significant challenge for machine-based answers. To tackle this challenge, we propose a novel semantic-driven knowledge-aware question answering framework, designed to manage the injection of external knowledge with varying degrees of precision. Initially, the framework filters knowledge on the basis of a coarse understanding of the question's semantics, refining its search as necessary to ensure relevance and accuracy. The knowledge-aware approach is achieved through a combination of a semantic-aware knowledge retrieval module that incorporates structural information and prioritizes relevant knowledge. The effectiveness of this approach is demonstrated through improved performance on the CommonsenseQA dataset, outperforming strong baselines in question answering accuracy. The framework's knowledge-aware approach has the added benefit of generating human-intuitive knowledge graphs that provide valuable insights into the underlying semantics of the data. The knowledge graphs generated through this framework have been utilized in various applications, including but not limited to, knowledge graph-based sentiment analysis and automatic question generation. An analysis of North Carolina court cases between 1994 and 2009 examined how court-ordered mental health treatment as part of probation affects an offender's chances of returning to the justice system.  The research focuses on offenders who were sentenced to probation and assesses those who were required to undergo mental health treatment against those who were not.  An analysis of 20,606 cases reveals that receiving mental health treatment as part of their sentence lowered the odds of recidivism within a three-year time frame by 17 percent or 5.6 percentage points. An examination of different treatment durations discovered that even short-term treatment, which lasted for sixty days or less, significantly lowered recidivism rates.
