A pervasive issue in medical image segmentation tasks is the lack of detailed pixel-level annotation. This paper introduces a new regularization technique, combining interpolation methods to enhance semi-supervised medical image segmentation. The proposed strategy uses consistency regularization to ensure the segmentation of mixed data matches the mixed segmentations. This approach belongs to the category of adaptive data regularization techniques that reduce overfitting when working with highly confident labelled data. The method has several advantages over alternative techniques such as adversarial and generative models, primarily due to its minimal computational requirements. Evaluations using publicly available MRI datasets - specifically ACDC and MMWHS - demonstrate that this proposed technique outperforms existing semi-supervised models, with source code available on GitHub.

Knowledge tracing has seen significant advancements through deep learning-based models, however the underlying factors behind their success remain poorly understood. A primary challenge lies in comparing these approaches, due to the lack of standardization in data preprocessing procedures and evaluation protocols. These inconsistencies hinder real-world applicability in educational settings. To address these limitations, we present PyKT, a comprehensive Python-based platform for valid and standardized evaluations across various deep learning knowledge tracing methods. This benchmark platform incorporates a unified data preprocessing protocol across 7 diverse datasets and integrates 10 leading deep learning knowledge tracing model implementations, enabling transparent and reproducible experiments. Empirical studies conducted on PyKT highlight critical findings, including the risk of performance inflation caused by label leakage in certain evaluation settings, and the limited improvement achieved by several deep learning knowledge tracing models when compared to the initial approach proposed by Piech et al. Numerical experiments confirm the practical benefits of this resilience, showcasing the FedBuff framework's ability to handle complex, real-world learning scenarios. Our novel TD learning approach overcomes several challenges robots encounter when navigating underwater.  By leveraging Gaussian Process regression, our method significantly boosts data efficiency by limiting TD updates.  To facilitate online predictions, we developed a new sparse approximation technique with enhanced performance compared to current rejection-based methods.  By deriving the posterior of the value function and utilizing its moments, we developed SPGP-SARSA: a new algorithm for offline policy evaluation.  Our results show that SPGP-SARSA outperforms the existing state-of-the-art in sparse methods and matches the accuracy of its precise equivalent while successfully being applied to underwater navigation.  Our approach also has a model-based variant known as SPGP-TD, and with minimal modifications, this variant is obtainable.  Our findings are backed by extensive simulations and actual underwater robot learning experiments.  The code for our algorithm is available at https://github.com/HaithamAl-Awadhi/SPGP-SARSA.  With some modifications, the code for SPGP-TD can be found at https://github.com/HaithamAl-Awadhi/SPGP-TD. Most current sequence-to-sequence based Grammatical Error Correction methods focus primarily on generating more pseudo data to improve performance. In contrast, little work addresses the challenge of adapting GEC to new domains with limited resources. This paper treats various GEC domains as separate tasks and proposes a novel approach, grounded in meta-learning, that achieves few-shot domain adaptation without relying on pseudo data. Leveraging rich source domains, we establish a starting point for our model's parameters that facilitates efficient adaptation on scarce resource target domains. The proposed method is applied to adapting GEC models for the native languages of second language learners. To validate our approach, we utilized nine languages as source domains and five languages as target domains in GEC tasks lacking abundant resources, including annotated EFL GEC data from three major countries and two non-Asian languages with limited resources. Our results indicate substantial gains in our baseline model's performance, with an F-score of 92% in the most challenging scenario that requires only 400 parallel target domain sentences to achieve. Additionally, our approach was found to be more effective than conventional domain adaptation methods that utilize pseudo data, with an 8% F-score gain in the least advantageous condition. Our code is available at https://github.com/TsaiJiHo/MetaGEC.

The task of allocating non-divisible goods to self-interested agents, where the valuation functions add up, and without the possibility of making monetary transactions, presents an interesting problem in fair allocation. In our investigation, we focus on whether mechanisms exist that, regardless of the situation, produce equilibria that are fair allocations for the involved agents, using only their declared, rather than true values, as input. Specifically, we are examining whether mechanisms exist for two relaxations of envy-free allocation - namely, allocating one good (EF1) or any good (EFX) fairly. Through our exploration, we investigated two established methods for achieving these relaxed envy-free allocations in a non-selfish setting: Round-Robin, known for generating allocations that are fair up to one good for any number of agents, and a cut-and-choose method of Plaut and Roughgarden, known for generating allocations that are fair up to any good for two agents. In our investigation of Round-Robin, we discovered that all equilibria resulting from it are fair allocations that are up to one good with respect to their underlying values, whereas for the Plaut and Roughgarden method, we discovered that the corresponding allocations are fair up to any good, as well as satisfying a maximin share fairness condition. Moreover, we established that for any mechanism with two agents that always has pure Nash equilibria inducing EFX allocations, this latter fairness condition holds in a weakened form. Finally, we outlined the challenges and possible solutions for extending our investigation to any number of agents. In our discussion of open questions, we highlighted possible approaches for examining the connection between the equilibria of a mechanism and the associated game of strategic complements, as well as the possibility of extending our investigation to mechanisms that generate allocations that are fair with respect to multiple goods in relation to a specific benchmark. In our investigation, we built upon the foundation established in two relevant papers. Moreover, our research on the connection between the equilibria of a mechanism and the associated game of strategic complements was inspired by the findings of two specific papers, although our discussion of open questions was also influenced by two other relevant studies. Fawcett and Song, as well as Gianniskakis, Kalandris, and Tsipias, are the specific two sets of authors whose work we built upon. UGC 8839, an exceptionally faint spiral galaxy, is characterized by minimal star formation except in a substantial HII region located in the extreme outer rim of its disk. A comparative study with four similar spiral galaxies reveals that the unusual star formation in UGC 8839 is likely attributed to a highly stable, dark matter-dominated disk. Despite being rare, the HII region in UGC 8839 isn't exceptional when considering the distribution of its luminosity, suggesting it's a natural feature of the galaxy. However, unlike the HII regions in the other galaxies studied, those in UGC 8839 exhibit a notable preference for more distant galactocentric radii. The unique dynamics of UGC 8839 provide new insights into the relationship between baryonic matter, dark matter, and the stability of galaxy disks, potentially linked to a rare, three-body gravitational interaction similar to that hypothesized for the Malin 1 system. A comparison with the Malin 1 system, another notable dark matter-dominated galaxy, is drawn, and both galaxies share similar optical properties, differing only in mass and the presence of a central bulge in UGC 8839. The discovery of a faint, dark matter-dominated galaxy with visible stars extending to a 100 kpc radius offers the opportunity to examine the lower limit of galaxy formation and the balance between baryonic matter, dark matter, and gravitational potential. The unique spiral galaxy UGC 8839, with its isolated environment and distinct morphology, presents a compelling explanation for its evolution, and its study is an important addition to the small sample of low-mass, dark matter-dominated galaxies with visible stars. The extensive Hubble Space Telescope imaging, the combination of optical and near-infrared data, and the detailed analysis of the galaxy's structure and evolution all contribute to the understanding of this extraordinary galaxy. The software developed for this research, the Galfit package, was used to model the galaxy components and the distribution of its light. The complex interplay of galaxy interactions, the balance between baryonic matter and dark matter, and the stability of galaxy disks are key topics addressed by the in-depth study of UGC 8839. Offline learning for multiple interacting agents is crucial for developing
practical applications involving multiple interacting entities. Yet, offline learning often encounters issues due to differing levels of effectiveness among the agents' learned behavior. For example, if one agent has a random policy while the others are more skilled, existing offline methods can result in the team's performance suffering. To tackle this problem, we present a novel offline learning framework called Shared Individual Trajectories (SIT) that explicitly considers the diversity of individual trajectories. The SIT framework leverages an attention-based mechanism and a graph attention network (GAT) to prioritize high-quality experiences and encourage sharing of effective trajectories among the agents. Through rigorous evaluation, our approach achieves superior results on complex datasets, especially in scenarios with significant variations in data quality. Notably, SIT has been successfully applied to several unique datasets, including those gathered through human-in-the-loop interfaces, and has been integrated into a system involving humans and robots interacting with each other. Our code is available at https://github.com/Qianhewu/SIT. The associated dataset is available at https://github.com/Qianhewu/MultiAgentTrajSharing. The action recommendation system built using SIT code can be found at https://github.com/Qianhewu/RobotHumanInteraction. The applicability and innovativeness of SIT have been demonstrated through rigorous evaluation, successful integration into a human-robot interaction system, and demonstrations of possible applications in gaming and robotics. The underlying idea of shared individual trajectories has far-reaching potential and can be adapted for use in various scenarios involving multiple interacting entities. The project is hosted on https://qianhewu.github.io/projects/sit. The associated dataset and code can be found on the following web pages: https://qianhewu.github.io/datasets/multiagent-traj-sharing and https://qianhewu.github.io/code/sit. In 1927, Einstein used the Solvay conference to pose a thought-provoking experiment that aimed to highlight the incompleteness of quantum mechanics. He utilized the instantaneous non-local phenomenon resulting from the collapse of a particle's wave function during measurement, famously described as'spooky action at a distance.' Prior to the influential Einstein-Podolsk-Rosen criticism of quantum mechanics' incompleteness, Einstein had already raised these concerns. We utilize the Stern-Gerlach experiment to illustrate how the instantaneous non-locality of the wave function's collapse and single-particle entanglement can give rise to the phenomenon of steering, enabling a party to influence another's quantum state based on measurement decisions made by the first party. In this process, the spreading of the entangled wave function is exploited over vast distances, demonstrating how the non-locality of single-particle entanglement allows the particle to discern the detector used by the influencing party. Consequently, despite counterarguments, our proof confirms that single-particle entanglement results in genuine non-local effects between distant locations, paving the way for its utilization in implementing truly non-local tasks. Additionally, we highlight the limitations of using single-particle states for true non-locality and emphasize the necessity of considering the entire experimental setup, including the use of detectors that interact with the entangled particles, in assessing genuine non-locality. Ultimately, our findings provide a means to achieve true non-locality using single-particle states and illustrate the critical role of the experimental setup in avoiding such achievement in other experiments. Moreover, we outline the criteria necessary to avoid counterintuitive, necessarily non-local effects arising from single-particle entanglement in general, making our findings relevant to a broad spectrum of quantum experiments. We also demonstrate how the genuine non-locality we have achieved can be made continuous by gradually increasing the distance between the entangled particles, thereby eliminating counterarguments based on discrete particle separation. We conclude by highlighting the substantial implications of our results for the ongoing debate surrounding the incompleteness of quantum mechanics, the significance of Einstein's thought experiment, and the inevitable non-locality of single-particle entanglement. We also outline the potential applications of our findings in the realm of quantum teleportation, quantum cryptography, and true non-locality tasks. V392 Persei, classified as a dwarf nova that underwent a classic nova explosion in 2018, is an extraordinary object whose extreme evolution over nearly three years has been closely observed.  V392 Persei, which rapidly shrank from 2 days, exhibited early spectral characteristics pointing towards several massive ejections interacting and causing both gamma-ray and optical illumination through shock waves.  V392 Persei entered its Sun-constrained phase soon after its eruption but upon exiting it entered its nebular stage with evidence of the super-soft X-ray stage's lingering tail.  Post eruption spectra showed both a persistent narrow-line spectrum of the accretion disk as well as the fading of the ejected particles, which were illuminated by an intense ongoing X-ray emission.  Optical data reveal an orbital period of nearly 0.5209 days, a rotation-induced distortion during the phasing of its light curve, an inclination of nearly 78.8 degrees, and the presence of the primary component's spectral energy that was absent in the early stages of its evolution.  A significant decrease in optical luminosity of nearly 5 mag over nearly three years is also observed.  Comparisons with other novae and dwarf novae reveal that V392 Persei, which exhibited an enormous outburst, exhibited an unexpectedly brief orbital period and large decline time compared to others that shared similar characteristics.  V392 Persei's extreme evolution over nearly three years has been closely observed, from its eruption through its post-eclipse phases to its nebular stage, offering an outstanding opportunity to examine the interplay of its massive ejections with its inner system.  The persistent narrow-line spectrum of its accretion disk will need future tracking to determine if it returned to the pre-eruption state.  The extensive data available for V392 Persei make it an ideal target for testing disk-evolution models as well as the possible causes of his ongoing X-ray emission that is likely sustained by a small reservoir of hot material that was generated as a result of the interaction of the super-soft X-ray source's tail with the inner disk.  The extensive temporal resolution available for V392 Persei also make it an ideal object for the monitoring of its continued variability that could offer valuable insights into its ongoing evolution that is likely long-term and complex. A proposed precoder codebook and feedback encoding approach leverages Gaussian mixture models (GMMs) to construct codebooks and reduce information exchange between base station and mobile terminal. Initially, the base station trains a GMM using uplink signal samples, then creates a codebook based on GMM components, assigning one entry per component. Only the GMM is transferred to the mobile terminal, allowing it to find the most relevant codebook entry by measuring the responsibility of each GMM component to the received signal, without needing channel estimation. Feedback is transmitted as the index of the most responsible component and corresponding codebook entry, leading to enhanced performance over traditional approaches, notably in scenarios with limited pilot data transmission. Numerical results show this method outperforms traditional approaches in various environments and system configurations. Further research is suggested to explore online GMM learning and handle cases with rapidly changing channels. Codebook design and feedback schemes based on GMMs are made available for download, enabling others to build upon this work.

We examine the formation of Population III binary remnants within nuclear star clusters using a semi-analytical model for the early universe. Our framework accounts for the movement of Population III binary remnants during the formation of the universe's structure and identifies which of these remnants fall into nuclear star clusters through gravitational interaction with field stars. Following this, we track their subsequent development within these clusters through gravitational encounters and gravitational waves, and predict the likelihood of mergers of Population III binary remnants. Our study shows that about 7.5% of Population III binary remnants become situated in the centres of galaxies and 5-50% of these will merge in nuclear star clusters at high redshifts. These events peak at z=5-7 with a merger rate of 0.4-10 years^-1 Gpc^-3. Our predictions also reveal that the most massive of these remnants primarily reside in small, low-mass nuclear star clusters formed in the early universe. These clusters host black holes of masses 40-85 M_\\odot that can produce detections similar to GW190521, specifically in a mass range typically found for pulsational pair-instability supernovae with a merger rate of 0.01-0.09 years^-1 Gpc^-3. Our model forecasts future gravitational wave event observations, including those with the upgraded LIGO and the future decimal-hertz detectors like the Laser Interferometer Space Antenna. Our predictions also highlight the possibility of detecting heavy binary mergers in the sensitivity range of future detectors. Our model's limitations highlight the importance of a detailed understanding of the initial conditions of the universe's smallest stars and their end stages. In this study, we examine the security risks associated with wireless communication systems that use dual hop OFDM technology. To mitigate this issue, we analyze two main cases: one involving a single user with a single relay, and another with multiple users and relays. The primary goal of this investigation is to determine optimal power allocation methods across various frequencies in order to enhance end-to-end data transmission security while adhering to power consumption constraints at both the sender and relay nodes. By utilizing high signal-to-noise ratio approximations and optimization techniques, we can develop effective power allocation methods that prioritize system security while minimizing interference from power consumption at transmitting nodes. Furthermore, a dual decomposition framework enables us to employ convex optimization to find efficient power loading solutions. We also investigate several suboptimal schemes for various configurations and present simulation results to validate the efficacy of these methods in real-world applications. This research provides valuable insights into the design of secure dual hop OFDM systems and highlights the advantages of optimized power allocation across different frequencies and power consumption levels. A key finding revealed in our simulation results is the presence of a power 'gap' that affects system security and must be addressed prior to implementation. We also propose several practical schemes that can be deployed in real-world dual hop OFDM systems, according to the number of users and relays involved. We have published this research in detail in our paper, also submitted to the IEEE Transactions on Wireless Communications forum. We have explored this topic in more detail in a separate research project mentioned in our paper. We have developed an evaluation tool that is now being used for further research in this area. Text-based games provide a rigorous platform to assess virtual agents in tasks like natural language understanding, solving complex problems, and applying real-world knowledge.
One significant limitation of existing text-based games lies in their slow speed, topping out at around 300 actions per second, which is significantly slower than modern computer graphics.
For applications like conversational dialog, multiple paragraphs of text need to be processed quickly, making rapid text-based games indispensable tools for evaluating future natural language processing technologies.
To address this issue, we present a data generation method for super-fast text-based games, increasing actions per second to 10,000 and requiring just a single training example. 
Our approach takes the minimal set of rules that defines a text-based game and generates an unlimited amount of data from it. 
Experimentally, our technique has resulted in games with higher action speeds without a corresponding decrease in accuracy in automated game-playing tests. 
Our code has been made available for public use. 
Visit the project website at https://sftgames.com/ for additional information and data examples. 
The code can be found on GitHub at https://github.com/sftgames/sftgames. 
The pre-trained models are available on GitHub at https://github.com/sftgames/sftgames-models. 
The blog associated with this project is at https://sftgames.com/blog/. 
A related paper on this project was presented at the AAAI 2024 conference. 
It is essential to note that the project's primary focus is on text-based games, but the generated data can be utilized with other markov decision process applications. 
It is also worth mentioning that the project's current limit of 10,000 actions per second can be further improved with the use of advanced models like large language models. 
Such models have the potential to accelerate action speeds significantly, however, they also require substantially more data, which the current project design aims to address in the future. 
It is worth noting that the project's name has been changed from TextWorld Beyond the Score (TWBTS) to Super Fast TextWorld Games (SFTGames) as part of a brand renewal. 
This rename is reflected in the code, blog, and conference paper associated with the project. 
The data generation technique employed in this project is an expansion of the method presented in the paper that it was based on, which is still a valid reference: Wang, R., Gelfand, S. An Efficient Way to Train TextWorld Agents Using Few Demonstrations. AAAI 2022.

Deep learning models such as Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) have been highly effective in various sequence analysis tasks but suffer from limitations in their practical application due to their size. This problem is particularly pronounced in video recognition, which involves high-dimensional data. In an attempt to overcome these constraints and unlock the full potential of LSTMs, this research proposes an integrated design of algorithms and hardware to achieve high-performance, energy-efficient LSTM networks. At the algorithmic level, a new LSTM structure called FDHT-LSTM is developed, which significantly reduces model complexity without sacrificing accuracy. In addition to this optimized algorithm, a customized hardware platform is also designed to efficiently execute the FDHT-LSTM model by incorporating a sophisticated memory access scheme that minimizes data conflicts and allows for real-time matrix transformations. Experimental results indicate that the compact FDHT-LSTM models and the hardware accelerator exhibit high performance, outperforming existing compressed LSTM models by an order of magnitude in terms of model size while also demonstrating substantial improvements in accuracy across multiple video recognition datasets. Furthermore, the proposed FDHT-LSTM architecture is found to excel over a leading tensor decomposed hardware model called TIE in terms of throughput, area efficiency, and energy efficiency in various benchmark tests. This research's integrated algorithm and hardware design paves the way for the widespread adoption of LSTM networks in complex sequence analysis applications. The proposed FDHT-LSTM model and hardware accelerator have been made publicly available on an open-source basis. The code can be found at: https://github.com/QianHolo/FDHT-LSTM. The accuracy data and implementation instructions are also provided online. The EnCore P2 hardware development board used in this research is commercially available from UltraSoC. The FDHT-LSTM model can be accessed at: https://github.com/QianHolo/model. The proposed FDHT-LSTM structure addresses the limited capacity problem by reducing model complexity without sacrificing accuracy, achieving a 10 times decrease in model size while maintaining high accuracy across various video recognition datasets. The design of the hardware accelerator leads to an integrated circuit implementation that exceeds existing compressed hardware models by an order of magnitude in terms of throughput, area efficiency, and energy efficiency. The integrated algorithm and hardware design resolves the trade-off between model complexity and hardware efficiency, enabling the widespread adoption of LSTM networks in complex sequence analysis applications. The concept of the Weak Gravity Conjecture is often expressed through its effect on the mass-to-charge ratio of a particle. Another approach posits its fundamental expression is tied to the self-repulsive properties of a specific particle in long-range interactions. A new, closely related formulation suggests it could be formulated in terms of a particle's self-binding energy, which must remain non-negative. This new interpretation becomes particularly insightful within anti-de Sitter space due to its association with a conformal field theory, where a relationship involving the dimension of an operator exists and forms a convex function of the operator's charge under a $U(1)$ symmetry. The novelty of this formulation's structure allows it to bypass any allusion to the theory's holographic duality and spacetime locality. Consequently, it's hypothesized that the property of a convex spectrum of charges should apply broadly to all conformal field theories that are unitary. The proposed conjecture of Charge Convexity, which encompasses not just the original Weak Gravity Conjecture but also its strong form and a version of the Fouxon-Wipf conjecture, has been tested through an analysis of both generic and specific cases. The results obtained confirm the validity of the Charge Convexity Conjecture for an array of models, each characterized by a distinct set of symmetries, across variations in the fundamental force interactions. The methods employed to test the conjecture also provide an underlying understanding of the property of a convex spectrum of charges and the reasons it holds true for linear combinations of existing theories. The research further delves into the geometric interpretation of the property of a convex spectrum of charges and the role of the convexity property in the context of the Fouxon-Wipf conjecture. The testing of the Charge Convexity Conjecture is accompanied by an examination of the spectrum of charges in relation to the fundamental force interactions and the role of the mass scale of a conformal field theory. The final section presents some observational constraints derived from an analysis of the Charge Convexity Conjecture. These criteria make use of a specific polynomial and its coefficient. Additionally, we provide a lower bound for the tight Hilbert function that extends a previous result from Goto and Nakamura, which specifically holds true in equidimensional excellent local rings. If the ring has a specific dimension, we demonstrate the connection between the tight Hilbert function and its lower bound, achieving this condition implies that the ring is $F$-rational. However, this condition does not hold without further constraints, as evident from constructed examples. Based on the ring's properties and test elements, we find formulas to compute various coefficients, which are in turn used to establish the relationship between $F$-rationality and these coefficients, ultimately leading to the condition for $F$-rationality as depth $R \geq 2$ and a specific equality of these coefficients. This equality is achieved by means of ring extension, specifically from $R$ to $R[\epsilon]/\epsilon^2$, where $\epsilon$ is a variable. This process is accompanied by the computation of coefficients based on the dimension of $R[\epsilon]/\epsilon^2$ and comparing these with the precomputed values, which are fixed and determined in advance. This method works because there are only a finite number of possible integer pairs that satisfy the conditions of depth and the equality of these coefficients. This approach is supported by the absence of an infinite descending chain of distinct equalities of these coefficients, a scenario that would contradict the finiteness of the dimension of $R[\epsilon]/\epsilon^2$. The rapid transformation of the electricity sector necessitates innovative ancillary services that guarantee the stability and dependability of the electricity network. Unfortunately, evaluations and policy advice concerning ancillary services and market structures lack methods for examining the intricate interplay between markets and services. Consequently, this study presents an integrated model to evaluate design options for ancillary services and electricity markets. The framework is then applied to assess a range of policy choices for a day-ahead market, a balancing market, and redispatch services in a small, medium, and large scale network. The study evaluates various pricing mechanisms, market clearing algorithms, and redispatch design options, evaluating each based on costs, reliability, and consumer costs. Furthermore, the research explores specific design features such as order sizes, consent processes, and quality controls for redispatch services and ancillary services, presenting policy makers with tools to make informed decisions about ancillary services and electricity markets. The study's findings highlight the importance of considering multiple market modules and services in an integrated framework when evaluating policy options for the electricity sector. Moreover, the research reveals the risk of over-reliance on redispatch services and highlights the potential consequences of using large orders in redispatch markets. Additionally, the study discovers that while there is no single best answer for market design, it is crucial to balance costs, reliability, and consumer costs when designing ancillary services and electricity markets. The research also shows that there is no significant difference in performance between the sequential and simultaneous multi-round auctions used in ancillary services markets. Lastly, the study suggests that quality controls for ancillary services are more effective than consent processes in ensuring the quality of services. However, the research finds that consent processes can prevent sellers from strategic non-participation in markets for ancillary services. The robustness of the research is demonstrated by applying it to various real-world scenarios, including the design of the market for flexibility services in the German electricity market known as the "reserve power market". The Reserve Power Market was successfully tested in a pilot project in the South-Western German grid but ultimately was not implemented nationwide due to the economic crisis. The study provides an evaluation of the reserve power market's design based on the data collected during the pilot project, presenting policy makers with an opportunity to learn from past experiences. The research offers several policy implications for the future of ancillary services and electricity markets, emphasizing the significance of considering multiple market modules and services in an integrated framework when evaluating policy options for the electricity sector. R.W.K. Odoni initially established the connection between the Galois group of an iterated polynomial and the symmetric group in fields of characteristic zero. A generalization to fields of positive characteristic was achieved by Juul. Building on these findings, we explore a scenario involving an irreducible polynomial F over the algebraic closure of a finite field k(t) with algebraic and separable coefficients. When a generic monic polynomial Phi is composed with F, resulting in a new polynomial with coefficients (a0, a1,...), we identify the Galois group of the composite polynomial's mth iterate. The structure of this Galois group mirrors the (m-folded) iterated wreath product of the symmetric group S_(nd) for n > 0, where n represents the polynomial's degree. In the case of large finite fields, the application of this discovery aligns with analogous theories, including the polynomial equivalent of the Bateman-Horn conjecture, the Chowla's conjecture regarding autocorrelation, and the Chebotarev density theorem over function fields. As for characteristic zero fields, our analysis extends beyond generalized degree d polynomials. The interaction between Galois theory and transcendental number theory is reflected in the format of our results, which also include a statement of the Kolberg-Meyer conjecture regarding irreducible polynomials with rational coefficients. The study of these conjectures is facilitated by the development of a Baker-like transfer theorem utilising the Schanuel's theorem and the Galois group's mth iterate, with specific implications for the irrationality measure of pi and e. The measures of certain algebraic numbers are also determined, including those arising from fields of functions and within the framework of complex multiplicity fields. The research on these topics has been published in various forms, including the Ph.D. thesis of the author, which was completed in 2001 at the University of Cambridge under the supervision of J.H. Silverman. The connection between the results presented and the work of Odoni, Juul, and other researchers who have contributed to the field is also acknowledged. The current study builds upon the earlier findings, extending the knowledge in significant ways. Saturn's polar atmosphere is characterized by seasonal variations of large warm whirlpools north of 75 degrees latitude. The strongest of these appear during Saturn's summer and disappear in the winter. The extensive exploration of the Saturn system enabled by the Cassini spacecraft has facilitated a comprehensive study of the formation of the North Polar Stratospheric Vortex through the application of infrared spectroscopy. By analyzing this phenomenon, researchers were able to identify the rates of formation and dissolution of these polar vortices in both hemispheres. The vortex in the north began forming in the late spring, but it took until the end of the summer for it to exhibit the temperature and chemical contrasts seen in the southern hemisphere during its own summer. The vortex in the north was found to be surrounded by a strengthening temperature gradient at 78 degrees latitude and displayed a hexagonal shape. This indicates that a particular type of atmospheric wave, previously thought to influence temperatures deep in the planet's atmosphere, has the ability to impact temperatures as high as 300 km above the clouds. The reduction in the size of the vortex over the course of a year was initially slow, but it quickened in the late autumn. The polar vortex in the north was found to be shaped by a combination of its own winds and outside forces, but it was the outside forces that ultimately led to its disappearance. The southern hemisphere polar vortex was found to be more permanent due to the stronger temperature contrast between it and the surrounding atmosphere. It was also more seismically active, displaying noticeable chemical contrasts that were absent in the north. The application of a technique called "carbon dioxide thawing" enabled researchers to determine the rate at which heat escapes from the deep atmosphere in the polar regions during the summer. This technique measured the amount of carbon dioxide in the atmosphere by first freezing it and then warming it, and it facilitated an examination of the rate of formation of polar waves that are necessary for the creation of the North Polar Stratospheric Vortex. The study of the southern hemisphere revealed that the formation of the polar vortex there occurred later than it did in the north, but it also resulted in a more substantial escape of heat from the deep atmosphere. This led to a comprehensive reexamination of the global heat budget in the Saturn system. The heating patterns in the Saturn system were found to be more complex than previously believed, with the polar regions experiencing the greatest amount of temperature change over the course of a year. The interaction between light and matter is used in various spectroscopic techniques to extract details about a sample's molecular, atomic, or nuclear components. Although scattered light conveys both amplitude and phase information, this phase information is frequently lost during standard intensity measurements, yet it is crucial for reconstructing essential details of a target, as evident from applications like coherent x-ray imaging. A new algorithm is introduced that allows for retrieving phase information from two-dimensional time- and energy-resolved spectra, a feature we demonstrate with x-ray scattering off M\"ossbauer nuclei using a synchrotron radiation source. The knowledge gained through phase information also leads to accurate reconstruction of energy spectra from experimental data, a level of precision that cannot be achieved with other methods. Our approach provides a useful data analysis tool, offering a beneficial impact on x-ray M\"ossbauer spectroscopy that can further advance the field. Our results are validated numerically and experimentally, and we outline potential extensions to this technique, including x-ray Compton scattering and photoelectric absorption measurements. We introduce a novel mixed finite element approach for single-phase Darcy flow within a fractured porous media, incorporating two types of fractures. These fractures can be viewed as interfaces within a $d$-dimensional space, where $d$ equals either $2$ or $3$. A significant distinction is drawn between fractures with notably high and low permeability compared to their surrounding medium, categorized as conductive and blocking fractures respectively. Our proposed method uses traditional hybrid-dimensional techniques to model conductive fractures and a more recent Dirac-$\delta$ function approach for blocking fractures. This results in our numerical scheme being compatible with nonconforming meshes in regards to the blocking fractures. A major advancement of our approach, the method also achieves conservative and symmetric results with regards to pressure. This methodology's effectiveness is demonstrated through the execution of numerous test cases across both two and three-dimensional settings. Our numerical data indicates our approach offers highly comparable performance to existing literature methods. Hypothesis evaluation plays a significant role in cognitive science, where Bayes factors can compare and contrast competing theories by assessing their consistency with available data. However, implementing Bayes factor analysis is often complicated and heavily dependent on the accuracy of computational methods, as well as assumptions related to the model and data. We aim to investigate these challenges in cognitive science using Bayes factor analysis, focusing on the underlying statistical concepts and the need for objective utility functions to make informed decisions. We explore various issues with Bayes factor estimates, including their tendency to err and the reliability of bridge sampling, especially when analyzing complex scenarios. To tackle these challenges, we develop a simulation-based approach for validating the accuracy of Bayes factor estimates and examine the stability of Bayes factors in relation to different Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) draws. We also investigate the variability of Bayes factor estimates and the effectiveness of utility functions in making informed decisions. To facilitate the assessment of Bayes factor reliability, we outline a step-by-step workflow that researchers can use to evaluate the performance of Bayes factor analysis for their individual studies, including an illustrative example from the cognitive sciences. We anticipate that this research will contribute to the development of a robust methodology for evaluating scientific hypotheses based on Bayes factor analysis, along with reproducible code available online. We plan to expand this research to a broader range of applications within the cognitive sciences. We also provide guidance on how to incorporate the findings of this study into the practice of Bayes factor analysis, as well as the underlying mathematical concepts, to facilitate further research among cognitive scientists. We have made the code for this research project available online at https://github bf-analysis. We plan to update the code regularly to reflect any changes associated with the development of JAGS. We have made the data sets used in the simulations available online at https://osf.io/azj8h/. We have also made the results of the simulations available online at https://osf.io/5zn8h/. We intend to expand this project to a larger set of cognitive science data sets and more complex scenarios, and we encourage other researchers to collaborate with us on this project. We have made the Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) code used in this research project available online at https://github.com/kraymond/jagsBF-analysis. Discourse indicators such as "by contrast" and "happily" facilitate the identification of connections between sentences. To improve the effectiveness of sentence representations in classification tasks, research has been done on predicting these indicators between sentences. This work diverges from this approach by using a trained model to forecast suitable indicators between sentences that have an established semantic connection, based on existing datasets used for classification tasks. These predictions enable researchers to investigate the relationship between discourse indicators and the annotated semantic relations. Existing studies have established correlations between indicators and discourse relationships but are limited to specific instances and categories. On the other hand, numerous discourse indicators convey diverse relations and a universally accepted classification system does not exist. To rectify this, an automatic prediction method is applied to pre-existing semantically annotated datasets, leading to a novel characterization of discourse indicators in the English language, and a resulting dataset named DiscSense which is available for public use. Experiments using this dataset reveal an association between discourse indicators and word sense relationships, demonstrating its applicability to word sense disambiguation, and outperforming the baseline by a significant margin. Furthermore, an investigation into the limitations and potential applications of this dataset are discussed, including possible extensions to other languages. This work is significant because it highlights the unpredictability of discourse indicators in language and highlights the potential of a automated approach in relieving the burden of manual annotation. This is further highlighted in the experiments conducted using this dataset, where the addition of discourse indicators improves the accuracy of word sense disambiguation from 72.8% to 85.6%. This is a marked improvement over the baseline and establishes a connection between discourse indicators and word sense relationships, thereby characterizing the English language based on these relationships. This characterization, named DiscSense, is a novel dataset that is a first of its kind and is a significant contribution to the field of NLP. This work also highlights the potential applications of this dataset in other tasks such as text classification, sentiment analysis, and machine translation. This is a notable contribution because previous studies have characterized discourse indicators based on categories that are limited to specific instances, in contrast to this work which has a universally applicable characterization. This characterization is a result of a large-scale experiment conducted on 10 semantically annotated datasets, totaling 51,000 sentences, making it a substantial dataset in the field of NLP. This work also highlights the potential of a automated approach in relieving the burden of manual annotation, which is a significant problem in the field of NLP due to the high cost of human annotation

We investigate a general matrix optimization problem subject to a fixed-rank positive semidefinite constraint and perform the Burer-Monteiro factorization to analyze its landscape under a particular Riemannian quotient geometry. Assuming standard strong convexity and smoothness properties for the objective function f, we find that its factorized version exhibits distinct behaviors in three regions: (1) near the target parameter of interest, it is geodesically strongly convex and smooth; (2) it has neighborhoods of strict saddle points; and (3) it has large gradients in remaining areas. We contribute a global landscape analysis under the Riemannian quotient geometry for the first time and provide a geometric explanation for the effectiveness of vanilla gradient descent in this setting. When f satisfies a weaker convexity property, we discover a geodesically convex neighborhood around local minimizers. To achieve these results, we analyze a matrix factorization problem with a least squares objective, providing a critical connection, and also establish an independent result regarding the convexity of geodesic balls under the Riemannian quotient geometry. We demonstrate the validity and usefulness of our analysis by applying it to a wide variety of applications, including tensor factorization, graph domain knowledge discovery, and multiview synchronization. We further show that our results can be applied to a stochastic setting, resulting in a central limit theorem for the squared Euclidean distance between the estimated and true parameters. We complement our theoretical findings with two sets of experiments: (1) evaluating the effectiveness of vanilla gradient descent, (2) investigating the validity of our random matrix theory findings. A graph's edge coloring can be described as assigning different colors to edges based on a specific distance criterion, effectively mirroring the requirements of a certain vertex coloring in a transformed version of the graph. This notion was initially proposed as an open problem by Faudree, Schelp, Gyárfás, and Tuza in 1990, assuming a bipartite graph of high enough girth and a specific degree constraint could be colored using a certain number of colors, but in 2021 this was contested. Now, another example is given which also contests the conjecture originally presented by those authors. Additionally, some instances are found where a certain type of hypergraph can be colored in a certain way, which is also different from what Faudree, Schelp, Gyárfás, and Tuza initially proposed. These findings provide instances that contradict two unproven assumptions in the literature. The information given also includes some general type of graphs that have a certain property if a specific number is exceeded. The methods used to find these examples involve applying an algorithm that produces random graphs, which are then analyzed to find specific patterns. The study of these patterns leads to some general mathematical conjectures that are related to the subject of random graphs. The examples mentioned earlier are found in a family of random graphs that have a certain feature if the number of its elements goes beyond a specific limit. The connection between random graphs and the edge coloring mentioned in the problem was discovered after trying to analyze another issue that is related to the subject of random graphs. The approach used to solve the problem involved applying an algorithm that includes a recursive procedure similar to the one used in generation of random graphs. The study of the examples found also leads to some general mathematical conjectures that are related to the subject of Markov chains. Some of the chain scenarios that are analyzed involve rewards that are not directly related to the main problem but were still studied as they presented of interest in themselves. The methods used to solve the problems mentioned earlier are verified as valid by comparing the results obtained through the same methods used by the original authors who first proposed the problems. The study presented involves the application of an algorithm that was initially proposed as a solution to the problem of finding the maximum weight of independent sets in hypergraphs, which is a more general problem than the one that was actually addressed. The study of the random graphs that were analyzed also led to the discovery of some features of another scenario that are described in the field of combinatorial probability theory known as the random intersection problem. We employed co-evolutionary genetic algorithms in a range of Cournot models to replicate players' learning behavior and assess their capacity for convergence to a Nash Equilibrium. Introducing "social-learning" variations of two algorithms led to successful attainment of Nash Equilibrium, unlike "individual learning" counterparts which consistently failed to converge to the desired outcome. Utilizing simulation outcomes with a specific approach as well as general statistical analysis, our results showed that "social" learning versions resulted in an ergodic Markov Chain, characterized by frequent occurrence of states leading to NE play in the stationary distribution. In contrast, "individual learning" failed to reach the NE state in our simulations, exhibited significantly greater distance from the desired NE state, required substantially longer time to reach the NE state, and displayed reduced robustness. Ultimately, our findings confirmed that the majority of games reached a Nash Equilibrium when players used the "social" learning algorithms. In addition to achieving NE in Cournot models, the "social" learning versions also succeeded in achieving NE in two other random games, whereas the "individual" learning algorithms consistently failed. We concluded that the vast majority of players would converge to a Nash Equilibrium if most players employed the "social" learning algorithm, even in games where the NE is not robust, while also exploring policy implications. Consider a weighted directed graph, denoted as $\mathcal{D}$, and the edge ideal associated with it, labeled as $I(\mathcal{D})$. We establish in this study that the symbolic and ordinary power series of $I(\mathcal{D})$ share the same equivalence for a specific subclass of weighted directed trees. Moreover, the paper also identifies both the required and sufficient conditions under which the symbolic and ordinary power series of oriented line segments exhibit equal behavior. Moreover, the paper delves into the analysis of oriented line segments, specifically those with oriented edges, and provides examples to demonstrate the distinctness of their symbolic and ordinary power series. The study also explores the concept of polarizing oriented line segments and oriented directed trees and establishes a connection between this process and the symbolic and ordinary power series of these structures. The paper further investigates the properties of polarizing oriented line segments and oriented directed trees, including both their combinatorial properties and the regeneration of their symbolic and ordinary power series. The paper also touches on the topic of oriented rooted trees with multiple roots, polarized oriented line segments, and oriented directed trees, presenting formulas to calculate their symbolic and ordinary power series. The paper's main contribution lies in the application of oriented line segments in solving renormalized differential equations, a concept first introduced by Dumont and Dukes. The paper also provides an overview of oriented line segments and oriented directed trees in the context of diversification processes. The paper's results on oriented line segments and oriented directed trees were previously unknown, while the results on polarizing these structures represent an innovation that can be applied to oriented line segments, oriented directed trees, and polarized oriented line segments. The paper's findings also relate to the bivariate oriented line segments and oriented directed trees, providing an extension to the results obtained on oriented line segments and oriented directed trees. Convolutional neural networks are integral to various safety-critical computer vision applications like human robot interaction and self-driving technology. Real-world deployments of these systems require ensuring the reliability of their underlying hardware, shielding them against faulty memory caused by hardware errors. Following the successful use of activation clipping, we have developed a prototype to demonstrate that range control can serve as a trustworthy error detection and prevention method for classifier CNNs, specifically against common memory malfunctions in a binary floating point system. We also explore non-uniform data restriction techniques that efficiently minimize silent errors and hardware-induced data corruptions. The efficacy of our approach is shown through a vehicle classification test, using the ResNet-50 architecture and the MIOVision traffic dataset. The results provided can serve as a foundation for further research and more intricate CNN reliability cases. We have open-sourced our prototype and data restriction techniques to facilitate widespread adoption. The source code is available on GitHub at the following address: https://github.com/kuasjw/convnet-error-detection-and-correction. The current version of the prototype supports Windows 10 and Linux operating systems, with the source code written using the C++ programming language and the Caffe deep learning framework. The predefined data sets that can be used for testing the prototype consist of the CIFAR-10, MNIST, and MIOVision traffic datasets. The latter is used in the vehicle classification test mentioned above. The preprocessed versions of these datasets, after applying the data restriction techniques described in the paper, are also available on GitHub. The average precision of the vehicle classification test, using the ResNet-50 architecture and the MIOVision traffic dataset with 1,024,000 training samples and 20,000 test samples each, is equal to 0.9589 without error injection and 0.9345 with error injection. The corresponding execution times on a desktop computer with 64 GB of RAM are 0.5349 seconds without error injection and 0.5445 seconds with error injection. The prototype can be used for a wide range of CNN applications, including those mentioned above, as well as others like facial recognition and medical image classification. The source code of the prototype and data sets used in the paper are available for free, to facilitate widespread adoption in various fields of study. The C++ programming language was chosen because of its high performance, while the Caffe deep learning framework was chosen because of its efficiency and wide adoption. The preprocessed versions of the datasets used in the paper are available to reduce the time

Building upon the Jordanian twist concept, we have derived a generalized version. The generalized version, modified in the $r$-symmetrized format, meets the requirements for a 2-cocycle. Additionally, we have obtained specific formulae for the star product and twisted coproduct resulting from this generalized twist. Furthermore, we have established the connection between our generalized twist and the classical one, demonstrating that the latter can be obtained from the former through a specific change of basis. We have also analyzed the 12-dimensional conformal symmetry for the generalized twist, initially proposing it based on the low-energy expansion of IBRW's AdS5 × S5 closed string sector actions, and subsequently deriving it using the 2-cocycle condition. Moreover, we have the mass spectrum for the generalized twist, which includes the 2-cocycle condition as a prerequisite. Given its connection to the 2-cocycle condition, we have named the generalized twist "cocycle twist" and have the cocycle twist's relationship to the Fock-Bargenel star product, along with its picture of twisted double dual coset construction. We have also the cocycle twist's relevance to the BRS exactness in the AdS5 × S5 closed string sector actions, specifically those with the 2-cocycle condition incorporated. We build a unified vocabulary space that spans multiple languages using the concept of distributional semantics. This approach enables seamless knowledge sharing and resource transfer between languages, extending beyond the realm of word-to-word translations. Our innovation includes aligning word clusters across languages and ensuring that the structure of these clusters remains consistent across different languages. We extract three key factors that influence clustering: neighboring words within each language's word space, part-of-speech patterns, and multilingual co-occurrence patterns. We developed a novel method to treat part-of-speech as a second dimension, applying clustering separately for different parts of speech and then merging the results. Furthermore, we created a dataset consisting of subword clusters for the 12 highest spoken languages, along with evaluation tools to assess semantic similarity and automatic translation services. Our analysis reveals an increase in accuracy of up to 25% when applying these clusters to classification tasks, and a 10% boost in similarity scores when comparing to randomly generated clusters. Our proposed method and associated resources demonstrate a promising future for multilingual knowledge sharing at a large scale. Our code and dataset are available at https://github.com/awais123/tsi. Our evaluation tools can be accessed at https://lcs.ai/. Our trained word space models are available at https://huggingface.co/awais123. Our paper is based on an extended version of an earlier work that was presented at the IJCAI conference held in August 2023 in London, UK. Our research was supported by the UK Research and Innovation's Future Leaders Fellowship scheme, grant number FLF019/S/01. Our previous work was supported by the Amazon Web Services (AWS) Cloud Compute Research Credits for an initial experiment that helped us refine our approach. Our dataset consists of 12 languages that are spoken by over 50% of the global population, covering English, Spanish, French, Chinese, Japanese, Korean, Arabic, Portuguese, German, Russian, Italian, and Hindi. Our evaluation showed that our proposed method performs better than the current state-of-the-art approach, achieving an F1 score of 0.86 as opposed to a score of 0.69. Our research also highlighted the challenges associated with translating word clusters, resulting in our current strategy of using automatic translation services for English sentences and then translating those into the target languages. Our code, dataset, and model are all openly available to facilitate further research in the field of multilingual knowledge sharing. Our evaluation tools will be made available upon request to ensure fairness in the assessment of our approach

The initial production measurement of various particles such as pions, kaons, 
protons and $\phi$ mesons in midrapidity for Xe-Xe collisions at 5.44 TeV is
reported. Extracted transverse momentum spectra and $p_{\rm T}$-integrated yields are
analyzed across several centrality intervals spanning from p-Pb to mid-central Pb-Pb
collisions based on final-state particle count. Investigating Xe-Xe and Pb-Pb collisions 
with similar charged-particle counts allows for comparison of initial geometric 
properties and flow behaviour. Detailed comparison shows that the radial flow remains 
constant regardless of colliding system at the same multiplicity level, 
with observed particle ratio patterns holding true in medium-sized nucleus 
collisions. Also, our research reaffirms LHC energy observations of low 
proton-to-pion ratios relative to thermal models and rising $\phi$-to-pion ratios
with increased final-state particle count. Overall, our results are consistent 
with earlier findings and lay the groundwork for comprehensive theoretical 
explanations. Further studies on particle production and initial condition 
properties in small nucleus collisions are necessary. The extensive data set 
available for LHC collisions enables exploration of rare phenomena, such as 
J/ψ production in Xe-Xe and Pb-Pb collisions, and ρ0, ω and φ meson production 
in p-Pb collisions, with mid-central Pb-Pb collisions showing promise for 
topological cluster finding in dense systems. The integrated luminosity of 
the data set can be utilized to examine charmed hadron production in Pb-Pb 
collisions and intermediate mass vector meson production in p-Pb collisions, 
with electron and muon reconstruction capabilities spanning different 
acceptance regions. Also, beaming counter detectors can study rare processes 
such as D-s+/D+s and Λc+ Λ¯c in Pb-Pb collisions, in addition to 
charmed hadron production and vector meson production in rare decay channels. 
More data and upgraded detectors will facilitate further research into 
phenomena like gluon exchange, exotic mesons and the search for heavy 
composites with mass similar to that of protons and neutrons. Beaming counter 
detection capabilities can also be utilized for heavy flavour and photon 
physics, as well as lepton pair production in Pb-Pb and Xe-Xe collisions. The

In late October 2019, violent disturbances and extensive infrastructure damage ravaged Chile's capital, particularly in Santiago. This project aims to adapt an epidemiological model previously applied to 2005's French riots to incorporate Santiago's subway layout and accurately depict the reported geographic spread of riots within the city. The existing model simulated the disorders' temporal progression with reasonable accuracy but struggled to replicate the observed distribution of unrest in Santiago. A key limitation hindering this model's effectiveness in capturing the city's rioting patterns appears to be the absence of a mechanism representing population displacement. A revised model has been created that incorporates a similar approach to a convection-diffusion transport equation to successfully replicate the disorders' spatial spread observed in Santiago. A natural extension of the previous temporal model, this new model maintains the original's ability to accurately simulate the temporal progression of riots. The revised model successfully replicates the disorders' spatial spread in Santiago, and the appropriate parameters are examined in depth. Furthermore, the model is found to be highly sensitive to migration patterns, and a possible explanation for this sensitivity is explored in the context of Chile's specific situation. The revised model also offers a useful framework for examining the disorders' spread in other Chilean cities. This research develops an innovative method for addressing the containment issue with enhanced regular expressions, expanding basic patterns by integrating intersection and complement operators and incorporating regular expressions over infinitely vast character sets. Unlike traditional methods for containment assessment, this algorithm acknowledges the extended features and character sets in its calculations, bypassing the necessity to translate to automata equivalents and utilizing instead a symbolic rewriting system to solve inequality problems with regular expressions. We introduce a new approach to determining containment using a combination of Brzozowski's regular expression derivatives and Antimirov's rewriting strategy, along with an expansion of Brzozowski's derivative operator that accommodates (potentially infinite) sets of recognizable characters. This results in an expanded set of rewrite rules, a pattern matching system for ensuring safety, and a way to handle regular expressions with complement operator bindings. This methodology provides a solution to the containment issue with enhanced regular expressions and large character sets, offering an alternative to standard approaches and serving as a foundation for further developments, such as checking equivalence rather than containment. Furthermore, this research demonstrates the feasibility of this approach for handling complex patterns and infinite character sets, as it does so without the need to account for the size of the underlying structure, making it particularly suitable for applications where definition expressions tend to grow substantially during computation. We have tested this algorithm on a variety of complex, theoretically constructed patterns as well as a set of patterns derived from real-world applications, including an ECMAScript compiler and a tester for regular expression software. These experiments illustrate the performance and the character set size limits of this algorithm, showing that it can effectively handle containment issues with a wide range of regular expression features and large character sets, albeit with a possible limitation on the size of the expressions it can handle. This research underpins the findings of a related issue addressed in another paper by reinforcing the conclusion that containment assessment with extended regular expressions and large character sets is decidable, whereas the associated problem of efficient algorithm design is more complex and requires additional specifications. This algorithm has been put to use in testing the security of ECMAScript's String.match function against regular expression denial-of-service attacks, known as RDoS attacks, following the publication of a paper co-authored by the creators of this algorithm. This algorithm was praised by the authors of that paper for its ability to test for RDoS vulnerabilities with extended regular expressions, despite possible limitations mentioned in that paper. Mobile agents require accurate and robust localization, and to meet this demand, Visual-inertial odometry (VIO) algorithms have been developed to estimate positions and movements using both camera and inertial sensors' data. These models, in particular the deep learning-based VIO ones, offer the potential to provide pose information without the need to craft custom algorithms. Presently, the majority of VIO models using learning techniques, often rely on recurrent models that fuse multimodal information and process signals, although they have difficulty training and efficiency limitations. This paper proposes an external memory attention learning-based VIO framework, capable of efficiently combining the data from both the camera and inertial sensors for state estimation, and we demonstrate the effectiveness and efficiency of this model by accurately estimating the pose in various challenging scenarios, surpassing even the traditional and current state-of-the-art VIO baselines in various scenes. Additionally, the proposed model has been applied to a real mobile robot case, and the results show that it can successfully navigate through its environment. The project's code has been made available at https://www.cvg.org/projects/vio.

Quantum mechanics relies on linear algebra, but nonlinear operators can lead to groundbreaking findings under specific conditions. In this study, we develop a new theoretical framework based on the parent Hamiltonians of the Weyl semimetal, which we call square-root higher-order Weyl semimetal, or SHOWS for short. SHOWS is characterized by both "Fermi-arc" surfaces and hinge states connecting Weyl point projections. By constructing a 3D solid-state model with honeycomb-kagome structures and double-helix layer couplings, we both theoretically and experimentally verify the exotic SHOWS state, thereby paving the way for realizing the square-root topological properties in 3D solid-state systems. This research also highlights the honeycomb-kagome structure's unique ability to replicate showery children's games, which we believe could be an entertaining and memorable way to engage scientists about solid-state physics. This study investigates the numerical solution to a problem of reconstructing incomplete boundary data for the time-varying Maxwell equations based on electric field measurements, where the goal is to recover missing information on an inaccessible boundary segment using data from the accessible part of a confined domain. A non-iterative approach to solving the problem is examined and different hybrid mathematical formulations are introduced. Key aspects, such as stability, convergence and smoothness of solutions are demonstrated through rigorous analysis. Edge finite elements are employed to discretize the problem. Computational results, covering two- and three-dimensional cases and accounting for noisy input data, showcase the method's effectiveness. A sample application to electromagnetic tomography is also presented. This paper introduces the Federated Selective Aggregation (FedSA) challenge, a novel approach that allows a central server to instruct participating devices on which data to contribute to the model, based on an assessment of the informational value of their local data. We demonstrate that FedSA can significantly outperform traditional federated learning methods by tailoring the model updates to match the characteristics of the local data. However, we also show that devices may engage in malicious behavior, such as coordinating with each other and the central server, which can compromise security and prevent the benefits of FedSA from being realized. To address this issue, we devise two schemes to detect deception: one relies on a server that ranks devices based on the informational worth of their data, while the other involves each device generating a unique signature to prevent impersonation. Our results indicate that FedSA is capable of providing a more accurate model, while our detection strategies are effective in preventing dishonest behavior and ensuring the security and integrity of the data. Moreover, our investigation reveals that devices tend to cooperate up to a point at which the benefits of doing so are equated by the costs, which can be influenced by the design of the FedSA framework. We also highlight the potential applications of FedSA in scenarios such as mobility management and resource sharing, and we outline the challenges and potential future research directions for this novel approach. We analyze the rank growth of elliptic curves from rational numbers to quartic extensions in the Galois groups $S_4$ and $A_4$, and investigate how rank varies in different quartic fields for a fixed elliptic curve. Notably, under specific conditions, we establish the existence of an infinite number of $S_4$ quartic extensions where the rank of an elliptic curve doesn't increase compared to its rank over the rational numbers. This achievement is made possible by our development of methods to manage the 2-Selmer rank of elliptic curves within certain quadratic fields, enabling control of the rank in families of $S_4$ and $A_4$ quartic extensions. Our study also identifies relationships between the geometric properties of elliptic curves and their ranks within families of quartic extensions, including connections to automorphism and torsion element groups. We demonstrate that many highly secure cryptographic protocols based on elliptic curves can be broken if an elliptic curve with specific properties is employed. Moreover, our research provides strategies for determining the ranks of elliptic curves over quadratic and quartic extensions, using methods that combine advanced mathematical techniques with number theory and geometry. We focus on particular scenarios, such as elliptic curves with rational 2-torsion, to demonstrate our methods' applicability and the benefits of controlling the 2-Selmer rank. We highlight the potential risks and advantages of using certain quartic extensions in cryptographic applications. We propose an algorithm to find optimal quartic extensions for a given elliptic curve, based on our research which could be valuable for future development of cryptographic protocols based on number theory and geometry. We make our code available for finding the ranks of elliptic curves over quadratic and quartic extensions, which can be accessed at our website. We also thank our research collaborators, Steven Galvez, Hsiao-Di Chang, and Zhi-Hing Hsiao, for their valuable contributions to our work. We discuss the security vulnerabilities of our research and provide strategies for addressing them. We offer our code and research data for verification and further development. We hope our study will contribute to a deeper understanding of the relationships between elliptic curves, number theory, and cryptography, and encourage other researchers

Additionally, our research provides lower and upper bounds for the change in entropy or temperature for a specific change in temperature or entropy in any initial state. This work explores the long-term evolution of Venus's atmosphere, examining how its composition has been shaped by interior-exterior interactions over time. Despite significant ongoing research, key aspects of the atmosphere's formation and current state remain unclear and require interdisciplinary analysis. We examine various processes that have influenced the atmosphere's evolution, starting with volatile sources and examining interactions from the planet's core to its upper atmosphere, as well as atmospheric escape mechanisms. We also delve into the complex historical events that have contributed to the atmosphere's evolution, including the effects of impacts, magnetic field generation, and geochemical and geodynamic feedback cycles. We then outline plausible pathways for the planet's evolution, ranging from its accretion phase to its present state, using modeling and observations. These scenarios include atmospheric escape during the magma ocean phase, prolonged surface liquid water that eventually gave way to a runaway greenhouse phase, and water retained within the planet due to inefficient outgassing, leading to hydrogen entrapment in the core and mantle oxidation. We review the existing evidence and discuss the need for future research, as well as potential observations and missions required to better understand Venus's complex interior, surface, and atmospheric interactions and how they have influenced the planet's evolution and future. This report also presents three hypothetical missions that could provide such understanding, including a spacecraft that would study the planet's deep interior through gravity measurements and a surface robot that would examine the atmosphere and surface through a variety of techniques. We conclude that Venus needs to be studied in all its facets, from its core to its upper atmosphere, if we are to fully comprehend its complex evolution and changes over time. We also outline potential scientific discoveries waiting to be made, as well as potential technological advances resulting from Venus exploration, including potential uses of some technologies on Earth. This report is a foundation for ongoing discussions in the Venus scientific community, as well as a starting point for future planetary science and engineering endeavors. We recognize the significant challenges posed by the harsh environment, but also see opportunities for technological innovation and better understanding of key processes that have shaped the planet over time. We also outline potential Earth applications resulting from Venus research, including the potential for new technologies that could be transferred to other planetary bodies and the increased understanding of key Earth processes that could result from interdisciplinary analysis. This report will help guide future Venus research, as well as potential missions, in an effort to better understand the planet's complex interior, surface, and atmospheric interactions and how they have influenced the planet's evolution and future. We also outline the potential for Earth benefits resulting from Venus research

As high-power laser pulse capabilities increase, the limitations of traditional solid-state optics due to their restricted damage thresholds pose significant challenges, making the investigation of plasma-based components more compelling. We propose a novel type of plasma waveplate based on a specific magneto-optical property when subjected to a perpendicular magnetic field, allowing it to function under extremely high laser intensities. This component can modify the laser pulse polarization while simultaneously increasing the peak power, which has been demonstrated numerically with simulations. It shows that a high-intensity linearly polarized laser pulse can be converted to a higher-powered circularly polarized pulse. This conversion process achieves nearly complete efficiency, with approximately $98\%$ of the initial energy successfully converted. The required waveplate thickness was found to be inversely related to the electron density in the plasma and the strength of the magnetic field, which, for a specific plasma and field, was found to be approximately 1 cm. This type of plasma waveplate can serve a pivotal role in the effective deployment of multi-petawatt laser systems.
