We investigate decoding of rank metric codes under the assumption of a symmetric error matrix. Our analysis yields two main conclusions. Firstly, we show that for code rates less than half, there is a diverse class of rank metric codes capable of accurately decoding any symmetric error, even those of maximal rank. Moreover, this code class includes, as a subset, the family of Gabidulin codes with rates less than half. Secondly, we propose a method for correcting symmetric errors of up to n-k rank, which can be applied for code rates greater than half. Both of these decoding strategies are deterministic and provide guaranteed performance in the worst-case scenario. Our method also involves a probabilistic approach that yields a randomised, efficient algorithm for decoding symmetric errors of maximal rank n, which can be applied for code rates greater than half. As evidence of our code class's versatility, we include a discussion on how these codes can be used to solve a specific type of system of equations that arises in the context of symmetric decoding errors. Our research was motivated by the study of a particular system of equations which, in turn, was inspired by a problem related to the Cayley-Hamilton theorem. Our results provide a decoding framework that is an expansion of the existing literature on the subject. Our work also offers an encoding approach that is an adaptation of the Gabidulin code construction method. Furthermore, our research offers an alternative explanation of the Reed-Solomon code's error-correcting capability, which is similar to the original explanation given by Elia. Building upon previous work by \cite{Ferrara:1971vh}, \cite{Ferrara:1973vz}, we develop a comprehensive integral representation of conformal block operators in CFT$_2$, specifically tailored for spinning primary fields. Notably, this integral expression can be re-expressed as a product of two weighted AdS$_2$ field combinations when the primary fields in question are conserved, which results in the representation of conserved current conformal block operators in CFT$_2$ in terms of geodesic operators defined within the AdS$_2$ framework rather than the AdS$_3$ framework. Moreover, this new perspective enables a direct link between the AdS$_2$ geodesic operator representation and massless higher-spin fields in the AdS$_3$ framework, facilitated by the HKLL bulk field reconstruction method. By harnessing this new picture, we are able to derive a closed-form expression for the four-point conformal block involving spinning primary fields as a product of two AdS$_2$ geodesic Witten diagrams. This development paves the way for extending our analysis to spinning conserved current blocks within the context of the AdS$_3$ CFT$_2$ correspondence. In 1992, Gelfand and MacPherson established a local and combinatorial approach to calculating Pontrjagin classes for differentiable manifolds. We delve into the specifics of their method and examine the underlying principles of their groundbreaking concept of combinatorial differentiable manifolds. Additionally, we provide a detailed analysis of how to extend their approach to calculating Gauss-Bonnet Chern classes and other geometric invariants. Furthermore, we outline possible applications of these developments to point clouds and other discrete geometric settings. Given the diversity of topics covered, we have structured the material into six consecutive sections. We begin with a brief overview of Pontrjagin classes and primary research findings. The second section examines the combinatorial realization of Pontrjagin classes through the Gelfand-MacPherson method. The third section focuses on extending this approach to calculate Chern classes for complex vector bundles and other classes. The fourth section explores the Gauss-Bonnet Chern class theorem and its applications. The fifth section investigates possible generalizations to be made within the current framework. The sixth and final section discusses the potential for adapting these findings to the study of discrete geometric settings. We also touch on a result from the work of Steve Ferry concerning combinatorial realization of Pontrjagin classes, which is distinct from the Gelfand-MacPherson method. This result forms the basis for Ferry's subsequent study on the subject in his 1980 paper. We have structured our narrative with an eye towards integrating these diverse topics and incorporating recent research findings that build upon the foundations established by Gelfand and MacPherson. We have aimed to create a self-contained exploration that can be understood without referencing the original 1992 paper, which was written by pioneering researchers in the field. We have also included a comprehensive bibliography to facilitate further exploration of these topics. We are confident that our abstract provides a substantial contribution to the existing body of knowledge and hope it will find value in the mathematical community. We would like to express our gratitude to Steve Ferry for his invaluable guidance throughout this journey. We are also indebted to the anonymous referee whose thoughtful feedback significantly enhanced the content of this paper. We would like to acknowledge the support we received from the National Science Foundation as part of the Geometry and Topology program. We are proud to report that we have made a genuine attempt to adhere to the advice provided by the referee, which has resulted in an improved version of the paper. We hope that this revised edition will find an even wider audience

We obtained high-cadence photometric and spectroscopic data for SN~2020jfo in various wavelengths starting around day 3 up to day 434 after its explosion. SN~2020jfo, classified as a hydrogen-rich Type II supernova with a short plateau duration, had a notably faint absolute peak magnitude compared to other similar supernovae. Observations during the plateau phase revealed characteristic H-alpha absorption similar to other SNe~II. Furthermore, SN~2020jfo exhibited a prominent [Ni~II] line in its nebular-phase spectra, often observed in low-luminosity SNe~II. Using the ratio of [Ni~II] and [Fe~II] line strengths, we determined a nickel to iron abundance ratio 1.5 times the solar value. Progenitor mass estimates from nebular-phase and semi-analytical modelling placed SN~2020jfo's mass within the 12 to 15 solar mass range. Semi-analytical modelling also suggested the presence of a substantial hydrogen envelope in SN~2020jfo's progenitor, which is unlikely for Type II supernovae with short plateau phases. Therefore, SN~2020jfo's characteristics challenge current theoretical understanding of low-luminosity SNe~II and it highlights the need for mass-loss history and hydrogen envelope evolution studies. Moreover, SN~2020jfo's evolution in the colour-magnitude plane was unusual, exhibiting a rapid colour transformation from blue to red in the plateau phase. This behaviour is exceptional among the large sample of SNe~II at our disposal. Additionally, SN~2020jfo's interaction with its surrounding environment is evident from its nebular-phase spectra and possible central compact object detection in X-rays. Furthermore, the SN~2020jfo system exhibits similarities with the Pulsar Supernova Remnants (PSRs) and massive young stellar objects. Given its proximity, SN~2020jfo's massive remnant, narrow central jet, and possible pulsar wind nebula, present a compelling opportunity for multi-wavelength studies in the future. To greatly decrease the number of image sensors required in wide-field X-ray monitors employing lobster-eye (LE) optics, we propose a concept called multiplexed lobster-eye (MuLE) optics. This configuration involves dividing an LE mirror into multiple sections and using each one to direct X-rays onto a single shared image sensor. If each LE section is positioned at a different rotation angle, the optical system can determine the exact section responsible for focusing X-rays on the sensor. A simulation showed that the proposed MuLE arrangement consisting of 9 segments can effectively detect a signal with an energy of ~10^-10 erg cm^-2 s^-1. Furthermore, this system is highly effective in determining the source direction of an X-ray transient, which is critical for its use in future wide-field X-ray transient monitoring missions on small satellites. A possible application of this system design is the Transient X-ray Surveyor (TXS), which is expected to have a detection power ~10 times greater than that of the current X-ray transient monitors. However, this will require MuLE to significantly improve its background count rate. To achieve this, we are exploring the use of low-background CMOS image sensors and optimizing the system to minimize unnecessary X-ray reflections. If successful, the MuLE design could be highly beneficial for future X-ray transient monitoring missions. A prototype of the MuLE optic with 9 segments has been manufactured and testing is ongoing. If the current design is found to have a significant problem with count rate, we plan to modify the optic to a single segment LE design. A segment of the LE optic with an aperture of 30 cm x 30 cm and a focal length of 0.5 m is also being tested for its imaging performance with a CCD camera. If the results are satisfactory, we may use this large segment LE optic for the future TXS satellite, which is expected to have a detection power ~10 times greater than the current X-ray transient monitors. This satellite is also expected to be able to determine the direction of an X-ray transient source with an error of ~10 degrees, which is critical for finding the same source in follow-up observations. This approach yields an alternative proof of existence for solutions to these equations within specified domains. Furthermore, we address the issue of partial uniform ellipticity in the context of viscosity solutions to the Monge-Ampere equation, obtaining an estimate for the number of solutions and characterizing them as the largest possible sub-solutions to a certain family of equations. These results may be viewed as an expansion on existing findings by G. Cordier and L. Jeanblang, as well as S. K. Ko, T. Parc, and J. G. Chen. The former's work focused on bounded and convex domains, whereas the latter examined domains with specific angular points. The current study builds upon their findings by providing a level set formulation, which enables the use of a suitable growth estimate to obtain the desired partial uniform ellipticity, thus extending their results to any polynomially bounded domain. The study on the Monge-Ampere equation has of its key findings a characterization of the set of possible solutions as the largest sub-family of partial differential equations that satisfy a certain growth condition, when considering a given domain. To investigate the structure of dark matter, a deep learning framework was implemented and used to explore the impact of velocity and density information on the formation of halos through $N$-body cosmological simulations. A Convolutional Neural Network was trained on an initial snapshot of a dark matter simulation, with the goal of predicting halo masses at a given point in time, in a specific range of masses. However, when testing the inclusion of velocity information with the standard model of cosmology, negligible improvements were found. By increasing the amplitude of initial scalar perturbations in the simulation, a significant improvement was observed in the halo mass prediction when adding velocity field information. Ultimately, when the simulation parameters were modified further, models trained on density information alone failed to predict halo masses accurately, demonstrating the importance of velocity field effects on the halo collapse, particularly in certain mass scales. Furthermore, the research highlights the difficulty in reconciling results with the overmerger issue encountered in certain mass scales. Ultimately, the study emphasizes the difficulty of accurately predicting halo masses without incorporating velocity field information, especially in scenarios with altered cosmological parameters. The most striking finding was the large overestimation in halo masses, particularly at the lower end of the mass spectrum, without the inclusion of velocity field information, even in the standard model of cosmology. The current approach was found to struggle with the recovery of halo masses below $10^{8}$ solar masses. The research underscores the value of incorporating velocity field information in the prediction of halo masses in dark matter simulations. We have developed a novel numerical approach for achieving equilibrium configurations in rotating stars under the principles of general relativity. This method, tailored for quasi-static evolution applications, utilizes a Lagrangian formulation where fluid elements are located by solving balance equations, in contrast to the conventional Eulerian method. This innovative approach eschews the use of the Euler equation's first integral, often obtained analytically under simplifying conditions, in favor of assigning unique specific angular momentum to each fluid element. This allows for the creation of equilibrium configurations even in situations where angular momentum is not uniformly distributed across the star. As a demonstration of this method's capabilities, we successfully constructed equilibrium configurations for rotating stars of varying densities, including neutron stars, proto-neutron stars, and massive, compact quark stars, with densities ranging from $10^{10}$ to $10^{18}$ g/cm$^3$. These configurations were obtained through a direct solution, without the need to adjust for density or angular momentum until the desired state was achieved. This approach has been incorporated into a code that can be used for postmerger neutron star evolution. This code has been utilized in a simulation of a binary neutron star merger, resulting in a rotating, compact star with a density of approximately $10^{14}$ g/cm$^3$, and has further been applied to a scenario involving a merger between a neutron star and a black hole. In both instances, this method has proven to be a reliable and versatile tool for achieving equilibrium configurations in rotating stars under general relativity. This work is significant as it paves the way for an in-depth examination of postmerger neutron star evolution, particularly in a scenario involving binary neutron star mergers. This research has been a part of a larger project that entails simulation runs requiring multiple equilibrium configurations for each run, and as such, this method has been optimized for efficiency with minimal computational overhead. This code has been tested on high-performance computing systems and has been found to scale well with an increasing number of processing units. A major challenge in creating AI models that can automatically process and analyze visually complex documents such as invoices is acquiring a large, high-quality dataset to train these models. Our proposed approach, known as Selective Labeling, streamlines the labeling process by limiting the labels to simple "accept/reject" confirmations for model predictions made on partially annotated documents. This is paired with a specialized strategy for active learning, designed to identify and target model predictions with the highest levels of uncertainty. Our experiments on multiple document types across three different fields have shown that selective labeling can cut labeling costs by tenfold, without a noticeable decline in accuracy. Furthermore, our findings indicate that the current state-of-the-art approach to active learning, known as Easiest-First, often prioritizes documents that are actually already highly confident in their annotations, leading to an opportunity for a novel metric called Easiest-Last to address this challenge. Our contributions to the field include both practical and theoretical guidelines for selective labeling, as well as a transparent framework for other researchers to build upon. Our proposed techniques have been successfully applied to multiple challenging document types, including those found in fields like medicine, finance, and logistics, and are available online for others to use. Our code is accessible on GitHub at https://github.com/ghaith/Selective-Labeling. Our results also highlight the significant potential cost savings and improved model performance that can be achieved through selective labeling, offering a tangible solution to the costly labeling challenges faced by many document analysis applications. Our study is an initial step towards addressing the labeling challenges of deep learning documents, and we encourage further research in this area to explore additional opportunities for label efficiency. Our approach and associated metrics are applicable to a broad range of tasks and datasets, and we have made our code publicly available to facilitate widespread adoption. Urban settings are known to benefit economically and socially due to their diversity of physical and social interactions, which also contribute to community resilience. However, COVID-19-related mobility restrictions significantly reduced urban face-to-face interactions, prompting concerns about their lasting social effects. To explore these changes, this study uses a vast dataset containing one million anonymized users in four major US cities, spanning pre-pandemic to post-pandemic periods. It reveals a significant drop (by 15% to 30%) in urban diversity during the pandemic and into late 2021, despite overall mobility rates recovering to pre-pandemic levels. Furthermore, counterfactual analysis shows that the primary factors contributing to decreased diversity included increased home isolation and lower willingness to explore new places, with altered visitation preferences exacerbating this decline in the long term. Consequently, this research implies that the pandemic may have long-lasting adverse impacts on the income diversity of urban settings, with resulting implications for managing public health policies in a way that balances strict measures with promoting diversity of urban encounters beyond the pandemic era. It also highlights the significance of examining physical interactions at various urban scales and intervals to prevent misunderstanding aggregation effects, as seen in previous mobile data analyses. Moreover, policy-makers should consider diversity of urban encounters as a vital indicator to monitor in the post-pandemic period, as it can significantly influence local economic resilience and community diversity. It is advisable to explore the societal implications of the pandemic on urban diversity further by conducting more in-depth qualitative research among residents, as well as business owners and community leaders, to gain a richer understanding of this topic. It is also possible to utilize mobile data more effectively by incorporating additional variables and conducting cross-validation to enhance the reliability of the data. It is essential to note that the term diversity used in this study refers to the variety of encounters in urban settings, which may be related to diversity in a broader sense but is more precise in this specific context. It is also worth mentioning that the methodology used in this study can be applied to examine diversity in other settings that involve geographical mobility, such as tourist behaviour or refugee migration patterns. It is also noteworthy that the mobile data used in this study does not include data from tourists or non-resident visitors, which might limit the diversity indicators in some cases, but it was considered necessary to exclude these users to examine diversity among local populations in the studied urban settings. It is also worth mentioning that the duration of the pandemic period included in this study was relatively long, which allowed the researchers to detect changes in diversity during different pandemic phases

This research investigates complex systems that follow stochastic patterns by using mathematical structures known as random field models. The study focuses on analyzing a specific aspect of these systems – the geometry of their parametric space – using statistical tools to simulate and model the systems' dynamics. The results revealed an intriguing phenomenon dubbed the "curvature effect," where a significant increase in a system's disorder is associated with an irregular geometric change, linked to the emergence of an internal timeline that influences the systems' progression over time. The findings are further demonstrated to be broadly applicable across various system types, including mechanical structures, biological processes, and material transformations, utilizing real-world data examples. The study presents a theoretical model that simulates the interactions between a system's geometry, its curvature, and the consequences of curve point failure, offering insights into the systems' stability, reliability, and evolution over time. The research proposes a new statistical method that can be applied to unconventional time series data derived from random field models, enabling the prediction of system failures and the identification of critical time points in their development. The study's conclusions are supported by numerical examples and graphical animations, in addition to theoretical model simulations. The proposed method has been tested on both synthetic and real-world data sets, leading to a system failure prediction accuracy of 80% in the data sets analyzed. Traditionally, annotated data have served as inputs for supervised machine learning models. Yet, contemporary pre-trained natural language processing models possess linguistic knowledge that can, in turn, be leveraged to guide the annotation process. In this work, we employ BERT to facilitate the semantic labeling of a game-based interaction dataset called EMO20Q. Following an in-depth analysis of BERT's performance on tasks within this dataset, we provide explicit labeling guidance to overcome limitations and improve accuracy. Our results indicate a significant reduction in labeling errors and demonstrate the potential for using such models as intermediate annotator guides across various interaction data sets. Furthermore, our optimized annotation framework yields a 24.7% increase in inter-annotator agreement among human annotators. We also present a unified labeling framework that we believe can be applied to other annotated data sets incorporating textual descriptions of behaviors and emotions. Our code and data are available at https://github.com/QiLi1991/EMO20Q-BERT.

For mobile robots to successfully navigate unfamiliar surroundings independently, having an effective mapping system is crucial. Current mapping approaches rely heavily on state estimation techniques that minimize drifting and produce a unified global map for navigation. Unfortunately, implementing these systems on a large scale can be challenging due to their tendency to deviate and slow build-up times. In response to these limitations, a novel map representation called HiTMap is presented, featuring a unique hierarchical structure that focuses solely on a local metric map for obstacle avoidance while navigating, without attempting to create an exhaustive representation of the environment. By reducing the map representation to a basic minimum, HiTMap significantly enhances building and tracking capabilities, thereby enabling mobile robots to efficiently navigate more complex and expansive unknown environments. Experimental data illustrates the advantages of HiTMap in comparison to conventional mapping methods, demonstrating its ability to successfully navigate areas up to 32 times larger than those mapped by the HiTMap system itself. Furthermore, HiTMap's scalability has been successfully demonstrated in both indoor and outdoor scenarios. A point of focus for this research was to ensure that the HiTMap system is computationally efficient and simple to implement, as evidenced by the fact that a hi-resolution HiTMap can be built and continuously updated by a robot within a matter of seconds. A key component of the HiTMap system is a novel mapping algorithm called HiTMapBuilder, which incorporates a unique hierarchical structure to prioritize map creation based on a risk assessment of each area, thereby ensuring that the robot explores the most informative regions first. In addition, HiTMap has been successfully applied to a variety of challenging navigation scenarios, including those that require crossing intersections, for which it has been found to be more efficient than HiTMap without a global map. In one such experiment, HiTMap was found to be 3.6 times more efficient in navigating a large, complex environment than the version without a global map. A related issue to mapping in independent mobile robots is the problem of place recognition, for which HiTMap has been found to be highly effective, with an 80% success rate in recognizing places that are up to 32 times larger than those originally mapped. In one such experiment, a robot was able to recognize a place that was 20 times larger than the map it was based on, after navigating it for an extended period of time. Despite this limitation, a range of applications, including real-world programs with inherent object structures, have been overlooked for parallelization opportunities.  Our research identified a particular subset of object-oriented programming called Single-Method Multiple-Objects (SMMO), which can be efficiently parallelized on SIMD devices by executing the same method across multiple objects of a given type.  To facilitate easy adoption of high-speed GPU programming for average developers, we created the DynaSOAr CUDA framework specifically tailored for SMMO applications.  This framework includes a dynamic memory allocator that is both lock-free and parallel, a data layout domain-specific language (DSL), and a do-all operation that is both parallel and efficient.  As a result, DynaSOAr offers improved memory usage, reduced fragmentation, and superior performance to leading state-of-the-art GPU memory allocators by concurrently managing both memory allocation and memory access through atomic operations.  Furthermore, DynaSOAr's approach allows for significant speedup and memory management efficiency gains, as demonstrated in our benchmark results, where it achieves application code performance improvements of up to 3 times and supports larger problem sizes of up to 2 times with the same memory.  As an added benefit, DynaSOAr's memory allocator can also be used independently as SpinLock-Free-MemoryAllocator (SFMA).  To facilitate easy adoption of high-speed GPU programming for average developers, we also established guidelines for converting existing applications to SMMO.  Our DynaSOAr framework and associated tools have been thoroughly tested and are now publicly available to support the scientific community in further enhancing SMMO applications. The NASA $TESS$ mission's comprehensive sky survey allows the detection of rarest transiting planetary systems. In a new discovery, we found a young star called TOI-712, hosting a system of four planets orbiting it. By analyzing $TESS$ data, the team established that the star rotates in about 12.48 days and has an age ranging from approximately $500$ million to 1.1 billion years. Observations from $TESS$ revealed three mini-Neptune-sized planets with distinct periods of $9.531$ days, $51.699$ days, and $84.839$ days. Additionally, the team detected an Earth-sized candidate called TOI-712.05 with a short orbital period of $4.32$ days. By calculating the habitable zone for this system, TOI-712 d appears to lie on the inner boundary, and further research into TOI-712, with a brightness of $9.9$, is worthwhile due to its relatively young and temperate conditions. This discovery was also presented in another study conducted by the same authors which explored the possible histories of the four-planet system based on planetary migration currents. According to their analysis, the team believed that the two smaller planets, with periods of $4.32$ days and $9.53$ days, might have experienced intense gravitational interactions that led to the ejection of TOI-712 d into an highly elliptical orbit and possibly TOI-712 b into a close orbit around the star. This scenario could have occurred as a result of a mean motion orbital resonance that was triggered by one of the smaller planets getting caught in the 12.48 day stellar tidal lock, and ultimately led to the destruction of one planet through gravitational interaction. This hypothesis is plausible given the detected star's characteristics, such as its rapid rotation and young age, and also considering the vast array of unstable orbital resonances that the planets could have encountered during their migration. If this hypothesis is confirmed, the TOI-712 system could serve as a prime example of how intense orbital resonances can lead to the formation of hot Jupiters and the eventual planetesimal disk migration current's power to reshape entire planetary systems even after the end of their formation. If the Earth-sized candidate's orbit is confirmed, the team suggested that TOI-712 could also represent a rare case where they were able to detect an Earth-sized planet that was affected by orbital resonance and ultimately survived it. We investigated the electronic and magnetic properties of carbon and nitrogen defects within rutile TiO2.  To accurately simulate these properties, we utilized a 48-atom supercell through the VASP code, relaxing both atomic positions and cell dimensions to minimize errors. The results indicate that substitutional carbon and nitrogen defects have a tendency for anti-ferromagnetic long-range ordering with corresponding magnetic moments of 2$\mu B$ and 1$\mu B$ for carbon and nitrogen respectively.  Conversely, nitrogen defects positioned interstitially possess a fixed magnetic moment of 1$\mu B$ whereas carbon defects positioned interstitially display no magnetism.  Moreover, calculations demonstrate that interstitial N defects lie at a saddle point in the total energy landscape, and that a more stable configuration is reached when these atoms bond with oxygen in a CO or NO dimer.  Notably, this outcome is consistent with earlier experimental findings utilizing XPS that also identified such N-O bonds, and could potentially be verified via spectroscopic techniques.  Moreover, both doped carbon and nitrogen defects reside within the band gap of TiO2.  We propose that tuning TiO2 by introducing such defects could enhance its photocatalytic properties.  To further analyze this, we calculated the CBM and VBM of TiO2 with defects and found that they could be tuned by up to 0.46 eV, and that this value is directly proportional to the distance of the defect from the surface.  We also investigated the mobility of these defects under applied electric fields and at 300K, and found that while some of the defects could become mobile, others could persist for extended periods of time.  We propose that these defects could reside within the interface of TiO2 and other materials, and that understanding their properties could be crucial for optimizing nanostructures based on TiO2. I demonstrate the feasibility of identifying the semi-elastic process using a dataset of 300 inverse picobarns of data, and the fully elastic process appears inaccessible. Finally, I show that the elastic process is too difficult to detect and the most promising application is effectively limited to semi-elastic production measurements or rare decay identifications in the elastic process with initial state radiation. In such cases, I outline the potential for limits on other rare decays like $t\rightarrow uW^-$ which could be $1.5$ times more stringent than the current limits set by the Tevatron. Our analysis highlights the benefits of using qudits instead of qubits in scalar Quantum Electrodynamics in $(1+1)$d, specifically regarding their tolerance to errors. When measuring the mass gap using an out-of-time correlator as noise increases from both amplitude damping and Pauli channels, our findings reveal that simulations utilizing qutrits can handle up to 10 to 100 times more gate noise than their qubit-based counterparts for the same mass determination error. Furthermore, while achieving a 20 percent accuracy for the mass gap may become achievable in the near future using qutrits, the same outcome seems unrealistic with qubits. These qudits' advantages can be attributed to qutrits' reduced entropy generation during operations, which directly influences the scalability of qudits in relation to their dimensionality. Moreover, our results demonstrate that dimensionality equivalent to qutrits, specifically using four-dimensional qudits, yield similar outcome patterns, allowing for a certain degree of replacement when studying qudits. Our research underscores the significance of fault-tolerance studies in quantum computations and provides actionable insights for developing future low-error quantum systems. Research indicates that positrons are efficiently produced through interactions between intense lasers and solid materials, specifically within the context of strong-field quantum electrodynamics. However, the polarization properties of these positrons remain unknown, hindering potential uses. Our study utilizes particle-in-cell simulations accounting for the polarization of photons and the spin of electrons and positrons to analyze the effects of an extremely intense linearly polarized laser on a thin, micrometer-scale target pre-heated by a thin layer of plasma. The results show that, when the number of generated positrons becomes substantial at intensities exceeding 10 to the power of 24 Watts per square centimeter, the produced positrons exhibit notable polarization properties. In fact, the polarization of the positrons can reach over thirty percent, with an accumulated charge exceeding 30 nanocoulombs, emitted with an enormous intensity of ten to the power of 12 per unit steradian. The degree of polarization is influenced by the angle of the emitted particles and their corresponding energies. In particular, the polarization is maximized at certain angles and reaches levels as high as sixty percent, primarily due to the unique interaction between the positrons and the intense laser fields within the overdense plasma. The occurrence of positron polarization is relatively robust, thereby likely manifesting in experiments using high-power lasers interacting with dense targets, with potential for a wide range of applications. The expected future increase in laser capabilities will only enhance the efficacy of these experiments. The degree of polarization can be further manipulated by modifying the target parameters, such as the thickness and size of the target. The findings of our research are supported by in-depth physical explanations obtained from reduced models, including the classic one-dimensional "pancake" model and the random laser-plasma interaction model. The discovered property of positron polarization opens up a new dimension for particle production in laser-plasma interactions, thereby paving the way for potential usage in quantum physics and matter production experiments. The impact of the polarization of electrons and positrons due to laser fields needs to be considered in various applications, such as quantum electrodynamics, where the collision of an electron and a positron with polarized spins may result in the production of particles like neutrinos and scalar Higgs bosons. The availability of polarized positrons will significantly broaden the capabilities of existing particle production experiments, such as those mentioned above, as well as those involving the production of exotic atoms, like positronium with zero total angular momentum. Given a finite group G and a subset S of G's generating elements, the smallest possible diameter is defined as the minimum number n, such that any element of G can be expressed as the product of up to n elements from S. This research focuses on characterizing groups with a diameter that scales polynomially for a fixed-sized generating set, and it demonstrates that these groups have a significant abelian subgroup close to their highest order, making up a substantial fraction of the group's total size. This finding reinforces an important result established by Breuillard and Tointon and implies that groups with a polynomial diameter contain multiple conjugacy classes and a large nilpotent subgroup with a maximum class of two. Furthermore, this result can be applied to provide evidence for the polynomial diameter conjecture when considering groups with a certain growth rate and those with a specific structure, including soluble groups and certain classes of finite simple groups. Additionally, it provides an explanation for the restricted diameters found in certain groups, including finite field multiplicative groups and specific classes of finite simple groups. Moreover, it gives an upper bound for the diameter of polynomial diameter groups, specifically it is less than sqrt(n), where n represents the number of generating elements. This research was initially presented at the 32nd British Combinatorial Conference held in 2022. Both the proof and its applications were jointly established with Thomas Breuer, Nadiya Dorid, Erika Meijer, Luke Tointon, and Thomas Weighill. This research develops a fully-integrated CMOS temperature sensor, enabling precise thermal monitoring in complex systems that employ adaptive voltage and frequency scaling. The temperature sensor module leverages a sub-threshold PMOS circuit to convert temperature readings into two corresponding biasing currents, which in turn influence two distinct oscillation frequencies in direct proportion to the absolute temperature. The resulting digital temperature value is obtained by converting the frequency ratio in the sensor module's digital backend. With a simple and efficient design, the temperature sensor offers a minimal footprint, extremely low power consumption, and accurate temperature readings over a broad temperature range. Moreover, the design includes a straightforward voltage regulation mechanism, enabling it to accommodate dynamic voltage scaling. The proposed design was implemented in a 180nm CMOS process, featuring a -100{\deg}C to 0{\deg}C temperature range, a wide supply voltage range from 0.6V to 1.8V, and an incredibly compact silicon area of 0.021$mm^2$. Experimental results from 20 test chips revealed outstanding performance characteristics, including a 0.24{\deg}C resolution, a 1.4{\deg}C maximum inaccuracy, a 1.5kHz sampling rate, and an energy per conversion of 1.06nJ at 30{\deg}C. The temperature sensor was successfully integrated into a voltage and frequency scaling system, demonstrating a 12{\deg}C thermal range without dynamic scaling, and displaying excellent energy and frequency scaling characteristics. In summary, this research presents a groundbreaking fully-integrated temperature sensor that can be employed in complex systems featuring adaptive voltage and frequency scaling, and boasts an unparalleled combination of precision, efficiency, and compactness. A functioning voltage and frequency scaling system based on this temperature sensor was also developed and tested. The design files for the temperature sensor have been made available online, and the research provides valuable insights for the creation of high-performance temperature sensors and voltage and frequency scaling systems. Furthermore, the temperature sensor microchip is available for research purposes at the TU Delft Solid-State Institute, and interested parties can contact the institute to request access. The research paper was published in the IEEE Transactions on Very Large Scale Integration (VLSI) Systems journal. A working voltage and frequency scaling system based on this temperature sensor was also developed and tested, and the design files are available online. A statistical analysis of 1.3 mm continuum cores from the Dragon infrared dark cloud reveals an interesting disparity between cores associated with molecular outflows, specifically protostellar and starless cores.  Protostellar cores are found to possess greater mass than their starless counterparts, with mass discrepancies holding true even after correcting for the effects of temperature and opacity.  We interpret this observed mass difference as a sign of mass growth among cores, with far-reaching implications for the origin of massive star formation.  In essence, it challenges the conventional view that massive star formation must originate from massive prestellar cores.  Further research is necessary to thoroughly explore this finding's effect on the established correlation between the mass function of prestellar cores and the mass function of the newly formed stars.  It's also crucial to investigate the possible role of turbulence in the formation of proto-stellar cores with reduced mass reservations, as this study's limitation of 10 solar masses is too low to encompass the C$^{18}$O integral intensity characteristics of many cores within the Dragon cloud.  Ultimately, the discovery of this mass distribution function could be a manifestation of a larger phenomenon, possibly linked to the massive molecular gas reservoirs found within infrared dark clouds.  As such, it's vital to explore the relationship between this mass distribution and the larger scale environment, as this could hold the key to understanding the complex formation processes of massive stars and gas reservoirs within infrared dark clouds.  It's also worth noting that this study's results are specific to the Dragon cloud, and more research is necessary to establish a universal core mass distribution. Recurrences in positive definite functions, especially concerning the underlying space dimension, have been widely utilized in various applications. These recurrences are often linked to the characteristics of a system of special functions, representing the geometric properties of the underlying space. The (strict) positive definiteness of zonal functions, defined on the sphere, relies on the expansion coefficients of these functions in Gegenbauer polynomials. The recent breakthrough demonstrates the applicability of conventional differentiation and integration methods that maintain positive definiteness, although they alter the space dimension by increments of two. To address the need for a dimension increase of one, this paper creates specialized operators acting on the Gegenbauer polynomials and guaranteeing the preservation of (strict) positive definiteness. The development of these operators is motivated by the theory of orthogonal polynomials, drawing on the characteristics of Jacobi polynomials. The resulting dimension increase method is applicable to a broad class of Gegenbauer polynomials, including those with polynomial factors. The applications of these operators are demonstrated through the examination of a specific example. The study acknowledges the contributions of H. G. Schmerer and modifies the dimension increase operator to accommodate the requirements of C. Rvaceva's construction, leading to the generation of positive definite functions with respect to the Lobachevski space characteristic. The discussion also delves into the characteristics of these operators within the context of the harmonic transform. The flow of complex liquids is significantly influenced by surface roughness, especially at interfaces. Through a combined approach using stress measurements and visual observations, we analyzed the effects of different surface roughness on dry liquid foams during motion. We have demonstrated the existence of three distinct friction modes: surface slippage, stick-slip behavior, and stationary soap films. The accuracy of our stress measurements has been validated for the surface slippage and stationary regimes by referencing existing models. Furthermore, we propose a new "leverage rule" to explain stress patterns during the stick-slip regime. The occurrence of the stick-slip or stationary regimes is governed by a roughness factor that considers the relationship between the size of surface asperities and the curvature of Plateau borders. The information we obtained is relevant to various applications involving the flow of complex liquids and could be extended to other non-newtonian fluids. Additionally, we highlight the fundamentals of surface physics that enable surfaces to slip and stick with respect to fluid interfaces. The distinct ways that surface roughness affects the stress experienced by dry liquid foams during motion have been highlighted, along with any observed patterns of stress displacement hysteresis in the stick-slip regime. The relevance of our findings to the work of others in the field has been emphasized, and the potential existence of the stationary regime has been proposed as an explanation for the stick-slip behavior observed in some experiments involving solid surfaces and fluids. The importance of considering surface roughness in modeling fluid mechanics has been discussed, along with the potential extensions of our research to other non-newtonian fluids and liquids within partially filled capsules. The existence of a minimum curvature threshold for the formation of hills during foam drainage has been confirmed. This report details our methods that led to 3rd and 4th place rankings in tasks 1 and 2 at the 2019 ISIC challenge, focused on using images and metadata for skin cancer diagnosis. A dataset with nine classes was utilized, although one class is considered anomalous and not included in the data. To address the challenge, we employed a multi-classifier ensemble consisting of 13 convolutional neural networks (CNN), and devised two methods to handle the outlier class. Additionally, we proposed an intuitive approach to integrate metadata with images. Our findings demonstrate consistency with previous challenges, and our strategies for identifying the outlier class and utilizing metadata were found to be effective. Furthermore, priority lists for addressing tasks 1 and 2 were determined through statistical analysis. Our results showed that models struggled with the outlier class and with distinguishing between classes that had similar visual and textual characteristics. This model has the ability to smoothly transition between the equations of state for dark energy and dust at different cosmological epochs, by asymptotically interpolating between two power laws. A constant viscosity coefficient underlies the model's dissipative component. Using a phase space analysis, we investigate the model's dynamics in a framework that is robust and solution-independent. Our analysis of the model relies on constraints derived from both its asymptotic behavior and numerous observational limits. Through numerical computations, we solve the Hubble parameter equation, which yields results when plotted against a set of current Hubble data. Our analysis of the model reveals that despite its quintessence-like nature, it surpasses the phantom barrier. To assess the model's predictions for the universe's evolution, we investigate the development of the deceleration parameter, the cosmic density, and the effective equation of state parameter for both the model and its embedded dark energy component. Our findings also support a value of 8 × 10^6 Pa.s for the model's current-day viscosity coefficient, which corroborates several past studies. This model has the capability to effectively explain the observed evolution of the cosmos. Our projection for the model's future predicts that the universe will eventually enter a stage of accelerated expansion similar to that simulated by a Lambda-CDM model, but with a constant acceleration that is instead driven by the model's viscous component. Our study concludes by outlining several open research questions, especially with regard to the model's predictions for certain gravitational waves signals and its ability to simulate the large-scale structure of the cosmos. Our research investigates the implications of the J/ψ particle decaying into invisible matter for light sterile neutrinos and sub-GeV dark matter. To understand these phenomena, we use low-energy effective field theories to describe general neutrino interactions and a type of dark matter linked to the charm quark. We analyzed J/ψ decay into a photon and invisible matter by conducting likelihood fits for individual neutrino and dark matter operators with varying Lorentz structures and photon spectrums. These analyses led to lower bounds on new energy scales based on neutrino or dark matter scenarios. Specifically, the most stringent limits on energy scales were found to be 12.8 GeV for neutrinos and 11.6 GeV for dark matter within their respective effective field theories. We also found that J/ψ decay into purely invisible matter imposes additional constraints on certain effective operators, with energy scales above 100 GeV for scalar and tensor operators that would contradict their own necessity. We have made our fitting code public to facilitate further research into related topics. Our study paves the way for J/ψ experiments to test light sterile neutrinos and sub-GeV dark matter connected to the charm quark, and we suggest combining searches for visible J/ψ decays to strengthen the limits further. Our research can be extended to other initial states, such as gluons, by incorporating relevant parton distribution functions. Our findings highlight the potential of J/ψ experiments to significantly constrain various neutrino and dark matter scenarios that cannot be tested by other existing experiments. Our code can be found at https://github.com/liyuanzheng/JPsi Invisible. This work introduces multivariate functional singular spectrum analysis (MFSSA) across various dimensional domains, building on the foundations of multivariate singular spectrum analysis (MSSA). We offer a comprehensive framework consisting of theoretical underpinnings and a step-by-step implementation guide for the algorithm. Our research demonstrates the effectiveness of MFSSA through comparative studies of reconstruction accuracy in multivariate functional time series (MFTS) and real-world applications, including the analysis of intraday temperature curves and remote sensing images of vegetation. Additionally, MFSSA is made available through the Rfssa R package for user convenience. 

Here is the code for the example discussed in the paper:

```r
library(rfssa)
library(fda)
library(mffda)

set.seed(1234)

n <- 100
t <- seq(0, 1, length.n = n)
f1 <- sin(2 * pi * 5 * t) + sin(2 * pi * 10 * t)
f2 <- sin(2 * pi * 3 * t) + sin(2 * pi * 15 * t)
f3 <- sin(2 * pi * 7 * t) + sin(2 * pi * 21 * t)

X <- cbind(f1 + rnorm(n) * 0.1, f2 + rnorm(n) * 0.1, f3 + rnorm(n) * 0.1)
X <- mffda(X, t)

ssa <- mfssa(X, nssa = 3, gamma = 0.1)
plot(sssa$reconstructed, main = "Reconstructed signals")
plot(sssa$trend, main = "Trend components")
```

To address this challenge, researchers have been exploring methods of automatic nucleus segmentation based on point annotation, which has been applied to various types of cancers, including lung, breast, and stomach cancers, among others. In the context of dynamic data streams, where Euclidean space points are added or removed from a dataset, we develop a one-pass coreset algorithm for solving the $k$-means clustering problem. Our solution employs storage capacity of approximately $k$ times a polynomial of $d$ dimensions and base-2 logarithm of $\Delta$, making it the first algorithm for this problem to utilize dimension-dependent storage while maintaining linear dependence on the target center count $k$. We construct this coreset using a single pass through the data, requiring only $O(kd^2 \log \Delta)$ updates and $O(kd^2 \log \Delta)$ queries among other operations. As a result, we surpass previous bounds on storage and time complexity in the coreset framework. Furthermore, we demonstrate how to adapt this coreset to solve the $k$-means clustering problem in the streaming setting, resulting in an algorithm with storage capacity of $O(kd^2 \log \Delta)$. We achieve this by creating a weighted version of the coreset, leading to a significant improvement over the current best solution, which has a storage capacity of $O(kd^2 \cdot \mathrm{poly}(\sqrt{d}))$, while maintaining a near-optimal time complexity of nearly linear with respect to the number of input points. We introduce a novel hierarchical strategy for large-scale discrete stochastic pursuit-evasion games on grid worlds by dividing the environment into macro-level sectors. This approach splits decision-making into two separate resolutions: a set of smaller-scale games at the sector level and a larger-scale game encompassing all sectors. Our method leverages the advantages of both small-scale and large-scale game solutions. The hierarchical approach enables us to tackle previously insurmountable large-scale games and our results reveal significant performance gains when compared to non-hierarchical implementations. Furthermore, our hierarchy can be easily extended to accommodate additional constraints such as observations and variable sector sizes. We demonstrate the efficacy of our hierarchical framework through extensive simulations and the capture or evasion of targets in grid worlds. Our data is available for download at https://doi.org/10.7910DEV/ASG. We also offer a Python implementation of our method at https://github.com/hgsong/hierarchicalPEG. Despite the grid world restriction, our framework provides a viable solution for a broader range of discrete state spaces. We highlight potential future applications and offer guidelines for their adaptation. We propose possible future adaptations for three such scenarios: a fully observable discrete state space, a semi-observable discrete state space, and a state space defined by a graph. We provide examples of such discrete state spaces including traffic flows, population dynamics, and social networks. We offer these examples as a starting point for further exploration in the context of our hierarchical PEG framework. We anticipate our hierarchical strategy could be beneficial in these scenarios following additional development. We intend to investigate these possibilities in the hope of expanding the scope of our hierarchical framework to a wider range of applications. In multi-task reinforcement learning, using shared representations can greatly
benefit a learner when it comes to solving a variety of tasks. While this
synergy is evident in model-free methods using shared policy networks, our study
investigates the benefits of shared dynamics models in model-based multi-task
reinforcement learning settings. Surprisingly, our findings indicate that using
a single learned dynamics model for multiple tasks may actually decrease the
performance and lead to task confusion. To overcome this, we show that isolating
sub-networks for each task, while keeping the parameter count constant, yields
substantial improvements in performance. We validate our approach by applying
these methods to both simple gridworld and more challenging multi-task Vizdoom
scenarios. Our approach is called separable recurrent multi-task agent (SeRMA)
and our results demonstrate significant performance gains over current state-of-the-
art multi-task dynamics models. Our code is available at https://github.com/tinghui/SeRMA.

We synthesize Godel's First Incompleteness Theorem from 1931, along with Tarski's Undefinability Theorem from 1933, the Diagonal Lemma attributed to Godel-Carnap in 1934, and a strengthened form of the first incompleteness theorem by Rosser from 1936, whose respective proofs show striking similarities and utilize the same fundamental techniques. We demonstrate how these theorems can be derived from a single, self-contained argument establishing the impossibility of creating a formal system that is capable of capturing basic properties of formal systems itself. This line of reasoning, which we call "metametarithmetic", consistently yields the following results: within a formal system, the inability to accurately define the notion of a formal system; the truth of any statement within the system is equivalent to the statement itself; the impossibility of proving any statement from the system's axioms; and most notably, the impossibility of creating a formal system that is both complete and consistent. These outcomes provide a concise and unified explanation for the fundamental limitations described by Godel's and Tarski's theorems. This research was initially presented as part of my PhD thesis at the Australian National University in 2010. This work has since been developed further in the book "The Incompleteness Theorems: A Source Book" where all relevant documentation can be found. This synthesis has been submitted to the arXiv repository and is a modified version of those previous works. This line of reasoning has significant implications for various areas of mathematics and philosophy, and it has been explored in detail elsewhere. This document is intended to serve as a concise introduction to these ideas rather than a comprehensive examination. This synthesis has been submitted to a number of academic journals for consideration. In solving inverse problems, researchers try to restore a degraded or incomplete image based on available data. This is crucial in imaging techniques such as MRI, computed tomography, deblurring and super-resolution, among others. Because there can be multiple plausible images given the measurements and prior information, the focus isn't solely on recovering a single ideal solution, but rather on exploring and sampling from a set of probable outcomes - the posterior distribution. We developed a method to generate a multitude of high-quality samples per second from the posterior distribution by using a regularized conditional Wasserstein GAN, which outperformed current methods according to Fr\'{e}chet inception distance metrics in applications like MRI with multiple coils and image inpainting. Additionally, our evaluations using quantitative measures such as structural and texture similarity indicated that our model produced results of equal quality when compared to the state-of-the-art. A regularized conditional Wasserstein GAN is simply a type of Wasserstein GAN with an additional constraint that ensures optimal transport plans between the target distribution and prior distribution are realized, which significantly slows down computation. However, by switching to a natural parameter update rule, we were able to derive a fast and efficient algorithm to train the model. The regularized version also significantly reduced artifacts in generated samples. The proposed method can be used in various inverse problems, including those mentioned above, as well as other image synthesis tasks. Code is available at https://github.com/lyh792/cwgan. The current implementation has limitations when applied to large images due to memory constraints. The suggested method can handle commodity-grade computer resolutions up to 512x512. The proposed CWGAN achieved the lowest FID scores to date on tasks like 'MRI with multi-coils' and 'image inpainting', and showed comparable performance on others when compared to the current state-of-the-art. This article examines the concept of invariant manifolds in dynamical systems from a stability perspective. We offer a concise overview of invariant sets, then proceed to explore conditions for specific invariant configurations in polynomial systems and fractional-order systems. Specifically, we outline the requirements for the preservation of invariant lines and parabolas in planar systems and the conditions under which linear subspaces remain invariant in fractional-order systems. We also discuss a notable result highlighting that in fractional-order systems, only linear subspaces can serve as invariant manifolds. Moreover, we highlight a key finding that parabolas or any nonlinear invariant set cannot exist in the presence of fractional derivatives. We also touch on the challenges faced in identifying methods for determining invariant sets in the presence of delayed terms. We review the relationship between invariant sets and equilibria, discussing how equilibria are specialized cases of invariant sets that are hyperbolic, where we also touch on the challenges faced in determining the stability of equilibria in the presence of delays. We also examine the dynamics on invariant manifolds in the presence of time delays, discussing the emergence of periodic oscillations in such systems. We review the core results obtained thus far, highlighting the difficulties faced in extending the current knowledge on the dynamics on invariant sets in the presence of time delays, and we also touch on the need for further research in this area. The interstellar medium is home to many scattering screens, most of which have unconfirmed origins. Pulsar scintillation observations can reveal these screens and their properties. This paper examines 34 years of data from Arecibo observations of the pulsar PSR B1133+16, resulting in detailed dynamic spectra and their associated scintillation patterns, likely created by screens in the line of sight to the pulsar. Six separate screens were identified that produce persistent scintillation patterns, enduring for several decades. Under the assumption that the screens remain largely unchanged over time, models of scintillation patterns throughout the Earth's orbit allowed for extraction of data about the screens, including their positions, distances, and velocities. The research yields measurements of six screens in the line of sight to PSR B1133+16, with four of these screens located within a few parsecs of the pulsar and two of these screens associated with molecular clouds. The study further reveals that these screens, even when unassociated with the nearby interstellar medium, still manage to create distinct scintillation patterns on Earth, demonstrating the interstellar medium's ability to generate lasting footprints, reflecting the persistent influence of scattering screens on the surrounding environment. The findings also highlight the capability to explore screens at greater distances, as demonstrated by the discovery of a screen around which a search was conducted following the initial detection of scintillation patterns, a search that was successful upon repetition of the observations two years later. The research highlights the significance of repeated long-term observations of pulsars, which can uncover intricate details of the interstellar medium, even in crowded regions of space. The data used in this study have been integrated into a new database known as ISCREEN, a collection of scattering screens in the interstellar medium. The database includes information about screen geometry, velocity, distance, mass, and density, alongside related data, which can be utilized for future research, including possible comparisons with molecular cloud databases, such as LISM walls and the Taurus wall. The relationship between the screens and the surrounding molecular clouds raises questions about the formation and destruction of these screens, which could be explored through further analysis of existing databases and future observations, possibly involving next-generation telescopes like next-generation Very Large Array. The most distant screen found in the research, at a distance of 5.7 parsecs, exhibits a screen mass of approximately 1.5 solar masses and a density of 10 particles per cubic centimeter, making it one of the most densely populated screens ever discovered.

This paper presents a generative model called Quasi-Periodic WaveNet (QPNet) to enhance the limited pitch control of WaveNet (WN) through pitch-dependent dilated convolution neural networks. WN achieves high-fidelity audio generation using stacked dilated convolution layers as an autoregressive probabilistic model. However, the lack of prior knowledge and the pure data-driven nature of WN lead to pitch control difficulties, particularly in modeling periodic signal components for inputs outside the training frequency range. To overcome this challenge, QPNet is proposed with two innovations. Firstly, the network adapts to given auxiliary frequency features via dynamic PDCNN architecture changes. Secondly, a cascaded network design is used to model long- and short-term signal dependencies in speech and other quasi-periodic signals. Experimental evaluations of QPNet demonstrate the benefits of PDCNNs for unseen frequency inputs and the cascaded structure's performance in speech synthesis. Additionally, QPNet is applied to generate unknown frequency speech and a nonlinear piano sound spectrum, showcasing its versatile quasi-periodic signal generation capabilities. Code is available at: https://github.com/kevin4898/Quasi-Periodic-WaveNet.

The theory of shadows constitutes an axiomatic bicategorical framework, extending and matching key characteristics of topological Hochschild homology (THH), notably preserving properties akin to Morita invariance. Through the incorporation of Berman's extension of THH to bicategories, it is demonstrated that functors from the THH of a bicategory are equivalent to shadows of that bicategory, ultimately establishing a direct relationship between them. Furthermore, this connection serves as the basis for an intuitive proof of the invariance of shadows under Morita equivalence. Additional results include the derivation of a composite functor from the THH of a bicategory to the shadow context, as well as an examination of the shadows associated with coherent functors, leading to the consideration of a projective model structure on coherent functors defined by Cartan-Eilenberg's descent theory. This, in turn, facilitates the retrieval of the THH of a coherent bicategory through the development of a left Quillen functor from the projective model structure on coherent functors to the shadow context. A concluding section explores the applicability of this framework to context-aware topological cyclic homology (TCHHC). A dedicated appendix addresses the challenge of categorifying coherent functors via monadic functors, ultimately arriving at a notion of shadows for coherent bicategories. A subsequent section in the appendix concentrates on the specific case of Bicategorical Recollement, presenting a representative application of the earlier developed shadows' framework. A second appendix provides the details for the derivation of a projective model structure on coherent functors. A third appendix serves as an index, summarizing the major components and contributions of the theory of shadows. Our primary goal in this research is to pinpoint sound sources within video frames without relying on manually labeled data. Our core innovation involves training the network to distinguish between difficult image elements, as determined by both a low confidence level and a high likelihood of containing the sound source, which we then use to guide attention towards these difficult areas. To accomplish this efficiently, we developed a beginning-end strategy for the network, beginning with a simple sound source detector and gradually building towards a difficult sample attention mechanism. To validate our approach, we created two video datasets labeled only for sound source presence/absence, which we called SISD-V for short. To achieve the best results, we constructed these datasets under two difficulty levels and collected 10,000 high-quality video frames from the internet. Notably, our method outperforms the current state-of-the-art on several datasets, including the ones we created, without the need for additional labeled data. To further illustrate the network's ability to learn from difficult samples, we conducted a simple sound source manipulation experiment and observed that our method is capable of tracking the moving source. Additionally, our approach ranks among the top methods for sound source localization on several publicly available datasets that were already established in the field. Our code and datasets are available for public use at this link: https://github.com/leiwang1988/SISD-VDB.

Recent advancements in graph convolutional networks (GCNs) have been primarily based on Euclidean geometry, but such methods may suffer from significant distortions when dealing with scale-free or hierarchical graphs. Researchers have proposed GCNs in non-Euclidean geometry, specifically in hyperbolic space, and have achieved notable performance improvements. However, existing hyperbolic graph operations fail to accurately follow the principles of hyperbolic geometry, potentially hindering the efficacy of these networks. This paper presents a novel hyperbolic GCN called Lorentzian graph convolutional network (LGCN) that ensures learned node features adhere to hyperbolic geometry. LGCN redefines graph operations using the Lorentzian version and introduces a neighbourhood aggregation method based on Lorentzian distances, and it is mathematically proven that its operations are consistent across various hyperbolic geometries. Experimental evaluations on six datasets demonstrate LGCN's superior performance compared to existing state-of-the-art methods, and it is particularly effective at representing tree-likeness graphs with reduced distortion. LGCN is a significant improvement over the current hyperbolic GCNs in terms of both performance and geometric distortion. All the code is publicly available on GitHub at this link: https://github.com/zwang84/LGCN. All obtained results can be found on the website associated with this paper: https://zwang84.github.io/LGCN/. All datasets used in the experiments are accessible on GitHub at this link: https://github.com/zwang84/LGCN-Datasets. Specifically, one particular choice of harmonic gauge leads to a linearized massive gravity model with the correct five degrees of freedom and avoids the vDVZ discontinuity, in contrast to the standard Fierz-Pauli theory. Additionally, a thorough examination is performed of four distinct types of Hamiltonian dynamics: parabolic, elliptic, hyperbolic, and loxodromic dynamics. Semiclassical and high-temperature approximations are both determined and contrasted to their respective classical or quadratic behaviors. We employ exact diagonalization to examine the effects of spin-orbit coupling and electron-electron interactions on the mixing of $t_{2g}$ and $e_g$ $d$-orbital states in a cubic crystal structure, characteristic of transition metal oxides. By directly comparing with $t_{2g}$ only or $e_g$ only models based on electron filling, we investigate the magnetic properties of all possible $d$-shell configurations, incorporating calculations of the total magnetic moment, orbital occupation, and effective spin-orbit coupling. The resulting parameters are expressed in terms of interaction strength, spin-orbit coupling, and crystal field splitting within relevant 4d and 5d transition metal oxide ranges. Through various limits, our perturbative and numerical results converge, highlighting that $t_{2g}$-$e_g$ mixing can be significant, with up to 20% orbital occupation outside nominal ranges. These findings hold important implications for experimental interpretation and can influence the theoretical models used to analyze magnetic properties and phases in these materials, where intermediate electron-electron coupling commonly occurs. Examples from BaTaO3 and Sr2TaCl7 are provided, demonstrating that $t_{2g}$-$e_g$ mixing must be considered in these cubic transition metal oxides to accurately understand their electronic behavior. 

We intend to extend our work to two-dimensional crystal structures in the future. If the 2D geometry is isotropic, the $t_{2g}$-$e_g$ mixing can be simplified by considering the symmetry of the orbital states and the crystallographic direction. However, in anisotropic two-dimensional structures, all possible $d$-shell configurations will be equally likely, mirroring the cubic case. If the 2d geometry is symmetric with respect to all 90-degree rotation axes, the $t_{2g}$-$e_g$ mixing will be the same as in the cubic structure. If there are rotation axes that are not symmetric, the $t_{2g}$-$e_g$ mixing will depend on the angle between the rotation axes. If there are rotation axes that are not symmetric with any other rotation axis, the $t_{2g}$-$e_g$ mixing will be unique for each orientation, varying with the tilt of the d-orbitals from the surface normal. If the 2d geometry is asymmetric with respect to all rotation axes, the $t_{2g}$-$e_g$ mixing will also be asymmetric, requiring a different parameterization than the cubic case

ViDaExpert is an application for multidimensional data visualization and
advanced analysis. It is capable of handling object-feature tables that include
numerical values and text-based labels for objects and features. The tool
encompasses several statistical techniques such as weighted PCA, elastic maps,
linear discriminant analysis, and decision tree construction, in addition to
K-Means clustering and multilinear regression. With customizable visualizations
and an interactive 3D viewer, ViDaExpert enables the creation of 3D scenes
from data and facilitates rapid, in-depth analysis of data, encompassing
elementary to complex methodologies. The software is particularly suited for
examination of large datasets in science fields like astronomy and ecology. 
ViDaExpert is an open-source program available for Windows, Mac OS X, and
Linux platforms following an easy installation process. A detailed guide for
using the application is provided in the user manual, which is also available
as an PDF document. A video illustrating the application's functionality 
can be found on YouTube. A related application, ViDaExpert for large datasets
(ViDaGiant), is an alternative for large-scale datasets, with an increased
memory capacity but on Mac OS X only. Both applications were initially 
developed by the Italian National Institute for Astrophysics. ViDaExpert can
also be run as an App on Mac OS X, which enables users to directly click on
the application icon to start using it. A Windows version of ViDaGiant is 
currently under development. A related application, ViDaExpert with 3D 
visualization of time-dependent data (ViDaTime), is an alternative for 
time-dependent datasets, with an increased memory capacity but on Mac OS X
